q: What is cloud computing?
options: A private network that connects a company's branch offices
Software installed from discs onto each employee's workstation
Purchasing physical servers to run in a company's own datacenter
The on-demand delivery of IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing
explain: Cloud computing delivers compute, storage, and services on demand over the internet — you pay for what you use instead of buying hardware. The distractors describe on-premises infrastructure, a WAN, and traditional licensed software.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Which statement BEST describes a public cloud?
options: A company's on-premises servers connected to the internet
Software that can only be installed on one computer at a time
Cloud infrastructure owned and operated by a third-party provider and shared by many customers
Cloud services dedicated to a single organization and hosted in its own datacenter
explain: In a public cloud such as Azure, the provider owns the infrastructure and many customers share it (multitenancy). The distractors describe a private cloud or things that are not cloud models at all.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A government agency runs cloud services on hardware dedicated solely to its own use, hosted in its own datacenter. This is a:
options: Public cloud
Hybrid cloud
Private cloud
Multicloud
explain: A private cloud is dedicated to a single organization, whether hosted on-premises or by a third party. Public clouds are shared; hybrid mixes models; multicloud means using more than one public provider.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company keeps its customer database on on-premises servers but runs its public website on Azure, with the two environments connected and managed together. This is an example of:
options: A public cloud
A private cloud
A community cloud
A hybrid cloud
explain: Hybrid cloud combines on-premises/private resources with public cloud services in one coordinated environment. Neither pure-public nor pure-private describes this mix.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: What is the difference between hybrid cloud and multicloud?
options: Multicloud means using services from more than one public cloud provider; hybrid cloud combines public cloud with private/on-premises resources
Hybrid cloud means using two public providers; multicloud means public plus on-premises
They are two names for exactly the same architecture
Multicloud is only for governments; hybrid cloud is only for retail companies
explain: Multicloud = multiple public providers (e.g., Azure plus another provider). Hybrid = public cloud plus private cloud or on-premises infrastructure. The terms describe different combinations.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Under the shared responsibility model, which of the following is ALWAYS the customer's responsibility, regardless of service model (IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS)?
options: Physical security of the provider's datacenters
The customer's data and the management of user identities and access
Patching the virtualization hypervisor
Maintaining the provider's backbone network
explain: No matter the service model, you always own your data, your accounts/identities, and who can access what. Physical security, the hypervisor, and the backbone network always belong to the provider.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs its application on Azure virtual machines (IaaS). Who is responsible for patching the guest operating system on those VMs?
options: Microsoft, because the VMs run in Azure datacenters
Nobody — virtual machines patch themselves automatically
The customer, because the OS is above the provider's responsibility boundary in IaaS
The internet service provider
explain: With IaaS, the provider manages the physical hosts, virtualization, and networking; the customer manages everything from the OS upward — including OS patches, middleware, and applications.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company uses a SaaS email service. Who is responsible for applying security patches to the email application itself?
options: The customer, because they own the mailboxes
The customer's internet provider
Both equally, under a split-patch agreement
The SaaS provider, because they manage the application layer
explain: In SaaS the provider manages nearly the entire stack — application, runtime, OS, and infrastructure. The customer remains responsible for their data and for managing user access to it.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Moving workloads to the public cloud typically shifts IT spending from capital expenditure (CapEx) to operational expenditure (OpEx). What does this mean in practice?
options: Replacing large upfront hardware purchases with ongoing pay-for-what-you-use bills
Eliminating all IT spending permanently
Paying for hardware with cash instead of credit
Hiring more datacenter technicians
explain: CapEx is money spent upfront on physical assets (servers). OpEx is ongoing spending on services consumed. Cloud converts the big upfront server purchase into a monthly usage bill — the core financial shift of cloud adoption.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Which pricing characteristic means you pay only for the resources you actually consume, and you can stop paying when you deallocate them?
options: Perpetual pricing
Flat-rate datacenter pricing
Fixed licensing
Consumption-based pricing
explain: Consumption-based (pay-as-you-go) pricing bills by actual usage — e.g., per hour a VM runs. Delete the VM and billing stops. This is the opposite of buying fixed capacity upfront.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Which Azure service is an example of Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?
options: Microsoft 365
Azure App Service
Azure Virtual Machines
Azure AI Services
explain: Virtual Machines are IaaS: you get virtualized hardware and manage the OS yourself. App Service is PaaS, Microsoft 365 is SaaS, and Azure AI Services are consumed as managed APIs (SaaS-like).
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Platform as a Service (PaaS) is BEST described as:
options: Renting virtual hardware where you install and patch the OS yourself
Buying a finished software application like email
Purchasing physical servers from a vendor
A managed platform where you deploy your code while the provider handles the OS, runtime, and infrastructure
explain: PaaS (e.g., Azure App Service) abstracts away servers and operating systems — you focus on code and data. The distractors describe IaaS, SaaS, and on-premises purchasing.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Which of the following is an example of Software as a Service (SaaS)?
options: Azure Kubernetes Service
A bare-metal server rental
Microsoft 365
Azure Virtual Machines
explain: Microsoft 365 is finished software delivered over the internet — classic SaaS. Virtual Machines are IaaS, AKS is a container platform, and bare-metal rental is IaaS-like infrastructure.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Serverless computing (for example, Azure Functions) is characterized by:
options: Renting physical servers by the month
Code that runs in response to events with no server provisioning or management, billed per execution
Virtual machines that never need patching
Databases with no storage limits
explain: Serverless means the provider fully manages the servers; your code runs when triggered by events and you pay per execution. Servers still exist — you just never manage them.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A development team wants to deploy a web API quickly and does not want to manage operating systems, patching, or servers. Which service model BEST fits?
options: On-premises virtualization
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
Platform as a Service (PaaS)
Bare-metal hosting
explain: PaaS removes OS and infrastructure management so the team ships code only. IaaS would still leave them patching operating systems, and bare metal is the most management-heavy option.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: High availability in cloud computing refers to:
options: The lowest possible monthly bill
The fastest possible processor speed
Unlimited storage capacity
Keeping services operational and accessible despite component failures, typically through redundancy
explain: High availability = maximizing uptime, usually by eliminating single points of failure with redundant components across zones or regions. It is about resilience, not price, speed, or capacity.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Scalability is the ability to:
options: Increase or decrease computing resources to handle changing workload demands
Automatically install security patches
Store data in multiple countries at once
Guarantee 100% uptime
explain: Scalability is adjusting capacity up or down as demand changes. Patching, data location, and uptime guarantees are separate concepts — and no provider guarantees 100% uptime.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Adding more CPU and memory to an existing virtual machine is an example of:
options: Horizontal scaling (scaling out)
Vertical scaling (scaling up)
Elasticity
Geo-distribution
explain: Making one instance bigger = vertical scaling (scale up). Adding more instances = horizontal scaling (scale out). Elasticity is the automatic aspect of scaling; geo-distribution is about location.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An online retailer uses Virtual Machine Scale Sets to automatically add instances during a holiday traffic spike and remove them afterward. This demonstrates:
options: High availability
Disaster recovery
Elasticity
Fault tolerance
explain: Elasticity is resources automatically expanding and contracting with demand. High availability/fault tolerance are about surviving failures; disaster recovery is about recovering after an outage.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Agility as a benefit of cloud computing means:
options: Automatic compliance with all regulations
Zero-cost computing
Running the fastest processors available
The ability to rapidly provision, change, and deprovision resources to respond to business needs
explain: Agility = speed of change: spin up test environments in minutes, experiment cheaply, and tear down what you don't need. It is about business responsiveness, not hardware speed or cost elimination.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company deploys its application to Azure regions in Europe and Asia so customers in each area get fast response times. This is an example of which cloud benefit?
options: Geo-distribution
Economies of scale
Predictable pricing
Serverless computing
explain: Geo-distribution = placing resources close to users to cut latency. Economies of scale is about provider cost savings; the other options don't describe location strategy.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Disaster recovery in the cloud typically relies on:
options: A single powerful server that never fails
Maintaining the ability to recover operations in a secondary location if the primary fails
Deleting backups to save money
Running all workloads in one availability zone
explain: Disaster recovery = a plan and secondary capacity (e.g., a paired region) to restore service after a major outage. No single server 'never fails' — that's why recovery planning exists.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Economies of scale benefit cloud customers because:
options: Each customer must buy their own datacenter
Providers operate at massive scale, lowering per-unit costs that are passed on as lower prices
Cloud resources are free for the first year
Small providers are always cheaper than large ones
explain: Hyperscale providers buy hardware, power, and bandwidth in enormous volumes, driving unit costs down — and competition passes much of that saving to customers. Resources are never free indefinitely.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A startup wants to avoid a large upfront purchase of servers and prefers a predictable monthly bill based on usage. This preference aligns with:
options: Capital expenditure (CapEx)
Perpetual software licensing
Operational expenditure (OpEx) with a consumption-based model
Buying reserved datacenter floor space
explain: The startup wants OpEx — ongoing operational spending tied to consumption — instead of CapEx's big upfront outlay. Usage-based monthly billing is the textbook OpEx pattern.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A hospital must keep patient records on its own servers for regulatory reasons but wants to run its public website and development environments in the cloud. Which cloud deployment model fits BEST?
options: Public cloud only
Hybrid cloud
Multicloud
Community cloud
explain: Keeping regulated data on-premises while using public cloud for other workloads — connected as one environment — is the classic hybrid scenario. Multicloud would mean two public providers, which isn't what's described.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A small retail business with no IT staff wants to host its online store without buying or maintaining any servers. Which approach BEST meets this need?
options: Buying mainframe computers
Running workloads on employee laptops
Building a private datacenter
Using public cloud PaaS or SaaS offerings
explain: Public cloud PaaS/SaaS removes hardware ownership and maintenance entirely — ideal with no IT staff. A private datacenter or mainframes demand exactly the expertise they lack.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Several regional hospitals share cloud infrastructure built specifically to meet common healthcare compliance requirements. This deployment model is called:
options: Public cloud
Private cloud
Community cloud
Hybrid cloud
explain: A community cloud is shared by organizations with common concerns (industry, compliance, security needs). It's distinct from public (open to all), private (one org), and hybrid (mixed models).
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: What is an Azure region?
options: A single physical server in a datacenter
A billing discount applied to long-term contracts
A geographical area containing one or more datacenters
A type of virtual machine
explain: A region is a geographic area with at least one datacenter (often several). You choose regions to place resources near users and meet data-residency needs. It is not a server, a discount, or a VM type.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Availability zones are best described as:
options: Discount pricing tiers for virtual machines
Separate Azure subscriptions for different departments
Physically separate datacenters within an Azure region, each with independent power, cooling, and networking
Time zones used for scheduling maintenance
explain: Availability zones are isolated datacenter locations inside a region. Deploying across zones protects against a datacenter-level failure. They have nothing to do with time, pricing, or subscriptions.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Why does Azure pair each region with another region at least 300 miles away?
options: To double the price of storage
To enable disaster recovery and to roll out platform updates to one region at a time
To allow customers to avoid paying taxes
To reduce the number of available services
explain: Region pairs provide a built-in disaster-recovery target far enough away to survive regional events, and Microsoft updates paired regions sequentially so at least one stays current. Distance is about resilience, not pricing.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure Government and Azure China are examples of:
options: Availability zones
Resource groups
Sovereign regions
Virtual networks
explain: Sovereign regions are isolated Azure instances built for specific governments' data-sovereignty and compliance needs (e.g., Azure Government for US agencies, Azure China operated by 21Vianet). They are separate from the global Azure cloud.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A large enterprise has 40 Azure subscriptions and wants to apply the same policies and access controls to all of them at once. Which feature should it use?
options: Resource groups
Availability sets
Virtual machine scale sets
Management groups
explain: Management groups sit above subscriptions in the hierarchy, letting you apply Azure Policy and RBAC once across many subscriptions. Resource groups organize resources within a subscription — they can't span this management need.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An Azure subscription is BEST described as:
options: A billing and management boundary that contains resource groups, with its own quotas and access controls
A single virtual machine
A type of storage account
A physical datacenter building
explain: Subscriptions are the unit of billing and a boundary for quotas, policies, and access. Resources live in resource groups inside subscriptions — a subscription is far more than one VM or one building.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Which statement about resource groups is TRUE?
options: All resources in a resource group must be in the same Azure region
Resource groups can only contain virtual machines
A resource can belong to multiple resource groups at the same time
Deleting a resource group deletes all the resources inside it
explain: A resource group is a logical container: each resource belongs to exactly one group, groups can hold resources from different regions, and deleting the group deletes everything in it — a favorite exam trap.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates are:
options: Pre-built virtual machine images sold in a marketplace
JSON files that declaratively define infrastructure so deployments are consistent and repeatable
Billing reports exported as spreadsheets
Physical documents signed during datacenter construction
explain: ARM templates are infrastructure-as-code: JSON files declaring the desired state of resources. Re-running a template produces the same environment every time (idempotent). They aren't images, bills, or paper.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: How does Bicep relate to ARM templates?
options: Bicep is a simpler domain-specific language that transpiles into ARM template JSON
Bicep replaces Azure subscriptions entirely
Bicep is a type of virtual network
Bicep is only used for on-premises servers
explain: Bicep offers cleaner, more concise syntax for defining Azure infrastructure and compiles down to standard ARM JSON. It's an authoring language for the same deployment engine, not a networking or subscription concept.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure Virtual Machines provide which service model, and what does the customer manage?
options: SaaS — the customer manages nothing
PaaS — the customer manages only application code
IaaS — the customer manages the operating system, middleware, and applications
Serverless — the customer manages only billing
explain: VMs are IaaS: Microsoft provides virtualized hardware while you own the OS upward — patching, configuration, apps, and data. That's the defining tradeoff of IaaS: maximum control, maximum management.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Virtual Machine Scale Sets are designed to:
options: Run a single VM at the lowest possible price
Automatically increase or decrease a group of identical, load-balanced VMs based on demand
Migrate physical servers to Azure
Provide file storage for applications
explain: Scale sets manage fleets of identical VMs behind a load balancer and autoscale them with demand — the backbone of elastic IaaS. Migration is Azure Migrate's job; file storage is Azure Files.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure App Service is BEST described as:
options: Infrastructure as a Service for running custom operating systems
A physical server rental program
A Platform as a Service for hosting web apps, APIs, and mobile backends without managing servers or operating systems
A desktop virtualization service
explain: App Service is PaaS: deploy code and Microsoft handles the OS, patching, and scaling. Desktop virtualization is Azure Virtual Desktop; custom OS control is the IaaS (VM) story.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants code to run automatically whenever a new file lands in storage, paying only for the milliseconds the code executes. Which service fits BEST?
options: Azure Virtual Machines
Azure ExpressRoute
Azure Bastion
Azure Functions
explain: This is the textbook serverless scenario: event-driven code with per-execution billing = Azure Functions (Consumption plan). VMs would idle and bill continuously; ExpressRoute and Bastion are networking services.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Which Azure service provides the fastest, simplest way to run a single container without managing servers or orchestration?
options: Azure Container Instances
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
Azure Virtual Machines
Azure App Service
explain: Container Instances runs containers on demand with no orchestrator to manage — ideal for simple, bursty container workloads. AKS is for orchestrating many containers at scale; VMs add OS management.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team needs to orchestrate hundreds of containers with automated scaling, self-healing, and rolling updates. Which Azure service should they choose?
options: Azure Functions
Azure File Sync
Azure Container Instances
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
explain: AKS is managed Kubernetes — built for orchestrating container fleets with scaling, healing, and deployment strategies. Container Instances runs containers but doesn't orchestrate them; Functions is serverless code, not containers.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure Virtual Desktop provides:
options: Virtual reality meeting rooms
Cloud-hosted Windows desktops and applications that users access remotely
Physical desktop computers shipped to offices
A VPN client for laptops
explain: Azure Virtual Desktop delivers Windows desktops and apps from Azure to any device — the desktop-virtualization (VDI) story. It doesn't ship hardware or provide VR; remote access happens over standard protocols.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An Azure Virtual Network (VNet) is:
options: A physical cable connecting two datacenters
A logically isolated network in Azure where you define IP address ranges, subnets, and routing
A billing report for network usage
A type of firewall appliance
explain: A VNet is your private network slice of Azure — you control addressing, subnets, route tables, and peering. It's software-defined networking, not a physical cable or a bill.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: What is the purpose of a subnet within a virtual network?
options: To provide DNS hosting for public domains
To encrypt data stored in Azure Storage
To subdivide the VNet's address space so resources can be segmented and controlled separately
To connect a VNet to the public internet
explain: Subnets carve a VNet's IP range into segments (e.g., web tier vs. database tier) so you can apply different network security groups and routing. Internet connectivity comes from gateways/NAT; DNS is Azure DNS's job.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: VNet peering allows you to:
options: Connect two virtual networks privately so traffic flows over the Microsoft backbone with low latency
Share a single virtual machine between two companies
Peer with on-premises networks without any gateway
Double the storage capacity of a virtual network
explain: Peering links VNets directly — private, low-latency, no internet traversal. On-premises connectivity still needs VPN Gateway or ExpressRoute; peering doesn't create VMs or storage.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants an encrypted connection between its on-premises office and Azure over the public internet. Which service should it use?
options: Azure DNS
Azure Content Delivery Network
VPN Gateway
Azure Front Door
explain: VPN Gateway builds encrypted site-to-site (or point-to-site) tunnels over the internet. DNS resolves names, CDN caches content, and Front Door is global load balancing — none create encrypted hybrid tunnels.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: How does Azure ExpressRoute differ from a VPN Gateway connection?
options: ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated connection through a connectivity provider — not over the public internet — with more predictable performance
ExpressRoute is free while VPN Gateway is expensive
ExpressRoute only works for storage accounts
There is no difference; they are two names for the same service
explain: ExpressRoute = private dedicated circuit (consistent bandwidth/latency, better for large or sensitive transfers). VPN Gateway = encrypted tunnel over the public internet (cheaper, faster to set up). They are distinct services with distinct tradeoffs.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure DNS is used to:
options: Host DNS domains and resolve names, including alias records that point directly to Azure resources
Encrypt network traffic between virtual networks
Filter inbound traffic with allow/deny rules
Provide private dedicated connectivity to on-premises
explain: Azure DNS hosts your DNS zones with fast anycast resolution and alias records for Azure resources. Encryption of hybrid links is VPN/ExpressRoute; traffic filtering is NSGs; private connectivity is ExpressRoute.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure Load Balancer operates at which network layer and what does it do?
options: Layer 2 — switches frames between physical servers
Layer 3 — assigns public IP addresses to virtual machines
Layer 7 — inspects HTTP content and applies web application firewall rules
Layer 4 — distributes TCP/UDP traffic across backend resources for availability and scale
explain: Load Balancer is a Layer 4 (transport) distributor of TCP/UDP flows — high throughput, zone-redundant. Layer 7 smarts (URL routing, WAF) belong to Application Gateway; it doesn't assign IPs or switch frames.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company needs Layer 7 load balancing with SSL termination, URL-based routing, and a web application firewall. Which Azure service fits BEST?
options: Azure Load Balancer
Azure VPN Gateway
Azure Application Gateway
Azure Bastion
explain: Application Gateway is the Layer 7 (HTTP/S) load balancer with WAF, SSL termination, and path-based routing. Load Balancer is Layer 4 only; VPN Gateway and Bastion solve connectivity, not web traffic management.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure Front Door is BEST described as:
options: A physical security gate for datacenters
A global Layer 7 entry point that routes users to the nearest healthy backend with instant failover
A firewall for a single virtual machine
A tool for migrating on-premises databases
explain: Front Door is Microsoft's global-scale entry point: it steers users to the closest/fastest healthy region and fails over instantly. It's not physical security, a single-VM firewall, or a migration tool.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A network security group (NSG) is used to:
options: Filter network traffic to and from Azure resources using allow/deny rules based on source, destination, port, and protocol
Encrypt data stored in Azure Storage
Manage user passwords in Microsoft Entra ID
Back up virtual machines automatically
explain: NSGs are packet filters with 5-tuple rules (source/destination IP and port, protocol) attached to subnets or NICs. They don't encrypt storage, manage identities, or back up VMs.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure Blob storage is designed for:
options: Relational database tables with SQL queries
Object storage of unstructured data such as images, videos, backups, and logs
Running virtual machines
Hosting Kubernetes clusters
explain: Blob = Binary Large Object storage for unstructured data at massive scale. Relational data belongs in Azure SQL; compute runs on VMs/AKS — storage and compute are separate services.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company stores security camera footage that is rarely viewed but must be kept for seven years, with retrieval in hours being acceptable. Which blob access tier is MOST cost-effective?
options: Hot
Cool
Archive
Premium
explain: Archive is the cheapest tier for rarely accessed data that can tolerate hours-long rehydration — perfect for long-term retention. Hot is for frequent access, Cool for infrequent (30+ days) with instant reads, Premium for low-latency workloads.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure Files provides:
options: A relational database engine
Temporary disk storage for virtual machines
Object storage for website images
Fully managed file shares accessible via SMB or NFS, suitable for lift-and-shift of on-premises file servers
explain: Azure Files offers cloud file shares over SMB/NFS — you can even mount them from on-premises. Object/image storage is Blob; databases are Azure SQL/Cosmos DB; VM disks are Managed Disks.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Locally redundant storage (LRS) keeps:
options: Copies in a secondary region hundreds of miles away
Only one copy of data with no redundancy
Three synchronous copies of data within a single datacenter, at the lowest cost
Copies across multiple availability zones
explain: LRS = 3 copies in one datacenter — cheapest, protects against drive/rack failure but not datacenter loss. Zones = ZRS; secondary region = GRS. There is always redundancy; 'one copy' isn't an Azure option.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company needs storage redundancy that survives the loss of an entire datacenter within its region, but does not need a secondary region. Which option fits BEST?
options: Locally redundant storage (LRS)
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS)
Geo-redundant storage (GRS)
Local disk storage with no replication
explain: ZRS replicates synchronously across availability zones (separate datacenters) in the same region — surviving a datacenter failure without cross-region cost. LRS can't survive datacenter loss; GRS adds an unneeded secondary region.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: What is the difference between GRS and RA-GRS storage redundancy?
options: GRS copies data to a secondary region; RA-GRS additionally allows read access to that secondary copy
GRS is cheaper than LRS
RA-GRS stores data only in the primary region
They are identical; RA-GRS is just the older name
explain: Both replicate to a paired secondary region, but RA-GRS (Read-Access GRS) lets you read the secondary copy — useful if the primary becomes unavailable. GRS alone keeps the secondary hidden until failover.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure Migrate is used to:
options: Assess on-premises servers and databases and migrate them to Azure
Migrate data between two Azure regions only
Manage user identities
Configure virtual networks
explain: Azure Migrate is the central hub for discovery, assessment, and migration of on-premises workloads to Azure. Identity is Entra ID's domain; networking is the VNet family's.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A research lab needs to move 500 TB of data to Azure but has very limited internet bandwidth. Which service should it use?
options: Azure Data Box
Azure VPN Gateway
Azure Bastion
Azure Policy
explain: Data Box is a ruggedized physical appliance Microsoft ships to you: load data offline, ship it back, and it's ingested into Azure. Network-based transfer of 500 TB over a thin pipe would take far too long.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure SQL Database is BEST described as:
options: A NoSQL document database
An on-premises database product
Infrastructure as a Service where you install SQL Server on a VM yourself
A fully managed Platform as a Service relational database with automated patching, backups, and scaling
explain: Azure SQL Database is PaaS: Microsoft handles patching, backups, and high availability while you work with the database. Installing SQL on your own VM is IaaS; NoSQL document storage is Cosmos DB's role.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A mobile game needs a database that serves players worldwide with single-digit-millisecond reads and automatic global distribution. Which Azure service fits BEST?
options: Azure Files
Azure Blob storage
Azure Cosmos DB
Azure Data Box
explain: Cosmos DB is the globally distributed, multi-model database with turnkey worldwide replication and millisecond latency. Blob/Files are storage, not databases; Data Box is offline transfer.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure Arc enables organizations to:
options: Run Azure virtual machines without paying
Extend Azure management, governance, and security to on-premises servers, other clouds, and edge devices
Replace all on-premises hardware automatically
Create virtual networks only
explain: Arc projects Azure control plane capabilities — Policy, Monitor, RBAC, Defender — onto resources anywhere: on-prem, multicloud, edge. It's about unified management, not free VMs or hardware replacement.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A developer wants to add image recognition to an app via an API call, without training any machine learning models. Which Azure offering fits BEST?
options: Azure AI Services (prebuilt vision, speech, language, and decision APIs)
Azure Virtual Machines
Azure ExpressRoute
Azure Policy
explain: Azure AI Services expose ready-made AI (computer vision, speech, language) through simple APIs — no ML expertise required. Training custom models is Azure Machine Learning's domain; VMs and networking don't provide AI.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) is:
options: A virtual machine image gallery
Microsoft's cloud-based identity and access management service
A storage redundancy option
A network load balancer
explain: Entra ID is the identity provider for Azure: single sign-on, MFA, and Conditional Access for users and apps. It's not compute, storage, or networking — identity is its own pillar.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication determines permissions; authorization verifies identity
Authentication applies only to on-premises systems
They are synonyms with no difference
Authentication verifies who you are; authorization determines what you are allowed to do
explain: Authentication (AuthN) = proving identity (sign-in). Authorization (AuthZ) = what that identity may access. Mixing them up is a classic exam trap — remember: AuthN first, then AuthZ.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Multifactor authentication (MFA) requires:
options: Entering your password twice
Two or more distinct verification methods, such as a password plus an authenticator app approval
Two different usernames
Answering the same security question repeatedly
explain: MFA combines factors — something you know, have, or are. Password + authenticator app = two factors. Typing one password twice is still single-factor.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Single sign-on (SSO) allows users to:
options: Bypass multifactor authentication permanently
Share one account among many employees
Sign in once and access multiple applications without signing in again to each one
Use the same password for every website on the internet
explain: SSO = one authentication grants access to many connected apps, improving both security and convenience. It doesn't weaken MFA or encourage password reuse/sharing — it reduces them.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Conditional Access policies in Microsoft Entra ID:
options: Evaluate signals such as user, device, location, and risk, then enforce controls like requiring MFA or blocking access
Only work for on-premises applications
Automatically approve every sign-in attempt
Replace the need for any passwords
explain: Conditional Access is an if-then policy engine: IF sign-in comes from an unfamiliar location on an unmanaged device, THEN require MFA or block. It's the automation layer on top of identity — not a blanket approval.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: The Zero Trust principle 'verify explicitly' means:
options: Trust all devices inside the corporate network
Always authenticate and authorize based on all available data points instead of assuming trust
Remove all passwords from the environment
Grant every user administrator rights for simplicity
explain: 'Verify explicitly' = never trust, always verify — every request is authenticated and authorized using identity, device, and risk signals. Trusting the internal network is the old perimeter model Zero Trust replaces.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Which TWO Zero Trust principles complete this pair: grant only the minimum access needed, and operate as if a breach has already occurred?
options: Single sign-on and passwordless
Encryption and compression
Verify explicitly and trust the perimeter
Least-privilege access and assume breach
explain: Zero Trust rests on three principles: verify explicitly, least-privilege access, and assume breach. 'Assume breach' drives segmentation, monitoring, and minimizing blast radius — the opposite of perimeter trust.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Defense in depth is a security strategy that:
options: Layers multiple defenses (physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application, data) so a single failure does not compromise everything
Relies on one extremely strong firewall
Removes all security controls to improve performance
Only protects the physical datacenter building
explain: Defense in depth = layered security: if one layer fails (e.g., perimeter breached), inner layers (identity, encryption, app controls) still protect. A single firewall is a single point of failure.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Microsoft Defender for Cloud is used to:
options: Host virtual machine images
Strengthen cloud security posture, assess compliance, and protect workloads — with a Secure Score showing improvement priorities
Manage DNS records
Calculate total cost of ownership
explain: Defender for Cloud provides cloud security posture management plus workload threat protection, summarized in a Secure Score. DNS is Azure DNS; TCO is the TCO calculator's job.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Microsoft Sentinel is BEST described as:
options: A virtual machine backup service
A cost management dashboard
A cloud-native SIEM and SOAR solution for intelligent security analytics and automated threat response
A tool for deploying ARM templates
explain: Sentinel collects security data at cloud scale (SIEM) and automates investigation and response with playbooks (SOAR). Backups are Azure Backup; costs are Cost Management; deployments are ARM/Bicep.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Azure Key Vault is used to:
options: Store virtual machine hard drives
Host public websites
Route network traffic between regions
Safeguard cryptographic keys, secrets, and certificates with hardware-backed protection
explain: Key Vault centrally manages secrets (passwords, API keys), encryption keys, and certificates — with HSM-backed options — so apps never hardcode them. Disks are Managed Disks; routing is networking's job.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: What is the difference between DDoS Network Protection and DDoS IP Protection in Azure?
options: Network Protection safeguards virtual networks (with always-on monitoring); IP Protection protects individual public IPs with simpler pay-as-you-go pricing
IP Protection is free and unlimited for all customers
Network Protection only works on-premises
There is no difference between them
explain: DDoS Network Protection covers VNets with adaptive tuning and cost protection; DDoS IP Protection secures individual public IPs with a simpler PAYG model. Both are cloud services — neither is on-premises.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Azure Firewall is:
options: A password manager for administrators
A backup service for firewalls
A host-based antivirus for virtual machines
A managed, stateful network firewall with built-in high availability, FQDN filtering, and threat intelligence
explain: Azure Firewall is a cloud-native network firewall (Layer 3–7) with FQDN filtering and threat-intel-based filtering, scaling automatically. Antivirus is Defender/endpoint protection; it has nothing to do with passwords or backups.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants administrators to connect to Azure VMs via RDP/SSH through the Azure portal without assigning public IP addresses to the VMs. Which service enables this?
options: Azure Data Box
Azure Migrate
Azure Bastion
Azure Front Door
explain: Bastion provides secure, browser-based RDP/SSH to VMs over TLS with no public IPs exposed — shrinking the attack surface. Front Door is global load balancing; Data Box and Migrate are data-transfer/migration tools.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Azure Policy is used to:
options: Enforce organizational standards and assess compliance across resources — for example, restricting VM SKUs or requiring specific tags
Grant users administrative access
Calculate monthly bills
Deploy virtual machines
explain: Policy = guardrails: define rules (allowed locations, required tags, approved SKUs), audit for violations, and optionally deny or remediate. Granting access is RBAC's job; billing is Cost Management's.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: What is the key difference between Azure Policy and role-based access control (RBAC)?
options: Policy defines rules that resources must follow; RBAC controls who can perform actions on resources
RBAC defines resource rules; Policy controls user access
They do exactly the same thing
Policy is only for storage accounts
explain: Policy governs WHAT resources can be/how they're configured (the rules); RBAC governs WHO can manage them (the people). Confusing the two is a classic exam trap — remember: Policy = resource rules, RBAC = user permissions.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A contractor needs to view resources in a resource group to audit them but must not be able to create, modify, or delete anything. Which built-in RBAC role fits BEST?
options: Owner
Reader
Contributor
User Access Administrator
explain: Reader grants view-only access. Contributor can create/modify (but not manage access), Owner can do everything including access management. Least privilege says: auditing = Reader.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company applies a CanNotDelete lock to a production resource group. What is the effect, and what happens to resources created inside it later?
options: Resources cannot be deleted but can still be modified; the lock is inherited by all current and future resources in the group
Everything in the group becomes read-only forever
The lock only affects resources that existed when it was applied
Locks have no effect on resource groups
explain: CanNotDelete blocks deletion while still allowing modifications; locks inherit down the hierarchy, so future resources are protected too. ReadOnly is the stricter sibling that also blocks modifications.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Resource tags in Azure are:
options: Passwords for administrative accounts
Firewall rules
Physical labels stuck on servers in datacenters
Name/value pairs applied to resources, resource groups, or subscriptions for organization, automation, and cost tracking
explain: Tags (e.g., Department=Finance, Environment=Production) organize resources and power cost reporting and policy enforcement. They're metadata — not physical labels, credentials, or firewall rules.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Microsoft Purview helps organizations with:
options: Unified data governance — discovering, classifying, and managing data across on-premises, multicloud, and SaaS sources
Running virtual machines
Balancing network load
Issuing SSL certificates
explain: Purview is the data-governance service: data discovery, classification, lineage, and compliance across the estate. Compute is VMs; load balancing is networking; certificates are Key Vault's domain.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Where can a customer find Microsoft's compliance reports, audit certifications, and security documentation for Azure?
options: The Azure pricing calculator
The Service Trust Portal
Azure Bastion
The Azure status page
explain: The Service Trust Portal publishes independent audit reports (ISO, SOC), compliance guides, and security documentation. The pricing calculator estimates costs; the status page shows service health.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A European bank requires customer data to remain stored within Europe. How can Azure meet this requirement?
options: By purchasing Azure Reservations
By using Azure Bastion
By enabling multifactor authentication
By deploying resources to Azure regions located in Europe, controlling data residency
explain: Data residency = you choose the region where data lives. Deploying to European regions keeps data in Europe. MFA, Reservations, and Bastion address identity, cost, and remote access — not data location.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Which statement about compliance in Azure is TRUE?
options: Microsoft owns all customer data stored in Azure
Compliance certifications eliminate the need for customer security controls
Azure holds certifications such as ISO 27001 and supports GDPR requirements, but the customer retains ownership and control of their data
Using Azure automatically makes any application compliant with all regulations
explain: Microsoft's certifications cover the platform, but compliance is shared: you own your data and must configure it compliantly. No cloud magically makes apps compliant, and Microsoft doesn't own your data.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Customer Lockbox for Azure ensures that:
options: Microsoft must request customer approval before accessing customer data during a support interaction
All customer data is automatically encrypted with customer-managed keys
Customers can never delete their own data
Support engineers have unrestricted access to customer data
explain: Customer Lockbox adds a human approval gate: Microsoft engineers get time-bound access only after the customer approves. It's the opposite of unrestricted access — it's customer-controlled access.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: The Azure pricing calculator is used to:
options: Pay your monthly Azure bill
Estimate the cost of Azure services before you deploy them, by configuring products, regions, and usage
Automatically reduce your bill by 50%
Compare Azure with on-premises datacenter costs
explain: The pricing calculator = pre-deployment estimate: pick services, regions, and usage to forecast cost. It doesn't pay bills or cut them; comparing with on-premises TCO is the TCO calculator's job.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator helps an organization:
options: Purchase reserved instances
Monitor real-time resource health
Calculate the exact monthly Azure bill in advance
Compare the total cost of running workloads on-premises versus running them in Azure
explain: The TCO calculator compares on-premises costs (hardware, power, labor) against projected Azure costs to build the migration business case. Exact monthly bills come from Cost Management; reservations are bought separately.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: With Microsoft Cost Management + Billing, an organization can:
options: Create budgets, set cost alerts, analyze spending by resource or tag, and forecast future costs
Patch virtual machines automatically
Enforce password complexity rules
Deploy resources with ARM templates
explain: Cost Management is the FinOps hub: budgets, alerts, cost analysis, and forecasting. Patching is Update Management/Automation; passwords are Entra ID; deployments are ARM/Bicep.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Azure Reservations allow customers to:
options: Book datacenter tours
Pay only with purchase orders
Commit to one- or three-year terms for services like VMs or SQL Database in exchange for significant discounts
Reserve IP addresses for free
explain: Reservations trade commitment (1 or 3 years) for steep discounts on predictable workloads — up to ~72% versus pay-as-you-go. They're about compute/data capacity commitments, not IPs or tours.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Azure Hybrid Benefit lets customers:
options: Run Azure services on any cloud for free
Apply existing on-premises Windows Server and SQL Server licenses to Azure workloads to reduce costs
Combine two subscriptions into one bill automatically
Get free ExpressRoute circuits
explain: Hybrid Benefit = bring your own licenses with Software Assurance to Azure and pay only the base compute rate. It's a licensing cost saver, not free multicloud or free networking.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Spot Virtual Machines offer deep discounts because:
options: They are only available on weekends
They include free premium support
They use slower processors
They run on unused Azure capacity and can be evicted on short notice when Azure needs the capacity back
explain: Spot VMs monetize spare capacity at up to ~90% off — the tradeoff is eviction with 30 seconds' notice. They're ideal for interruptible batch work, not for anything requiring guaranteed uptime.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Which factors affect the cost of Azure resources?
options: Only the number of users in Microsoft Entra ID
Resource type and size, Azure region, usage meters, and outbound data transfer (ingress is free, egress is billed)
The color scheme of the Azure portal
Only the time of day resources are created
explain: Azure cost = what you run (type/size) × where (region pricing varies) × how much (meters) + outbound bandwidth. Data going in is free; data going out is metered. Portal themes and creation time don't matter.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An Azure service-level agreement (SLA) is:
options: A formal Microsoft commitment describing expected uptime/connectivity for a service, with service credits if the commitment is missed
A marketing brochure with no obligations
A contract signed in person at a datacenter
A guarantee of 100% uptime
explain: SLAs define the uptime target (e.g., 99.9%) and the remedy — service credits — if Microsoft misses it. No SLA promises 100%; and the remedy is credits, not cash refunds.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An application depends on two Azure services: one with a 99.9% SLA and one with a 99.99% SLA. What is the application's composite SLA?
options: 199.89% (the sum)
99.9% (the lower of the two)
99.99% (the higher of the two)
explain: Composite SLA = multiply the individual SLAs: 0.999 × 0.9999 ≈ 0.9989 (99.89%). Every dependency lowers the total — a key reason architects minimize critical dependencies.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Azure Advisor provides personalized recommendations across which categories?
options: Only virtual machine sizes
Cost, Security, Reliability, Operational Excellence, and Performance
Only billing contact information
Only deprecated services
explain: Advisor scores your environment across five pillars — Cost, Security, Reliability, Operational Excellence, Performance — and suggests concrete improvements. It's far broader than VM sizing alone.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: How do Azure Monitor, Azure Service Health, and Azure Resource Health differ?
options: Service Health monitors your VMs; Monitor tracks Microsoft's datacenters
Resource Health is only available on-premises
They are three names for the same dashboard
Monitor collects metrics and logs from your resources; Service Health reports Azure-wide service issues and planned maintenance; Resource Health shows the health of your specific resources
explain: Monitor = telemetry about YOUR resources (metrics, logs, alerts). Service Health = Azure platform status (outages, maintenance) affecting regions. Resource Health = per-resource diagnosis ('your VM is unavailable because of a platform event').
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A university's enrollment portal runs quietly all year but gets slammed during a two-week registration window, then drops back to normal. The university wants capacity to adjust automatically and to pay only for what it uses during the rush. Which cloud characteristic BEST meets this need?
options: Overprovisioning servers for peak load year-round
Purchasing additional physical servers every semester
Rapid elasticity — scaling resources out during the rush and back in afterward
Running the portal on staff laptops during registration
explain: Rapid elasticity automatically scales resources with demand and releases them afterward, so you pay for peak capacity only while you need it. Overprovisioning wastes money year-round; buying hardware is slow CapEx; staff laptops are not enterprise infrastructure.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A development team needs a full test environment for three days to validate a release, then wants it gone entirely. Which pricing approach makes this cheapest and simplest?
options: Buying servers as a capital expense
Signing a three-year reserved capacity contract
Consumption-based pricing — paying only for the three days the environment exists
Purchasing perpetual software licenses
explain: Consumption-based (pay-as-you-go) pricing means no upfront cost and billing stops when resources are deleted — ideal for short-lived workloads. CapEx and three-year reservations assume long-lived use; perpetual licenses cover software, not infrastructure.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company migrates its databases to Azure SQL Database, a platform-as-a-service offering. A critical security patch is released for the database engine. Who is responsible for applying it?
options: The customer's database administrators
Microsoft, because the database engine sits below the customer's responsibility boundary in PaaS
Nobody — PaaS databases never need patching
The company's internet service provider
explain: In PaaS the provider manages the platform — operating system, runtime, database engine, and patching — while the customer manages data, access, and application logic. The 'nobody' option tests the misconception that managed services are maintenance-free for everything.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A bank must migrate a legacy trading application that requires a specific operating system kernel version and custom hardware drivers. The IT team needs full control of the OS. Which service model should they choose?
options: Infrastructure as a Service, using Azure virtual machines
Software as a Service
Platform as a Service
Serverless computing
explain: Only IaaS gives OS-level control for custom kernels and drivers. PaaS and serverless abstract the OS away entirely, and SaaS provides finished software — not a place to run a custom legacy application.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A startup is building a mobile app backend. It has no operations team and wants to deploy code without ever managing servers, operating systems, or patching. Which service model BEST fits?
options: Infrastructure as a Service
On-premises servers
A private datacenter
Platform as a Service
explain: PaaS abstracts servers and OS management so developers focus on code — the right fit with no ops team. IaaS still requires OS management, and on-premises or private datacenters demand exactly the operations expertise the startup lacks.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An online ticket seller automatically adds server instances as concert tickets go on sale and removes them when the rush ends. This automatic scaling with demand is called:
options: Scalability
Elasticity
Agility
Fault tolerance
explain: Elasticity is scaling out AND back in automatically as demand changes. Scalability is the ability to scale (not necessarily automatically); agility is speed of change; fault tolerance is surviving failures.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A virtual machine is already using the largest size available in its series, but the application still needs more CPU and memory. Vertical scaling is no longer possible. What should the architect do?
options: Keep adding memory — virtual machines have no size limits
Restart the machine to unlock more capacity
Scale out by adding more instances behind a load balancer
Move the application to a SaaS product
explain: Vertical scaling (scaling up) hits hardware and series limits, so the answer is horizontal scaling — more instances. VMs do have size limits and restarts change nothing; switching to SaaS is a different service model, not a scaling strategy.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company deploys its application across multiple availability zones in a region. One datacenter loses power completely. What happens to the application?
options: It keeps serving users from the remaining zones
It goes offline until power is restored
All customer data is lost
It automatically fails over to a different cloud provider
explain: Availability zones are independent datacenters with separate power, cooling, and networking, so the application survives a datacenter-level failure. Data is not lost because storage is replicated, and failover to another provider is never automatic.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An e-learning company hosts its platform in a US Azure region, but students in Japan report slow page loads. Which cloud benefit BEST solves this problem?
options: Economies of scale
Capital expenditure
Serverless computing
Geo-distribution — deploying resources in regions close to users
explain: Geo-distribution places resources near users to cut latency, which follows physical distance. Economies of scale lower costs; CapEx is a spending model; serverless is a compute model — none address distance-based latency.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A German manufacturer will only use cloud services if customer data never leaves the European Union. How can Azure address this requirement?
options: Geo-distribution with data residency — choosing EU regions so data stays in the EU
Deploying to whichever region is closest regardless of location
Using only serverless services
Encrypting data but storing it anywhere
explain: Azure lets customers choose regions, and data-residency commitments keep customer data within the chosen geography. The 'closest region' trap ignores the compliance constraint, and encryption alone does not satisfy a residency requirement.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company replicates its databases to a paired region and documents the exact steps to restore service there after a major outage. This planning is an example of:
options: High availability
Disaster recovery
Fault tolerance
Elasticity
explain: Disaster recovery is the plan plus secondary capacity to restore service after a disaster. High availability keeps a system running through minor failures; fault tolerance avoids interruption from component failure; elasticity scales with demand.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A developer provisions a complete test environment through the Azure portal in ten minutes. The same request through corporate procurement used to take six weeks. This speed of provisioning demonstrates:
options: Fault tolerance
Geo-distribution
Agility
Economies of scale
explain: Agility is the ability to provision, change, and experiment quickly — minutes instead of weeks. The scenario is about speed, not surviving failure (fault tolerance), location (geo-distribution), or bulk pricing (economies of scale).
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A CFO is comparing two proposals: buying $200,000 of servers outright versus paying a monthly cloud bill based on usage. The outright purchase is classified as:
options: Capital expenditure (CapEx)
Operational expenditure (OpEx)
Consumption-based spending
Serverless spending
explain: CapEx is large upfront spending on physical assets owned by the company. OpEx and consumption-based spending describe the monthly-bill model; serverless is a compute model, not a spending classification.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A cloud bill itemizes every gigabyte stored and every hour of compute used, and the customer pays exactly for those metered amounts. This reflects which cloud characteristic?
options: Resource pooling
Broad network access
Rapid elasticity
Measured service
explain: Measured service means usage is metered and billed accordingly. Resource pooling is shared infrastructure; broad network access is availability over the network via standard devices; rapid elasticity is scaling — none describe metering.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A cloud provider runs thousands of customers' virtual machines on shared physical servers, with each customer's workloads isolated from the others. This sharing of the provider's infrastructure is called:
options: Multicloud
Resource pooling
Geo-distribution
Vertical scaling
explain: Resource pooling (multitenancy) means provider resources are shared across customers with logical isolation. Multicloud is using multiple providers; geo-distribution is about location; vertical scaling is resizing a single resource.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A developer creates a new virtual machine at 2 AM through a self-service portal, with no ticket to IT and no call to the provider. This demonstrates:
options: Community cloud
Hybrid cloud
Disaster recovery
On-demand self-service
explain: On-demand self-service is provisioning without human interaction with the provider — anytime, through a portal or API. The distractors are deployment models or unrelated concepts, not provisioning characteristics.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Employees access company applications from phones, tablets, and laptops over the internet, from the office and from home. This capability reflects:
options: Broad network access
Resource pooling
Fault tolerance
Capital expenditure
explain: Broad network access means services are available over the network through standard devices and connections. It is about reach — not shared hardware (pooling), surviving failure (fault tolerance), or spending (CapEx).
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A hospital needs cloud infrastructure dedicated solely to its own use for compliance reasons. A provider hosts and manages it in the provider's datacenter, but no other customer shares it. This is a:
options: Public cloud
Hybrid cloud
Private cloud
Multicloud
explain: Private cloud means single-tenant, regardless of who hosts it or where it lives. The trap is assuming 'provider-hosted' means public — it is the sharing, not the hosting, that defines public cloud. Hybrid mixes models; multicloud means multiple providers.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A retailer runs its steady year-round workload in its own datacenter but 'bursts' into the public cloud each December to handle holiday traffic. This architecture is an example of:
options: Public cloud only
Hybrid cloud
Multicloud
Community cloud
explain: Cloud bursting — on-premises plus public cloud working as one environment — is the textbook hybrid pattern. It is not public-only (on-premises is involved), not multicloud (one provider), and not community (not shared with peers).
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs its data analytics on one public cloud provider and its machine-learning workloads on a different public cloud provider, choosing each for its strengths. This strategy is called:
options: Hybrid cloud
Private cloud
Community cloud
Multicloud
explain: Multicloud is using more than one public cloud provider. Hybrid requires private cloud or on-premises in the mix; private and community describe tenancy, not how many providers are used.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Several universities share cloud infrastructure built to support joint research grants with common security requirements. This deployment model is called:
options: Community cloud
Public cloud
Private cloud
Hybrid cloud
explain: A community cloud is shared by organizations with common concerns, such as research compliance here. Public cloud is open to all; private serves one organization; hybrid mixes deployment models rather than sharing one.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company uses a SaaS customer-relationship system. Sales reps enter customer records into it daily. If customer data is entered incorrectly, who is responsible for the data's accuracy?
options: The SaaS provider's support team
The internet service provider
The customer — data is always the customer's responsibility, even in SaaS
Nobody, because SaaS includes data management
explain: The shared responsibility model always leaves data with the customer, in every service model including SaaS. The provider manages the application; it does not own the meaning or accuracy of what the customer puts into it.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A team deploys custom application code to Azure App Service (PaaS). A new version of the underlying runtime is released. Who applies the runtime update?
options: The development team, during their next sprint
Microsoft, because the runtime is part of the managed platform
The company's network administrator
Nobody — runtimes update themselves with no involvement
explain: In PaaS the provider manages the platform — operating system, runtime, and patching — while the customer manages code and data. Treating PaaS like IaaS, where the customer would patch, is the classic exam trap.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs its workloads on Azure virtual machines (IaaS) inside a virtual network it designed. Who is responsible for configuring the network security group rules that filter traffic to those VMs?
options: Microsoft's network operations team
The internet service provider
The virtual machine's guest operating system
The customer, because networking above the virtualization layer is the customer's responsibility in IaaS
explain: In IaaS the customer owns everything from the OS upward, including virtual networking and firewall rules. Microsoft provides the physical network fabric; it does not write your NSG rules.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A stock-trading platform must keep processing orders with zero interruption even if an individual server fails. The ability to continue operating through a component failure without any disruption is called:
options: Fault tolerance
High availability
Disaster recovery
Elasticity
explain: Fault tolerance means no interruption despite a failure. High availability minimizes downtime but may allow a brief failover; disaster recovery restores service after a major event; elasticity scales capacity.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A photo-sharing app runs a small piece of code each time a user uploads a picture — resizing it, then shutting down. The company pays only for the milliseconds the code runs. This is an example of:
options: Infrastructure as a Service
Platform as a Service
Serverless computing
A virtual machine scale set
explain: Serverless is event-driven code execution billed per use with no server management. IaaS and scale sets keep servers running and billing; PaaS still runs an always-on platform beneath the code.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A finance director wants the company's cloud spending to be as predictable as possible for budgeting. Which approach BEST delivers predictable costs?
options: Pay-as-you-go pricing with constantly changing usage
Spot virtual machines
Reserved capacity — committing to one or three years for a discounted fixed rate
Deleting resources every night
explain: Reservations trade a one- or three-year commitment for discounted, predictable pricing. Pay-as-you-go varies with use; Spot prices fluctuate and VMs can be evicted; nightly deletion is an optimization tactic, not a budgeting model.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An administrator wants to stop incurring compute charges for an Azure virtual machine that won't be needed for a month, but wants to keep its disks and configuration. What should they do?
options: Shut down the operating system from inside the VM
Stop (deallocate) the VM in the Azure portal
Delete the virtual machine's data disks
Pause the Azure subscription
explain: Only deallocating releases the VM's compute allocation and stops compute billing. Shutting down from inside the OS leaves the VM 'Stopped' but still allocated — and still billed. Deleting disks destroys data, and subscriptions cannot be paused.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A 15-person company has no datacenter staff and doesn't want to hire any. Which cloud benefit BEST addresses this situation?
options: Geo-distribution
Reduced management burden — the provider maintains the physical infrastructure
Capital expenditure
Fault tolerance
explain: The provider handles facilities, hardware, and physical maintenance, so a small team can focus on its business instead of datacenters. Geo-distribution is about location; CapEx is the spending model they want to avoid; fault tolerance is about resilience.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A startup launches its product worldwide on day one, serving users on five continents, without building a single datacenter. Which cloud benefit makes this possible?
options: Global reach through the provider's worldwide regions
Operational expenditure
Resource pooling
Serverless computing
explain: The provider's global region footprint gives instant worldwide presence with no datacenter investment. OpEx describes spending; resource pooling describes shared hardware; serverless is a compute model — none explain global presence.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A cloud provider employs full-time physical security teams, biometric access controls, and redundant power at every datacenter — far beyond what any single mid-size customer could afford. Customers benefit from this through:
options: Capital expenditure
The provider's economies of scale applied to security
Measured service
On-demand self-service
explain: Economies of scale let the provider spread massive security investments across millions of customers, giving each enterprise-grade protection cheaply. The distractors are unrelated characteristics or spending models.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A nonprofit has no capital budget at all, but its board approved monthly operating funds. Why is the public cloud a good fit for this organization?
options: It requires buying servers with operating funds
It converts infrastructure spending into operational expenditure with no upfront cost
It eliminates the need for any IT spending
It requires a three-year contract paid upfront
explain: The cloud's OpEx model needs no upfront hardware purchase — spending comes from operating funds as usage occurs. Cloud does not eliminate IT spending, and it does not require upfront contracts.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: After adding more instances behind a load balancer, an application successfully handles ten times its previous user load. The application's ability to handle increased load by adding resources demonstrates:
options: Scalability
Agility
Fault tolerance
Disaster recovery
explain: Scalability is the ability to increase capacity to meet demand — here by scaling out. Agility is speed of change; fault tolerance and disaster recovery concern failures, not growth.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An enterprise wants to move company email, calendars, video meetings, and file sharing to the cloud with minimal administrative effort. Which service model BEST fits?
options: Infrastructure as a Service
Platform as a Service
On-premises Exchange servers
Software as a Service, such as Microsoft 365
explain: Email and collaboration are classic SaaS — finished applications consumed over the internet with minimal administration. IaaS or PaaS would require building and maintaining the systems themselves.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's customers are concentrated in Japan and complain about slow response times from an app hosted in a US region. What should the architect do?
options: Enable a larger VM size in the US region
Deploy the application to an Azure region in Japan, closer to the users
Add more users to the US deployment
Switch the app to a SaaS product
explain: Latency follows physical distance, so deploying to a region near the users cuts round-trip time. A bigger VM does not fix distance; adding users makes it worse; switching service models is irrelevant to latency.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A hospital's patient portal must stay online even if an entire datacenter in its Azure region fails. Which feature should the architect use?
options: A resource group
An Azure subscription
A management group
Availability zones — deploying across physically separate datacenters within the region
explain: Availability zones isolate datacenter-level failures because each zone has independent power, cooling, and networking. Resource groups, subscriptions, and management groups are management and billing boundaries — not resilience mechanisms.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: During Azure platform maintenance, Microsoft updates only one region of a pair at a time. Why?
options: So that at least one region in the pair remains available and current during the rollout
To reduce the customer's bill
Because paired regions cannot communicate with each other
To force customers to use both regions
explain: Sequential updates across a region pair keep a current, available disaster-recovery target at all times. It has nothing to do with billing, and paired regions absolutely communicate — replication depends on it.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A US federal agency needs cloud services that meet strict government compliance requirements and are operated solely for government customers. Which Azure environment fits?
options: Azure China
A standard public Azure region
Azure Government — a sovereign cloud built for US government workloads
Any region, since all regions are identical
explain: Azure Government is a separate sovereign cloud dedicated to US government with its own compliance attestations. Azure China serves China under a local operator; standard regions do not carry the same government compliance posture; regions differ in services and certifications.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A multinational needs to serve customers in mainland China in compliance with Chinese regulations. What should it know about Azure China?
options: It is identical to global Azure in every way
It is a separate cloud instance operated in China by 21Vianet, with its own compliance posture
It is only available to the Chinese government
It cannot be used alongside any other Azure cloud
explain: Azure China is physically and operationally separate, run by 21Vianet under Chinese law, with some service differences from global Azure. It is not government-only, and hybrid architectures can span the two clouds.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A holding company owns five subsidiaries. Each subsidiary needs separate billing, but the parent company must enforce the same security policies across all of them. How should Azure be organized?
options: One resource group for the entire holding company
Five subscriptions with no shared management
One subscription per employee
A management group hierarchy with one subscription per subsidiary
explain: Management groups apply policy and RBAC across many subscriptions, while separate subscriptions give each subsidiary its own billing boundary. A single resource group cannot span that structure, and ungrouped subscriptions lose central governance.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A consulting firm starts a new client project and needs isolated billing, quotas, and access control for everything the project uses. What should it create?
options: A new Azure subscription for the project
A new availability zone
A new Azure region
A new virtual machine
explain: Subscriptions are the billing, quota, and access boundary in Azure. Zones and regions are infrastructure placement choices, not billing boundaries, and a VM is a single resource.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team deploys a web app, its database, and its storage account together for a marketing campaign site that will be deleted entirely when the campaign ends. Where should these resources live?
options: In three different subscriptions
Each in its own region
In the same resource group, so they share one lifecycle
Directly under the management group
explain: Resource groups bundle resources with a shared lifecycle — deploy, manage, and delete them together. Scattering resources complicates cleanup, and resources cannot live directly under a management group.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company must deploy 20 identical development environments, and every deployment must produce exactly the same configuration. Which approach guarantees this?
options: Clicking through the portal 20 times
Infrastructure as code with ARM templates — declarative files deployed identically every time
Emailing setup instructions to each developer
Taking screenshots of a working environment
explain: ARM templates are declarative and idempotent: the same file yields the same result on every deployment. Manual portal work drifts between environments; instructions and screenshots are not executable or reliable.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services
