q: A team finds raw ARM JSON templates too verbose to write by hand, but still wants the reliability of ARM deployments. What should they use?
options: The Azure pricing calculator
Azure Policy
A spreadsheet of resource names
Bicep — a simpler language that transpiles into ARM templates
explain: Bicep offers cleaner syntax and compiles down to standard ARM JSON for deployment. The pricing calculator estimates cost; Policy enforces rules; a spreadsheet is not deployable.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A manufacturer must migrate a legacy inventory application that requires administrator access to the operating system and custom kernel drivers. Which Azure compute option fits?
options: Azure virtual machines (IaaS), which give full OS control
Azure App Service
Azure Functions
Microsoft 365
explain: Only IaaS virtual machines provide OS-level access for drivers and kernel requirements. App Service and Functions abstract the OS away; Microsoft 365 is SaaS productivity software, not a compute platform.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An e-commerce company runs a stateless web tier that must automatically grow from 4 to 40 identical instances during flash sales and shrink afterward. Which service is designed for this?
options: A single virtual machine
Azure Virtual Desktop
Virtual Machine Scale Sets
Azure Bastion
explain: Virtual Machine Scale Sets manage fleets of identical VMs with built-in autoscaling. A single VM cannot scale out; Virtual Desktop serves remote desktops; Bastion provides secure admin access — not scaling.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An architect wants virtual machines protected against a single server rack failing inside a datacenter, using fault domains and update domains. Which feature provides this?
options: Availability zones
Availability sets
Region pairs
Resource groups
explain: Availability sets spread VMs across fault domains (racks, power) and update domains (maintenance groups) within a datacenter. Availability zones — the almost-right trap — protect across datacenters instead; region pairs serve disaster recovery; resource groups are management boundaries.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team needs to deploy a web API that automatically scales, with no server or OS management and built-in deployment slots for staging. Which service fits?
options: Azure virtual machines
Azure Container Instances
Azure Arc
Azure App Service (PaaS)
explain: App Service is the PaaS web-hosting platform with autoscaling, no OS management, and deployment slots. VMs require OS management; Container Instances run containers rather than PaaS web apps; Arc extends management to hybrid environments.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A logistics company wants a small piece of code to run automatically every time a new file arrives in blob storage, paying only for each execution. Which service fits BEST?
options: Azure Functions — event-driven serverless compute
A continuously running virtual machine
Azure Virtual Desktop
Azure ExpressRoute
explain: Functions triggers on events like blob creation and bills per execution. A VM idles and bills continuously; Virtual Desktop delivers desktops; ExpressRoute is private network connectivity — neither runs event-driven code.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A developer needs to run a single container for a one-off data-processing job — no orchestration, no always-on servers. Which service is the fastest, simplest fit?
options: Azure Kubernetes Service
Virtual Machine Scale Sets
Azure Container Instances
Azure App Service
explain: Container Instances runs individual containers on demand without orchestration overhead. AKS orchestrates many containers; scale sets manage VM fleets; App Service hosts web apps rather than arbitrary one-off containers.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company is breaking its monolith into dozens of microservices that need automated scaling, self-healing, and rolling updates across hundreds of containers. Which service should it choose?
options: Azure Container Instances
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
Azure Functions
Azure Virtual Machines
explain: AKS is the managed Kubernetes orchestrator built for scheduling, scaling, and self-healing at this scale. Container Instances runs single containers without orchestration; Functions is event-driven code; raw VMs mean building orchestration yourself.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A startup wants to run containerized services without managing Kubernetes or any servers, scaling to zero when idle. Which Azure service fits?
options: Azure virtual machines
Azure Container Instances
Azure Arc
Azure Container Apps — serverless containers without Kubernetes management
explain: Container Apps abstracts Kubernetes away while keeping container semantics and scale-to-zero. VMs and Container Instances still leave host-management decisions with you; Arc is hybrid management, not container hosting.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company with a remote workforce needs to give employees secure Windows desktops accessible from anywhere, without shipping laptops. Which service provides this?
options: Azure Virtual Desktop
Azure Functions
Azure DNS
Azure Front Door
explain: Azure Virtual Desktop delivers virtualized Windows desktops and apps from Azure. Functions runs code; DNS resolves names; Front Door is global load balancing — none deliver desktops.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company designs a virtual network with separate subnets for web servers, application servers, and databases. What is the purpose of these subnets?
options: To increase the internet bandwidth
To reduce the Azure bill to zero
To segment the network so traffic between tiers can be isolated and controlled
To replace the need for firewalls
explain: Subnets segment a VNet's address space so each tier can carry its own security controls, such as NSGs. They do not add bandwidth, do not eliminate cost, and do not replace firewalls — they work alongside them.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company has virtual networks in two Azure regions and needs private, low-latency connectivity between them without traffic crossing the public internet. What should it use?
options: A network security group
VNet peering
Azure DNS
A storage account
explain: VNet peering connects virtual networks privately over Microsoft's backbone network. NSGs filter traffic but do not connect networks; DNS resolves names; storage accounts store data.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Developers working from home need encrypted access from their laptops to Azure virtual networks, with no dedicated telecom circuit involved. Which service fits?
options: Azure Firewall
Azure Bastion
Azure Front Door
A VPN Gateway — supporting point-to-site encrypted tunnels over the internet
explain: VPN Gateway supports point-to-site connections so individual devices tunnel in securely over the internet. Firewall filters traffic; Bastion gives portal-based VM admin access; Front Door is global web load balancing.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A bank needs a connection to Azure with consistent latency that never traverses the public internet, for regulatory reasons. Which service fits?
options: Azure ExpressRoute — a private dedicated connection
A VPN Gateway over the public internet
VNet peering
Azure DNS
explain: ExpressRoute is a private circuit with predictable performance that does not cross the public internet. VPN Gateway does traverse the internet — the trap; VNet peering connects VNets, not on-premises; DNS resolves names.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants virtual machines in its VNet to resolve each other's names privately, without exposing those names on the public internet. Which service fits?
options: Public Azure DNS
A hosts file on every VM
Azure Private DNS zones
Azure Front Door
explain: Private DNS zones provide name resolution scoped to virtual networks. Public DNS would expose names internet-wide; hosts files do not scale; Front Door is a global load balancer.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company must distribute incoming TCP traffic across a pool of virtual machines at the network layer, with health probes removing failed instances. Which service operates at Layer 4 to do this?
options: Azure Application Gateway
Azure Load Balancer
Azure Front Door
Azure Firewall
explain: Azure Load Balancer is the Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) distributor with health probes. Application Gateway and Front Door operate at Layer 7 (HTTP); Firewall filters traffic but does not load-balance.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company needs HTTPS load balancing with URL-based routing, SSL termination, and a web application firewall to block SQL injection. Which service fits?
options: Azure Load Balancer
Azure DNS
Azure Bastion
Azure Application Gateway with WAF
explain: Application Gateway is the regional Layer 7 load balancer with URL routing, SSL offload, and integrated WAF. Load Balancer is Layer 4 only; DNS and Bastion perform none of these functions.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A global SaaS company needs users worldwide routed to the nearest healthy regional deployment, with instant failover if a region goes down. Which service is designed for this?
options: Azure Front Door — global Layer 7 load balancing across regions
A regional load balancer
VNet peering
Azure Private DNS
explain: Front Door is the global entry point with worldwide routing and instant regional failover. Regional load balancers do not span regions; peering and Private DNS do not route user traffic.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A security team wants to block all inbound SSH traffic from the internet to a subnet, while allowing it from the corporate office range. Where should this rule be enforced?
options: In the Azure pricing calculator
In Azure Advisor
In a network security group (NSG) attached to the subnet
In Azure Key Vault
explain: NSGs filter traffic to subnets and network interfaces with allow/deny rules. The pricing calculator and Advisor do not enforce anything; Key Vault stores secrets, not traffic rules.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company needs to filter outbound traffic by fully qualified domain name (for example, allowing only update domains) and wants built-in threat intelligence. Which service fits?
options: A network security group
Azure Firewall
Azure Bastion
Azure DDoS Protection
explain: Azure Firewall does FQDN-based filtering and integrates threat intelligence; NSGs filter by IP address and port only. Bastion is admin access; DDoS Protection mitigates volumetric attacks, not URL filtering.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company's partner firewalls only allowlist a single IP address, but all outbound traffic from an Azure subnet currently uses many unpredictable public IPs. Which service gives the subnet one predictable outbound IP?
options: Azure Firewall
A VPN Gateway
ExpressRoute
Azure NAT Gateway
explain: NAT Gateway provides a single static public IP (or prefix) for all outbound traffic from a subnet. Firewall filters traffic; VPN Gateway and ExpressRoute connect networks rather than consolidating outbound IPs.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An accounting firm stores client tax documents that auditors access a few times per year. When accessed, the files must open immediately. Which blob access tier is MOST cost-effective?
options: Hot
Cool
Archive
Premium
explain: Cool is the lower-cost tier for infrequently accessed data that still needs millisecond retrieval. Hot fits frequent access; Archive is cheaper but takes hours to rehydrate — the trap; Premium is for high-performance block blobs.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company is migrating on-premises file shares to Azure and needs the applications to keep using the SMB protocol. Which storage service fits?
options: Azure Blob storage
Azure Queue storage
Azure Files
Azure Table storage
explain: Azure Files exposes SMB (and NFS) file shares in the cloud — the lift-and-shift file-share service. Blob is object storage without SMB; Queue is messaging; Table is NoSQL.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company needs its storage to survive the complete loss of one datacenter within its Azure region, but it does not need a secondary region. Which redundancy option fits at the lowest cost?
options: Locally redundant storage (LRS)
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS)
Geo-redundant storage (GRS)
Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS)
explain: ZRS synchronously replicates data across three availability zones in the region, surviving a datacenter loss. LRS protects only within one datacenter; GRS and GZRS add a secondary region the company does not need, at higher cost.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants every employee to use one identity to sign in to Microsoft 365, Azure resources, and third-party SaaS apps. Which service provides this?
options: Azure Key Vault
Azure Policy
Microsoft Defender for Cloud
Microsoft Entra ID
explain: Microsoft Entra ID is the cloud identity provider enabling single sign-on across applications. Key Vault stores secrets; Policy enforces configuration rules; Defender for Cloud secures workloads — none provide identity.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An employee types a username and password to sign in (proving who they are), and then the system checks whether they may open the finance folder (deciding what they can do). These two steps are:
options: Authentication, then authorization
Authorization, then authentication
Encryption, then decryption
Two unrelated logins
explain: Authentication verifies identity; authorization grants permissions based on that identity. The order matters — the system must know who someone is before deciding what they may do.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company requires administrators to approve sign-ins with an authenticator app in addition to their passwords. This requirement is an example of:
options: Single sign-on
A Conditional Access policy
Multifactor authentication (MFA)
Passwordless backup codes
explain: MFA requires two or more verification factors — here, something known (password) plus something possessed (the app approval). SSO reduces sign-in friction; Conditional Access is the policy engine that can require MFA; backup codes are a recovery method.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Employees complain about signing in separately to twelve different cloud applications every morning. Which feature lets them sign in once and access them all?
options: Multifactor authentication
Single sign-on (SSO)
A VPN Gateway
Azure Bastion
explain: SSO federates one sign-in across applications. MFA adds security without reducing sign-in count; VPN Gateway and Bastion are network access technologies, not application sign-in.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants to block sign-ins from devices that are not marked compliant in its device management system. Which Entra ID feature enforces this?
options: Single sign-on
Azure Bastion
Azure Policy
Conditional Access policies
explain: Conditional Access evaluates signals — device compliance, location, risk — and enforces allow, block, or require-MFA decisions. SSO simplifies sign-in; Bastion is VM access; Azure Policy governs Azure resources, not user sign-ins.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants administrators to receive elevated rights only when needed, for a limited time, with approval and auditing. Which Entra ID feature provides this just-in-time access?
options: Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
Single sign-on
Azure resource locks
A Conditional Access policy
explain: PIM provides eligible, just-in-time role activation with approval workflows and audit trails. SSO is sign-in convenience; locks protect resources from changes; Conditional Access controls sign-in conditions, not time-bound elevation.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company designs its network so that every access request is authenticated and authorized based on identity and device health — never trusted just because it comes from inside the corporate network. This reflects which Zero Trust principle?
options: Assume breach
Least-privilege access
Verify explicitly
Defense in depth
explain: Verify explicitly means always authenticating and authorizing based on all available signals, never granting implicit trust by network location. Assume breach is operating as if compromised; least privilege is minimal access; defense in depth is layered controls.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A contractor is given read-only access to a single resource group — nothing more — while the security team continuously hunts for threats on the assumption that an attacker may already be inside. These two practices reflect:
options: Verify explicitly and defense in depth
Least-privilege access and assume breach
High availability and elasticity
Authentication and single sign-on
explain: Least privilege grants only the minimum access needed; assume breach means operating as if compromise has already occurred. The other pairs describe different principles or unrelated cloud concepts.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company protects its systems with MFA for identities, NSGs for the network, disk encryption for data, and Defender for Cloud monitoring — so that if one control fails, others still stand. This strategy is called:
options: Zero Trust
Single sign-on
Shared responsibility
Defense in depth
explain: Defense in depth layers independent controls so no single failure is fatal. Zero Trust is the never-trust verification model (related but distinct); SSO is sign-in convenience; shared responsibility divides duties between customer and provider.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A CISO wants a single dashboard showing the security posture of all Azure workloads, with prioritized recommendations and a secure score to track improvement. Which service provides this?
options: Microsoft Defender for Cloud
Microsoft Sentinel
Azure Monitor
Azure Service Health
explain: Defender for Cloud is the cloud security posture management tool with Secure Score and hardening recommendations. Sentinel is SIEM/SOAR for threat detection; Monitor tracks performance metrics; Service Health reports Azure platform outages.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A security team needs to collect logs from Azure, on-premises servers, and SaaS apps into one place, detect threats with AI, and automatically isolate compromised machines. Which service combines SIEM and SOAR to do this?
options: Azure Key Vault
Azure Policy
Microsoft Sentinel
Microsoft Entra ID
explain: Sentinel is the cloud-native SIEM (collect and detect) plus SOAR (automate response). Key Vault stores secrets; Policy enforces configuration; Entra ID manages identities — none analyze threats across sources.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A development team hard-codes database connection strings into its application code. The security team wants those secrets stored centrally with audited access instead. Which service fits?
options: Azure Blob storage
Azure Key Vault
Azure Policy
Microsoft Defender for Cloud
explain: Key Vault centrally stores secrets, keys, and certificates with access policies and auditing. Blob storage lacks secret-specific access control; Policy enforces rules; Defender for Cloud monitors posture — none vault secrets.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A public-facing web application needs always-on protection against large network-layer DDoS attacks, with a cost-protection guarantee if an attack drives up scaling costs. Which Azure offering fits?
options: The free basic DDoS protection on virtual networks
Azure Firewall
A network security group
DDoS Network Protection
explain: DDoS Network Protection adds adaptive tuning, attack telemetry, and the cost-protection SLA guarantee. Basic protection is automatic but carries no guarantee; Firewall and NSGs filter traffic but do not mitigate volumetric DDoS attacks.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company must ensure no virtual machine is ever deployed outside approved European regions. Which governance tool automatically blocks non-compliant deployments?
options: Azure Policy with a deny effect
Role-based access control (RBAC)
A resource lock
A resource tag
explain: Azure Policy evaluates deployments against rules and can deny non-compliant ones automatically. RBAC controls who may act, not whether the action complies; locks prevent deletion or changes; tags organize but do not enforce.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A compliance team needs to apply fifteen related policy definitions — covering regions, encryption, and tagging — as a single assignable package. What should they create?
options: Fifteen separate RBAC role assignments
A management group
An Azure Policy initiative
A resource lock
explain: An initiative bundles multiple policy definitions into one set for assignment and compliance reporting. RBAC manages access, not configuration rules; management groups scope assignments; locks prevent changes.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A team lead must be able to create resources AND grant other team members access to the subscription. Which built-in RBAC role provides both abilities?
options: Reader
Owner
Contributor
Virtual Machine Contributor
explain: Owner grants full access including managing access for others. Contributor — the classic trap — can manage resources but cannot grant access. Reader is view-only.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An external auditor needs to manage user access reviews but must not be able to create, modify, or delete any Azure resources. Which built-in role fits BEST?
options: Owner
Contributor
Reader
User Access Administrator
explain: User Access Administrator manages access (role assignments) without resource-management rights. Owner and Contributor can change resources; Reader cannot manage access at all.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: During a financial audit, a company must guarantee that no one can modify or delete production resources for two weeks. Which lock should it apply?
options: ReadOnly
CanNotDelete
A resource tag
An Azure Policy
explain: ReadOnly blocks all updates and deletes while still allowing reads; CanNotDelete still permits modifications — the trap. Tags organize; Policy enforces configuration rules, not a freeze on changes.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A CanNotDelete lock is applied to a production resource group. An administrator then tries to resize a virtual machine inside it. What happens?
options: The resize fails — the lock freezes everything
The administrator is locked out of the portal
The resize succeeds — CanNotDelete prevents deletion, not modification
All resources in the group are deleted
explain: CanNotDelete blocks delete actions only; reads and modifications still work. The trap is assuming the lock freezes all changes — that behavior belongs to ReadOnly.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: The finance department needs cloud costs broken down by department and project for chargeback. Which feature should the company use to label resources for this?
options: Azure Policy
Resource tags
Resource locks
Availability zones
explain: Tags are name-value labels used for cost allocation, organization, and automation. Policy enforces rules; locks prevent changes; availability zones provide resilience — none label resources for billing.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An architect needs to find every virtual machine across 40 subscriptions that is missing a required tag. Which service can query resources at that scale?
options: The Azure pricing calculator
Azure Advisor
Azure Service Health
Azure Resource Graph
explain: Resource Graph runs fast, powerful queries across subscriptions and management groups. The pricing calculator estimates cost; Advisor gives recommendations; Service Health reports platform outages.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A department wants an email alert when its cloud spending reaches 80% of its monthly budget. Which Cost Management feature provides this?
options: Budgets with alerts
Azure Reservations
The TCO calculator
Spot virtual machines
explain: Budgets track spending against thresholds and trigger alerts. Reservations pre-commit to capacity; the TCO calculator compares on-premises with cloud; Spot VMs are discounted interruptible compute.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A startup wants to estimate what its planned architecture — 10 VMs, a database, and storage — will cost per month in Azure. Which tool should it use?
options: The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator
Microsoft Cost Management
The Azure pricing calculator
Azure Advisor
explain: The pricing calculator estimates the cost of planned Azure services. The TCO calculator compares on-premises with cloud; Cost Management analyzes actual spending; Advisor recommends optimizations.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A CIO must present a three-year cost comparison of keeping workloads on-premises versus moving them to Azure. Which tool is built for this?
options: The Azure pricing calculator
The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator
Azure Monitor
Microsoft Sentinel
explain: The TCO calculator compares on-premises costs (hardware, power, staff) against Azure over time. The pricing calculator prices Azure services alone; Monitor tracks performance; Sentinel is security.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company runs 50 virtual machines at steady utilization and expects the workload to remain unchanged for three years. How can it significantly reduce compute costs?
options: Switch to Spot virtual machines
Delete and recreate the VMs nightly
Move the VMs to a different region each month
Purchase Azure Reservations for a one- or three-year term
explain: Reservations exchange a capacity commitment for deep discounts on steady workloads. Spot VMs can be evicted at any time — wrong for steady workloads; nightly deletion adds churn without commitment pricing; moving regions changes nothing about pricing.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company owns Windows Server licenses with Software Assurance and wants to use them for Azure virtual machines instead of paying for new Windows licenses. Which benefit enables this?
options: Azure Hybrid Benefit
Spot virtual machines
Azure Reservations
The TCO calculator
explain: Azure Hybrid Benefit lets customers apply existing eligible on-premises licenses to Azure. Spot and Reservations are pricing options, not license reuse; the TCO calculator is a comparison tool.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A media company runs overnight video-rendering batch jobs that can tolerate interruptions and restarts. Which VM purchasing option offers the deepest discount for this workload?
options: Pay-as-you-go
Reserved instances
Spot Virtual Machines
Dedicated hosts
explain: Spot VMs use spare Azure capacity at deep discounts, with the tradeoff that they can be evicted when capacity is needed. Interruptible batch work is the textbook Spot scenario; pay-as-you-go and reserved are pricier; dedicated hosts are the opposite of cheap shared capacity.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company is surprised by a large bill after users downloaded terabytes of data from Azure storage to on-premises systems. Which cost factor caused this?
options: The number of resource groups
The Azure region's time zone
Data egress (bandwidth) charges for data leaving Azure
The number of availability zones
explain: Inbound data transfer is free, but outbound (egress) data transfer is billed — a classic surprise. Resource group count, time zones, and zone counts do not drive bandwidth bills.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Azure fails to meet the uptime guaranteed in a service's SLA during a given month. What is the customer entitled to?
options: A full refund of all Azure spending
Automatic migration to another cloud
A lawsuit settlement
Service credits, as defined in the SLA
explain: SLAs define service credits — a percentage of fees — as the remedy for missed targets. The trap is expecting full refunds or dramatic remedies; the SLA is a financial-backing commitment, not a migration promise.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A service advertises a 99.9% monthly SLA. Approximately how much downtime does that allow per month?
options: About 43 minutes
About 7 hours
About 4 minutes
Zero — 99.9% means no downtime
explain: 0.1% of a roughly 30-day month is about 43 minutes of allowed downtime. Seven hours would be closer to a 99% SLA, and the trap is reading 99.9% as 'basically 100%.'
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Azure Advisor flags a virtual machine running at 5% CPU utilization for the past month. Which recommendation category does this fall under, and what will Advisor likely suggest?
options: Security — enable disk encryption
Reliability — add an availability zone
Cost — resize or shut down the underutilized VM
Operational excellence — apply a tag
explain: Underutilized resources are Cost recommendations: right-size or deallocate to stop paying for idle capacity. The distractors name real Advisor categories, but the wrong ones for this finding.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An administrator asks: 'Is Azure itself experiencing an outage in my region right now?' Which service answers that question?
options: Azure Service Health
Azure Monitor
Azure Resource Health
Microsoft Defender for Cloud
explain: Service Health reports Azure platform issues by region and service. Monitor tracks your own resources' metrics; Resource Health reports the health of your specific resources; Defender for Cloud covers security posture.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An external auditor asks for Microsoft's ISO 27001 certificates and SOC reports for Azure. Where can the company direct the auditor?
options: The Azure pricing calculator
Azure Advisor
The Azure portal dashboard
The Microsoft Service Trust Portal
explain: The Service Trust Portal publishes compliance reports, audit certifications, and security documentation for Microsoft cloud services. The calculator prices services; Advisor optimizes; the portal manages resources.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company is launching a new product and has no idea whether it will attract 100 users or 10,000. Buying servers for the worst case would waste money if demand is low. How does the consumption-based model solve this capacity-guessing problem?
options: It requires committing to maximum capacity upfront at a discount
The consumption model does not apply to new products
The company provisions what it needs now, scales up or down as real demand appears, and pays only for what it uses
Cloud providers give unlimited free capacity to new products
explain: Consumption-based pricing removes the need to predict capacity: start small and scale with actual demand, paying only for consumed resources. Upfront commitment is the old CapEx guessing game, and cloud capacity is metered — never unlimited or free.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's disaster recovery plan states: 'After an outage, systems must be back online within 4 hours, and no more than 1 hour of data may be lost.' The 'back online within 4 hours' requirement is the:
options: Recovery Time Objective (RTO)
Recovery Point Objective (RPO)
Service-level agreement (SLA)
Backup retention policy
explain: RTO is the maximum tolerable downtime — how fast service must be restored. RPO is the maximum tolerable data loss (the 1-hour figure here). An SLA is the provider's uptime commitment, and retention is how long backups are kept — different concepts.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: After a ransomware attack, a company restores last night's database backup — but the business stays down for two days because its servers, network, and applications must all be rebuilt. This illustrates the difference between:
options: IaaS and PaaS
RTO and SLA
Hot and cold storage tiers
Backup (recovering data) and disaster recovery (restoring full business operations)
explain: Backup restores data; disaster recovery restores the entire operating environment — servers, networking, apps, and processes. Having backups without a tested DR plan still leaves the business down, which is exactly what happened here.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company stores files in cloud storage. An employee misconfigures a storage container as publicly readable, and sensitive data leaks. Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for this misconfiguration?
options: Microsoft, because the data sits in Azure datacenters
The customer — data and access configuration are always the customer's responsibility
The company's internet service provider
Nobody, because cloud storage is secure by default
explain: The provider secures the underlying platform, but the customer always owns its data and how access to it is configured — in every service model. A public container is a customer configuration error, not a provider failure.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A bank's online portal is designed so that if one server fails, traffic automatically shifts to a healthy server within seconds, with only a brief interruption for users. This design provides:
options: Fault tolerance
High availability
Disaster recovery
Elasticity
explain: High availability minimizes downtime through redundancy and automatic failover — a brief interruption is acceptable. Fault tolerance would mean zero interruption. Disaster recovery restores service after a major event; elasticity scales capacity with demand.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A retailer's servers are aging and fully depreciated. The CFO refuses another large capital purchase and wants IT costs to appear as a monthly operating expense tied to actual usage instead. Which move fits this preference?
options: Buying new servers with a five-year loan
Extending hardware warranties for three more years
Leasing servers with a buyout clause
Migrating workloads to public cloud services with consumption-based (OpEx) billing
explain: Public cloud converts the big upfront server purchase (CapEx) into ongoing usage-based bills (OpEx). Loans, extended warranties, and leases on owned hardware all keep the spending in the capital-expenditure world the CFO wants to leave.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A CIO is evaluating private cloud and wants an honest assessment of its trade-offs. Which statement about private cloud is TRUE?
options: It offers cloud-style self-service and elasticity, but the organization still bears the cost and maintenance of dedicated infrastructure
It is always cheaper than public cloud
It eliminates the need for IT staff
Its infrastructure is shared with other companies to cut costs
explain: Private cloud delivers cloud operating models (self-service, automation) on single-tenant infrastructure — but you still buy, house, and maintain that infrastructure. It is not inherently cheaper, still needs skilled staff, and is never shared with other tenants.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Several regional banks share a cloud platform built specifically to satisfy common financial-services regulations, isolated from the provider's general commercial customers. This deployment model is called:
options: Public cloud
Private cloud
Community cloud
Hybrid cloud
explain: A community cloud is shared by organizations with common concerns — here, banking compliance. Public cloud is open to all customers, private serves one organization, and hybrid mixes deployment models rather than sharing one platform.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A law firm keeps confidential client files on its own servers to satisfy client contracts, but runs its public website, email, and development environments in the public cloud — all managed through one console. This is an example of:
options: Hybrid cloud
Multicloud
Private cloud only
Community cloud
explain: Hybrid cloud combines on-premises/private resources with public cloud services as one coordinated environment — exactly this split. Multicloud would require two or more public providers; neither pure-private nor community describes the mix.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: To avoid depending on a single vendor, a company deliberately runs its Windows workloads on one public cloud provider and its analytics on a different public cloud provider, with no on-premises infrastructure. This strategy is called:
options: Hybrid cloud
Private cloud
Community cloud
Multicloud
explain: Multicloud means using more than one public cloud provider — here, as a deliberate hedge against vendor lock-in. Hybrid requires private cloud or on-premises in the mix, which this company does not have.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs a report that takes five minutes every night. On virtual machines it pays for a server running 24/7; with a serverless function it pays only for the five minutes the code executes. This illustrates which serverless characteristic?
options: Servers are eliminated entirely from the architecture
Pay-per-execution billing with no charges for idle time
Unlimited performance at a fixed price
Code runs without being written
explain: Serverless bills per execution, so idle time costs nothing — the five-minute job costs five minutes. Servers still exist behind the scenes (the provider manages them), performance is not unlimited, and code must still be written.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A marketing team wants to build a custom customer portal. Its developers will write all the application code, but nobody wants to manage servers, operating-system patching, or runtime updates. Which service model BEST fits?
options: Software as a Service (SaaS)
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
Platform as a Service (PaaS)
On-premises servers
explain: PaaS is the 'write code, skip the servers' model — the provider manages OS, runtime, and patching while the team owns the application. SaaS would mean buying a finished portal, IaaS would leave them patching servers, and on-premises maximizes their management burden.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Rank these from MOST to LEAST management responsibility for the customer: Azure Virtual Machines, Azure App Service, Microsoft 365.
options: Microsoft 365 > Azure App Service > Azure Virtual Machines
All three require exactly the same management effort
Azure App Service > Azure Virtual Machines > Microsoft 365
Azure Virtual Machines (IaaS) > Azure App Service (PaaS) > Microsoft 365 (SaaS)
explain: Responsibility decreases up the stack: IaaS (VMs) leaves you the OS and above; PaaS (App Service) leaves you code and data; SaaS (Microsoft 365) leaves you mainly data and user access. Reversing the order is the classic exam trap.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A consultant wants project-management software she can use immediately through a browser, with the vendor handling all hosting, updates, and maintenance. Which service model is she describing?
options: Software as a Service (SaaS)
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
Platform as a Service (PaaS)
Bare-metal hosting
explain: Finished software consumed over the internet with zero installation or maintenance is SaaS. IaaS rents infrastructure, PaaS hosts custom code, and bare metal is the most hands-on option of all.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A streaming service sees viewership drop 80% the week after a hit finale airs. It wants server capacity to shrink automatically so it stops paying for idle resources. This automatic scale-in demonstrates:
options: High availability
Elasticity
Fault tolerance
Geo-distribution
explain: Elasticity works in both directions: scaling out for demand and scaling back in when demand falls, so you stop paying for what you no longer need. High availability and fault tolerance concern failures, not demand; geo-distribution concerns location.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An architect says, 'Our system is scalable but not elastic.' What does this mean?
options: It cannot handle any increase in load
It automatically fails over between regions
Capacity can be increased — for example, by manually adding bigger virtual machines — but it does not automatically grow and shrink with demand
It is deployed in multiple geographies
explain: Scalability is the ability to add capacity; elasticity is doing it automatically in response to demand. A system you must resize by hand is scalable without being elastic — an important distinction the exam loves to test.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A retailer wants to test a risky new checkout design with 5% of its traffic for two days, then roll it back instantly if conversion drops. The cloud's ability to support this fast experiment-and-revert cycle demonstrates:
options: Agility
Elasticity
High availability
Fault tolerance
explain: Agility is the speed of change: provision, test, adjust, and tear down in hours or days instead of months. Elasticity is about capacity tracking demand; high availability and fault tolerance are about surviving failures.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company deploys its application in both US and European Azure regions so European users get fast responses, and so US traffic can fail over to Europe if the US region suffers a major outage. This primarily demonstrates:
options: Elasticity
Economies of scale
Serverless computing
Geo-distribution supporting disaster recovery
explain: Geo-distribution places workloads near users (cutting latency) and across regions (enabling failover) — one strategy serving both performance and resilience. Elasticity, economies of scale, and serverless address capacity, cost, and compute models instead.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An Australian retailer wants local shoppers to get fast page loads, and its legal team requires customer data to stay inside Australia. Which approach meets BOTH requirements?
options: Deploying in US regions and encrypting the data
Deploying resources in Australian Azure regions — close to users and keeping data resident in-country
Using ExpressRoute to connect Australian users to US servers
Enabling geo-redundant storage only
explain: Deploying in-country regions solves latency (proximity) and data residency (location control) at once. Encryption does not change where data lives; ExpressRoute does not shorten intercontinental distance; storage redundancy alone does not move the application.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A CFO wants the company's cloud bill to stay stable month-to-month despite variable usage. Which combination BEST delivers cost predictability?
options: Pay-as-you-go pricing for everything with no monitoring
Spot virtual machines for all workloads
Reserved capacity for steady baseline workloads, plus budgets and alerts to catch unexpected spikes
Deleting resources at random to keep spending down
explain: Predictability comes from committing to discounted steady-state capacity (reservations) and governing the rest with budgets and alerts. Pure pay-as-you-go varies with usage, Spot prices fluctuate and can be evicted, and random deletion is not a strategy.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A cloud provider buys 100,000 servers at once, negotiating bulk discounts on hardware, power, and bandwidth that no single mid-size company could obtain. Customers benefit from this purchasing power through:
options: Higher prices to fund the provider's growth
Free hardware for every customer
Mandatory long-term contracts
Economies of scale — bulk purchasing lowers per-unit costs, which flow through as lower prices
explain: Economies of scale let hyperscale providers drive unit costs down and pass savings to customers through competitive pricing. The hardware is not free, contracts are not mandatory for the benefit, and the effect lowers — not raises — prices.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A virtual machine is deallocated for an entire month and shows $0 in compute charges, yet the company's bill still includes a small storage charge for the VM's disks. This illustrates:
options: Measured service — each meter (compute, storage) is billed independently based on actual usage
Flat-rate pricing regardless of usage
A billing error that should be disputed
That deallocated virtual machines are entirely free
explain: Measured service meters each resource separately: zero compute hours means zero compute cost, but the disks still exist and still consume metered storage. It is not flat-rate, not an error, and deallocation stops compute billing — not storage billing.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Unlike a $200,000 server purchase that must be capitalized as an asset and depreciated over several years, monthly cloud bills are treated as:
options: Capital expenditure (CapEx)
Operational expenditure (OpEx)
A bank loan
An intangible asset
explain: Cloud usage bills are operating expenses — incurred and accounted for in the period of use, with no asset to depreciate. The server purchase is the textbook CapEx counterpart: a large upfront asset investment.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A business worries that ransomware could encrypt not only its primary data but also its connected backups. Which backup approach BEST protects against this?
options: Keeping backups on the same network for fast restores
Deleting backups after one week to limit exposure
Storing backups unencrypted for simplicity
Immutable, isolated backup copies that cannot be modified or deleted during their retention period
explain: Immutable backups (such as Azure Backup's immutable vaults) cannot be altered or deleted by anyone — including ransomware — during retention. Same-network backups get encrypted alongside primaries, short retention weakens recovery options, and encryption-at-rest is about confidentiality, not tamper-resistance.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company stores customer records in Azure SQL Database, a PaaS offering. A database administrator misconfigures the server firewall, exposing the database to the public internet, and data is stolen. Who is responsible for the misconfiguration?
options: Microsoft, because it manages the PaaS platform
The company's internet service provider
The customer — configuring access to its data is always the customer's responsibility, even in PaaS
Nobody, because PaaS is fully managed
explain: PaaS shifts platform management (patching, engine updates) to the provider, but data and access control never transfer. 'Fully managed' never means the provider configures your firewalls or owns your data.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company stops buying servers entirely. Instead it rents virtual machines by the hour, scales them up for marketing campaigns, and shuts them down afterward — paying only for what it uses. This shift best illustrates:
options: Cloud computing — on-demand delivery of IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing
Building a private wide-area network
Traditional perpetual software licensing
Server colocation
explain: On-demand resources, rapid scaling, and usage-based billing are the defining traits of cloud computing. A WAN is networking, perpetual licensing is software purchasing, and colocation still means owning the servers.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company moves its on-premises virtual machines to Azure virtual machines with minimal changes, planning to modernize the applications later. This migration approach is called:
options: Refactoring
Rehosting (lift and shift)
Rebuilding as cloud-native
Retiring the workload
explain: Rehosting — lift and shift — moves workloads as-is for speed, deferring modernization. Refactoring and rebuilding change the application architecture; retiring eliminates the workload instead of moving it.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's e-commerce site slows down during a sale. The team adds more identical virtual machine instances behind a load balancer, and performance recovers. The team scaled:
options: Vertically (up)
Down
Horizontally (out)
They did not scale at all
explain: Adding more instances is horizontal scaling (scaling out). Vertical scaling would mean making the existing VM bigger. The load balancer distributes traffic across the new instances.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An architect must choose between scaling up (a bigger virtual machine) and scaling out (more virtual machines). Which statement is TRUE?
options: Scaling up has no limits
Scaling out requires rewriting every application from scratch
Only scaling up improves availability
Scaling out adds redundancy — if one instance fails, the others keep serving traffic — while a single scaled-up VM remains a single point of failure
explain: Scale-out distributes load and eliminates the single point of failure; one big VM can still fail entirely. Scaling up does hit size limits, scaling out does not always require rewrites (stateless apps scale naturally), and it is scaling out that typically improves availability.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company moves to a private cloud expecting public-cloud-like cost savings, but its infrastructure spending barely changes. What is the most likely reason?
options: Private cloud keeps infrastructure ownership — and its costs — with the organization; the dramatic economies of scale belong to public providers
Private clouds are always misconfigured
Public cloud is free, so any private spending looks high
The company should have bought even more servers
explain: The public cloud's cost advantage comes largely from the provider's massive scale spread across millions of customers. A private cloud is still your own dedicated hardware with your own capital and maintenance costs — the cloud operating model without the hyperscale economics.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs its entire workload on a single virtual machine with no redundancy. The physical host server fails. What happens to the application?
options: Traffic automatically fails over to another instance
The application goes offline — a single VM is a single point of failure, and high availability requires redundant instances
All application data is permanently lost
Azure automatically doubles the company's bill
explain: One VM means one point of failure: when its host fails, the app is down until the VM restarts elsewhere. Failover requires a second instance (availability set, zone, or scale set). Data is not lost — disks persist independently — and billing does not punish failures.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Which of the following is a genuine benefit of public cloud compared with building a private datacenter?
options: You must purchase all hardware upfront
You manage physical security of the facility yourself
You wait weeks for procurement whenever you need servers
You avoid upfront hardware costs and can deploy resources globally in minutes
explain: Public cloud removes the capital outlay and procurement delays of datacenter building, with global deployment in minutes. The other options describe the burdens of the private-datacenter path, not benefits of cloud.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A hospital runs its electronic health records on a private cloud for strict control, while staff use a cloud-based email and collaboration suite. The email suite is an example of:
options: SaaS consumed within a hybrid strategy
Infrastructure as a Service
An on-premises application
A community cloud
explain: The overall strategy is hybrid (private cloud plus public cloud), and the email suite itself is SaaS — finished software delivered over the internet. It is not infrastructure rental, not on-premises, and not shared with peer organizations.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A developer says, 'With serverless, there are no servers.' What is wrong with this statement?
options: Nothing — it is entirely accurate
Serverless always costs more than virtual machines
Servers still exist — the provider provisions and manages them; the developer is simply abstracted from that work
Serverless platforms cannot execute code
explain: 'Serverless' means no server management for you, not no servers at all. The provider runs the underlying fleet, scales it, and patches it. Cost depends on the workload pattern, and executing code on demand is precisely what serverless does.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company needs Azure services inside its own datacenter with no internet connectivity, for regulatory reasons. Which offering brings the Azure cloud into its datacenter?
options: Azure Arc
Azure Stack Hub
Azure Migrate
Azure ExpressRoute
explain: Azure Stack Hub runs Azure services on hardware in your own datacenter, including disconnected scenarios. Arc extends Azure management to existing infrastructure but does not deliver Azure services; Migrate moves workloads to Azure; ExpressRoute is connectivity.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company has web applications deployed in three Azure regions. It wants users' DNS queries to automatically resolve to the closest healthy region, with failover if a region goes down. Which service provides DNS-based global traffic routing?
options: Azure Load Balancer
Azure Front Door
Azure DNS
Azure Traffic Manager
explain: Traffic Manager is the DNS-based global router with health checks and routing methods (priority, weighted, performance, geographic). Front Door routes at the HTTP layer rather than DNS; Load Balancer is regional Layer 4; Azure DNS hosts zones but does not do health-based routing.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A media company serves large video files to a global audience and wants content cached close to viewers to cut latency and reduce load on its origin servers. Which service fits?
options: Azure Content Delivery Network (CDN)
Azure Files
Azure ExpressRoute
Azure Backup
explain: CDN caches static content at edge points of presence near users. Azure Files is cloud file shares, ExpressRoute is private connectivity, and Backup protects data — none cache content at the edge.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An architect is comparing Azure's traffic-distribution options. Which pairing is CORRECT?
options: Load Balancer provides global HTTP routing
Application Gateway operates at Layer 4
Front Door is a global Layer 7 entry point with instant failover, while Traffic Manager routes at the DNS layer
Front Door works only within a single region
explain: Front Door is the global HTTP(S) entry point with instant regional failover; Traffic Manager makes DNS-level routing decisions. Load Balancer is regional Layer 4, and Application Gateway is regional Layer 7 — the distractors swap these roles.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants its virtual network to reach Azure Storage using a private IP address inside the VNet, so storage traffic never traverses the public internet and the storage account has no public exposure. Which feature provides this?
options: Virtual network service endpoints
A network security group
A VPN Gateway
Azure Private Link (private endpoints)
explain: Private Link assigns a private IP from your VNet to the PaaS service, removing public exposure. Service endpoints keep traffic on the Microsoft backbone but the service retains its public endpoint — the key distinction the exam tests.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company is comfortable with its Azure SQL Database keeping its public endpoint, but wants all traffic from its VNet to reach the database over the Microsoft backbone network instead of the public internet. Which feature fits?
options: Azure Private Link
Virtual network service endpoints
Azure ExpressRoute
Azure Firewall
explain: Service endpoints extend the VNet identity to the PaaS service so traffic stays on the backbone, while the service keeps its public endpoint. Private Link would instead give the database a private IP; ExpressRoute connects on-premises; Firewall filters traffic.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A network engineer needs to capture packets from a virtual machine, verify network security group flow logs, and run connection troubleshooting between two VMs. Which Azure service provides these network diagnostics?
options: Azure Network Watcher
Azure Monitor metrics
Azure Service Health
Azure Policy
explain: Network Watcher is the network monitoring and diagnostics service: packet capture, NSG flow logs, connection troubleshoot, and topology views. Monitor metrics track resource performance, Service Health reports platform issues, and Policy enforces configuration rules.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A data-science team needs to run big-data analytics over petabytes of unstructured data using a hierarchical file-system namespace with fine-grained access control. Which storage option fits?
options: Azure Files
Azure Queue storage
Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2
Azure Table storage
explain: Data Lake Storage Gen2 builds a hierarchical namespace on top of Blob storage, designed for analytics at massive scale. Azure Files is SMB/NFS shares, Queue is messaging, and Table is NoSQL key-value storage.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company stores virtual machine disk (VHD) files in Blob storage and needs efficient random read/write access to fixed-size pages. Which blob type underlies VM disks?
options: Block blobs
Page blobs
Append blobs
Archive blobs
explain: Page blobs provide random access to 512-byte pages and back all Azure VM disks. Block blobs store objects like images and videos, append blobs are optimized for logging, and Archive is a cold access tier rather than a blob type.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants blobs automatically moved from the Hot tier to the Cool tier after 30 days without access, then deleted after 365 days. Which feature automates this data lifecycle?
options: Azure Policy
Manual scripts run by administrators
Soft delete
Azure Blob lifecycle management policies
explain: Lifecycle management policies define rule-based actions — tier to Cool/Archive or delete — triggered by age or last access. Policy governs resource configuration, soft delete only protects against accidental deletion, and manual scripts defeat the purpose of automation.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A financial firm must retain transaction records for seven years in a way that keeps them readable but impossible to modify or delete during the retention period, to satisfy regulators. Which feature meets this requirement?
options: Immutable blob storage with time-based retention (WORM)
The Cool access tier
Locally redundant storage (LRS)
Azure Files snapshots
explain: Immutable storage enforces write-once-read-many retention: data cannot be altered or deleted until retention expires. The Cool tier only changes pricing, LRS only changes redundancy, and snapshots are point-in-time copies that do not enforce immutability.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An administrator needs to copy 2 TB of files from an on-premises file server to Azure Blob storage over the internet as fast as possible. Which tool is purpose-built for high-performance data transfer to Azure Storage?
options: Azure Bastion
Remote Desktop
AzCopy
Azure Migrate
explain: AzCopy is the command-line utility optimized for fast, resumable transfers into and out of Azure Storage. Bastion and Remote Desktop provide admin access to machines, and Azure Migrate moves servers and workloads rather than bulk-copying files.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A software-as-a-service company hosts 200 small customer databases. Each database's usage is unpredictable, but total usage across all of them is stable — provisioning each database separately wastes capacity. What should it use?
options: 200 separate SQL Managed Instances
SQL Server on Azure virtual machines
Azure Cosmos DB
An Azure SQL elastic pool, so the databases share provisioned compute resources
explain: Elastic pools let many databases share a pool of resources, absorbing individual spikes within predictable totals. Separate instances or per-database provisioning pay for 200 peaks; Cosmos DB is a NoSQL/global-distribution service, not a SQL Server pool.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants to lift-and-shift its on-premises SQL Server to a fully managed PaaS database with near-100% compatibility — including SQL Agent jobs and cross-database queries — without managing virtual machines. Which service fits?
options: Azure SQL Database (single database)
Azure SQL Managed Instance
Azure Cosmos DB
Azure Database for PostgreSQL
explain: SQL Managed Instance is the PaaS option closest to on-premises SQL Server, supporting Agent jobs and cross-database queries. Single databases lack those features, Cosmos DB is multi-model NoSQL, and the PostgreSQL service is a different engine entirely.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A startup's application is built on PostgreSQL, and the team does not want to manage database servers, patching, or backups. Which Azure service fits BEST?
options: Azure Database for PostgreSQL — a fully managed PaaS database
PostgreSQL installed on Azure virtual machines
Azure Files
Azure SQL Managed Instance
explain: Azure Database for PostgreSQL is the managed PaaS service: Microsoft handles patching, backups, and high availability. Running PostgreSQL on VMs keeps all management with the team, Files is storage, and Managed Instance is SQL Server — the wrong engine.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company is migrating a MongoDB workload to a globally distributed Azure database and wants to avoid rewriting its application code. Which Azure Cosmos DB capability enables this?
options: Automatic indexing only
The Table API
Multi-model APIs, including a MongoDB-compatible API that works with existing drivers and queries
The Gremlin API only
explain: Cosmos DB exposes multiple wire-compatible APIs — MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table, and its core SQL API — so existing applications migrate with minimal changes. Indexing and any single non-Mongo API would not preserve the application's MongoDB code.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A retailer wants to combine its data warehouse with big-data analytics, running SQL queries over petabytes of data stored in a data lake. Which Azure analytics service is designed for this?
options: Azure Data Factory
Azure Cosmos DB
Power BI alone
Azure Synapse Analytics
explain: Synapse Analytics unifies data warehousing and big-data analytics, querying petabyte-scale data lakes with SQL. Data Factory orchestrates data movement (ETL), Cosmos DB is an operational database, and Power BI visualizes rather than processes at that scale.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company needs a scheduled pipeline that copies data nightly from on-premises SQL Server to Azure, transforms it, and loads it into a data warehouse. Which service orchestrates this ETL workflow?
options: Azure Logic Apps
Azure Data Factory
Azure Event Hubs
Azure Functions
explain: Data Factory is the data-integration service for building scheduled ETL/ELT pipelines. Logic Apps orchestrates business workflows across SaaS connectors, Event Hubs ingests streaming data, and Functions runs event-driven code — none is the ETL orchestrator.

q: A factory has 100,000 sensors each sending telemetry every second, and needs to ingest millions of events per second for real-time analytics. Which messaging service is built for this big-data streaming ingestion?

Azure Service Bus
Azure Event Grid
Azure Queue storage
explain: Event Hubs is the big-data streaming platform, ingesting millions of events per second. Service Bus is enterprise messaging with ordering and transactions, Event Grid routes discrete events to handlers, and Queue storage is simple message queuing.

q: A company wants its inventory system to react the instant a new order file lands in Blob storage — routing that event to both an Azure Function and a Logic App. Which service routes events from sources to handlers?
options: Azure Event Hubs
Azure Service Bus
Azure Event Grid
Azure IoT Hub
explain: Event Grid is the event-routing service: publishers emit events and Grid delivers them to subscribers like Functions and Logic Apps. Event Hubs ingests high-volume streams, Service Bus handles enterprise messaging, and IoT Hub connects devices.

Azure Service Bus
Azure Event Hubs
Azure Notification Hubs

Azure OpenAI Service
Azure AI Search

Azure Machine Learning
Azure Functions
Azure DevOps

Azure Cosmos DB
Azure AI Search
Azure Data Factory

Azure Sphere
Azure Notification Hubs
Azure IoT Hub

Azure IoT Central
Azure IoT Edge
Azure Digital Twins

Azure Arc
Azure Policy
Azure Blueprints

q: A developer needs to monitor a live web application's request rates, failure rates, and slow external dependencies to diagnose performance problems. Which Azure Monitor feature is built for application performance monitoring?
options: Log Analytics
Azure Advisor
Azure Service Health
Application Insights
explain: Application Insights is the APM feature: request telemetry, dependency tracking, and failure analysis for live apps. Log Analytics queries collected logs, Advisor gives optimization recommendations, and Service Health reports platform issues.

q: An operations team collects logs from virtual machines, containers, and Azure resources into a central workspace and needs to analyze them with a powerful query language. Which workspace — and language — do they use?
options: Application Insights with SQL
Microsoft Sentinel only
A Log Analytics workspace, queried with KQL (Kusto Query Language)
Azure Resource Graph
explain: Log Analytics workspaces centralize operational logs and are queried with KQL. Application Insights focuses on app telemetry, Sentinel is the SIEM built on top of Log Analytics, and Resource Graph queries resource inventory — not logs.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company needs to continuously replicate its Azure virtual machines to a secondary region so it can fail over within minutes during a regional outage — and fail back afterward. Which service orchestrates this disaster-recovery replication?
options: Azure Backup
Azure Site Recovery
Azure Migrate
Azure Traffic Manager
explain: Site Recovery orchestrates DR: continuous replication, planned failover, and failback. Backup restores data from recovery points, Migrate performs one-way migrations, and Traffic Manager routes user traffic via DNS — it does not replicate machines.
