q: A company wants automated daily backups of its Azure virtual machines with a 30-day retention policy, managed centrally. Which service and construct should it use?
options: Azure Backup with a Recovery Services vault and a backup policy
Azure Site Recovery
Manual disk snapshots only
Azure Files
explain: Azure Backup stores protected copies in a Recovery Services vault, with backup policies defining schedule and retention. Site Recovery is for disaster failover, manual snapshots do not scale or centralize, and Files is file storage.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company must run its virtual machines on physical hardware dedicated solely to its organization — never shared with other customers — to satisfy licensing and compliance requirements. Which option provides this?
options: Spot virtual machines
Availability zones
Azure Dedicated Host
B-series burstable virtual machines
explain: Dedicated Host provides a physical server devoted to one organization, so no other tenant shares the hardware. Spot VMs are cheap spare capacity, availability zones are separate datacenters, and B-series VMs are shared burstable sizes — none dedicates hardware.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team hosts its web app on Azure App Service and wants a staging slot to validate changes before swapping to production, plus automatic scaling. Which tier capability do they need?
options: Free tier
Shared tier
Basic tier
Standard tier or higher — deployment slots require Standard and above
explain: Deployment slots are a Standard-tier-and-above feature; Free and Shared tiers do not support them. Basic allows some scaling but no slots — a frequent exam trap for teams planning safe release workflows.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants partner organizations' employees to sign in to its Azure apps using their own company credentials, while customers signing up for its public web app use social accounts. Which Microsoft Entra External ID offerings map to these two scenarios?
options: Both scenarios use B2C
Partners: B2B collaboration; customers: B2C
Both require on-premises Active Directory
Partners use Privileged Identity Management
explain: B2B collaboration invites partner users to access your resources with their own identities; B2C provides customer-facing sign-up/sign-in with social and local accounts. B2B is not for public customers, and neither scenario requires on-premises AD or PIM.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company runs on-premises Active Directory and wants employees to sign in to Microsoft 365 with the same credentials, keeping identities synchronized to the cloud. Which tool provides this hybrid identity synchronization?
options: Microsoft Entra Connect
Azure Arc
Azure AD B2C
Azure Key Vault
explain: Entra Connect synchronizes on-premises AD users, groups, and password hashes to Entra ID for hybrid sign-in. Arc manages hybrid infrastructure, B2C serves external customers, and Key Vault stores secrets — none syncs directory identities.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants to domain-join Azure virtual machines and apply Group Policy without deploying and managing its own domain controllers on VMs. Which managed service provides this?
options: Microsoft Entra Connect
Azure Bastion
Azure DNS
Microsoft Entra Domain Services
explain: Entra Domain Services offers managed domain-join, LDAP, and Group Policy without running domain controllers. Entra Connect syncs identities, Bastion provides secure VM admin access, and DNS resolves names — none delivers managed domain services.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A security team wants automatic detection of risky sign-ins — such as leaked credentials or impossible-travel logins — with policies that can block or step up authentication in response. Which Microsoft Entra ID feature provides this risk-based protection?
options: Single sign-on
Access reviews
Microsoft Entra Identity Protection
Self-service password reset
explain: Identity Protection detects sign-in and user risk and automates remediation through risk policies (a P2 capability). SSO simplifies sign-in, access reviews recertify access, and self-service password reset helps locked-out users — none detects risky sign-ins.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company gives guest users access to a project site and wants managers to periodically confirm each guest still needs access, automatically removing those who no longer do. Which feature automates this recertification?
options: Conditional Access
Microsoft Entra access reviews
Privileged Identity Management
Resource locks
explain: Access reviews schedule recurring recertification of guest and user access, removing access that reviewers deny. Conditional Access controls sign-in conditions, PIM manages just-in-time admin roles, and locks protect resources from changes.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Employees who get locked out at midnight need to reset their own passwords after verifying with an authenticator app, instead of waiting for the help desk to open. Which feature enables this?
options: Privileged Identity Management
Identity Protection
Conditional Access
Self-service password reset (SSPR)
explain: SSPR lets users reset passwords themselves after proving identity through registered verification methods. PIM manages admin role elevation, Identity Protection handles sign-in risk, and Conditional Access enforces access policies — none resets passwords.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An application running on an Azure virtual machine needs to read secrets from Azure Key Vault, but the security team forbids storing any credentials in code or configuration files. What should the application use?
options: A managed identity — Azure gives the app its own Entra identity, so no credentials need to be stored
A shared administrator password in the config file
A hardcoded connection string
Anonymous access to the vault
explain: Managed identities provide Azure resources with an Entra identity and handle credential rotation automatically — nothing secret lives in code. Shared passwords, hardcoded strings, and anonymous access are exactly the anti-patterns Key Vault plus managed identities eliminate.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company needs one identity shared across several Azure resources (VMs and Functions) with a lifecycle independent of any single resource, so deleting one VM does not remove the identity. Which managed identity type fits?
options: System-assigned managed identity
A service principal with a client secret
User-assigned managed identity
A guest user account
explain: User-assigned identities are standalone resources with their own lifecycle and can be attached to multiple Azure resources. System-assigned identities die with their resource, service principals require secret management, and guest accounts are for external users.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A user has the Reader role at the subscription scope, and is then granted the Contributor role scoped to a single resource group. What can the user do inside that resource group?
options: Only read resources — the subscription-level role wins
Create, modify, and delete resources in that resource group — role assignments are additive, so the narrower Contributor grant applies there
Nothing — conflicting assignments cancel out
Manage access for other users
explain: RBAC is additive: effective permissions are the union of all assignments, and the resource-group-scoped Contributor grants full resource management within that group. The narrower scope does not override the wider one — they combine. Managing access still requires Owner or User Access Administrator.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants to guarantee that even subscription Owners cannot delete a critical production database. Which mechanism overrides allow-assignments — even Owner?
options: An Azure RBAC deny assignment — deny takes precedence over allow
Assigning everyone the Reader role
Applying a resource tag
A policy with the audit effect
explain: Deny assignments explicitly block actions and take precedence over any allow, including Owner. Reader alone cannot stop an Owner, tags organize without enforcing, and audit-effect policies only report non-compliance.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A user with the Reader role on a storage account can see the account in the portal but gets an authorization error when trying to open blob files. Why?
options: The Reader role is broken
The user needs the Owner role
The storage account is offline
Reader grants management-plane access only; reading blob data requires a data-plane role such as Storage Blob Data Reader
explain: Azure has two permission planes: management plane (manage the resource) and data plane (access the data inside). Reader covers the management plane; blob contents need a data role like Storage Blob Data Reader. Owner is overkill, and the account is not offline — the portal lists it fine.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company needs a role that can restart virtual machines but cannot delete them or manage access — and no built-in role matches exactly. What should it create?
options: An Azure Policy
A management group
A custom RBAC role, defined in JSON with precisely the allowed actions
A resource lock
explain: Custom roles define exact permission sets (actions, notActions, assignable scopes) in JSON for least-privilege needs no built-in role covers. Policies govern resource configuration, management groups scope governance, and locks prevent changes rather than granting granular rights.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants non-compliant resources flagged in the compliance dashboard but NOT blocked, so teams can remediate gradually without breaking deployments. Which policy effect should it use?
options: Deny
Audit
Append
Modify
explain: The audit effect reports non-compliance without blocking anything — ideal for gradual rollouts. Deny would block deployments, while append and modify change resource properties rather than simply flagging violations.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company requires every virtual machine to have the monitoring agent installed, and wants Azure to automatically install it on any VM missing it. Which policy effect enables this automatic remediation?
options: Audit
Deny
Disabled
DeployIfNotExists — with a remediation task that deploys the missing configuration
explain: DeployIfNotExists evaluates resources and deploys the required configuration (via a remediation task) when it is absent. Audit only flags, deny only blocks new non-compliant deployments, and disabled turns the policy off — none remediates.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A policy denying public storage accounts is assigned at the subscription scope, but one legacy application needs a six-month exception for a single storage account. How can the company exclude just that account?
options: Create a policy exemption scoped to that storage account
Delete the policy assignment entirely
Move the storage account to another tenant
Assign the Reader role to the application team
explain: Exemptions (and exclusions) carve out specific scopes from a policy assignment, optionally with an expiration. Deleting the policy removes protection everywhere, moving tenants is drastic and unnecessary, and RBAC roles do not affect policy evaluation.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A CanNotDelete lock protects a production resource group, but an urgent migration requires deleting it. Who is able to remove the lock?
options: Any user with the Reader role
Any user with the Contributor role
Only users who can manage locks — such as Owners or User Access Administrators
Nobody — locks are permanent once applied
explain: Removing a lock requires the Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* permission, which Owner and User Access Administrator hold — Contributor does not. Locks are never permanent; they are designed to be removable by sufficiently privileged users.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company applies CostCenter and Environment tags to a resource group, expecting every current and future resource inside it to inherit those tags for billing. What actually happens?
options: Tags inherit automatically to all resources in the group
Tags do NOT inherit automatically — they must be applied per resource, or enforced with Azure Policy
Only virtual machines inherit the tags
Tags apply retroactively to already-deleted resources
explain: Resource groups do not propagate tags to their contents — a very common misconception. Tag each resource directly, or use Azure Policy (append/modify effects) to require and auto-apply tags. Nothing inherits silently, and deleted resources are out of scope entirely.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A finance analyst wants to see last month's cloud spending grouped by the Department tag so costs can be charged back to each department. Which Cost Management capability provides this?
options: Cost analysis with grouping and filtering by tag
The Azure pricing calculator
Azure Advisor
The TCO calculator
explain: Cost analysis slices actual spending by dimensions including tags, resource groups, and services — the chargeback workflow. The pricing calculator estimates future costs, Advisor recommends optimizations, and the TCO calculator compares on-premises with cloud.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants its development VMs automatically shut down when the monthly budget forecast reaches 100% — not just an email warning. How can budgets drive this automation?
options: Budgets can only send emails; automation is impossible
Purchase reservations instead
Ask Azure Advisor to shut them down
Configure the budget alert with an action group that triggers an automation runbook or Logic App
explain: Budget alerts support action groups, which can invoke runbooks, Logic Apps, or webhooks — turning a spending threshold into automated remediation. Alerts alone only notify; reservations and Advisor do not react to budget thresholds.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants discounted compute pricing with a one-year commitment, but its VM sizes and regions change frequently as projects evolve. Which option gives discounts with flexibility across VM families, sizes, and regions?
options: Reserved virtual machine instances scoped to one size and region
Spot virtual machines
An Azure savings plan for compute
Pay-as-you-go pricing
explain: Savings plans commit to an hourly spend amount rather than specific VMs, so the discount follows usage across sizes, families, and regions. Reservations lock to a scope, Spot VMs can be evicted, and pay-as-you-go carries no discount.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A development team with Visual Studio subscriptions wants discounted Azure rates for its non-production dev and test workloads. Which offer is designed for this?
options: Azure Hybrid Benefit
Azure Dev/Test pricing
Spot virtual machines only
The Azure free account only

domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A student wants to learn Azure hands-on. Which statement about the Azure free account is TRUE?
options: Every Azure service is free forever
It requires no payment method and includes a $500 credit
It is only available to enterprise customers
It includes 12 months of popular services free, a $200 credit for the first 30 days, and 55+ always-free services
explain: The free account bundles 12 months of free popular services, a $200 credit usable in the first 30 days, and 55+ services free within limits every month. It is available to individuals, requires a payment method for identity verification, and most services are metered beyond the free quantities.

q: Azure misses a service's SLA in a given month. How does the customer actually receive the service credit defined in the SLA?
options: The customer must submit a claim requesting the credit — it is not applied automatically
Microsoft automatically refunds the customer's bank account
The credit arrives as cash by mail
Credits apply automatically to the next invoice
explain: SLA service credits must be claimed by the customer following the process in the SLA terms; they are issued as credits against future Azure consumption, not automatic refunds or cash. Assuming automatic compensation is the exam trap.

q: A team builds a production workload on an Azure service that is still in public preview because it has attractive features. What should the team understand about SLAs for preview services?
options: Preview services carry higher SLAs than generally available ones
Preview services have the same SLA as generally available services
Preview and beta services are excluded from SLAs — there is no uptime commitment
The SLA doubles during the preview period
explain: SLAs apply only to generally available services; preview features are provided as-is with no uptime commitment. Building production workloads on preview services means accepting that risk — a key governance consideration.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants its Azure Storage data encrypted at rest but does not want to manage encryption keys itself. What happens by default?
options: Data sits unencrypted until the customer configures encryption
Storage Service Encryption automatically encrypts the data with Microsoft-managed keys
The company must store keys in Key Vault first
Only premium storage accounts encrypt data
explain: Azure Storage encrypts all data at rest by default using Microsoft-managed keys — no action required. Key Vault enters the picture only when the customer wants to manage its own keys (CMK), and encryption applies across performance tiers.

q: A bank requires that it — not Microsoft — controls the encryption keys protecting its storage accounts, with the keys safeguarded in a hardened vault. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Customer-managed keys stored in Azure Key Vault (or Managed HSM)
Microsoft-managed keys
Disabling encryption at rest
Storing the keys in Blob storage
explain: Customer-managed keys (CMK) let the customer own key lifecycle — creation, rotation, revocation — with keys protected in Key Vault or Managed HSM. Microsoft-managed keys keep control with the provider, disabling encryption violates the requirement, and storing keys alongside data defeats the purpose.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants RDP and SSH ports on its virtual machines closed by default, opened only temporarily upon an approved request, to shrink its attack surface. Which Microsoft Defender for Cloud feature provides this just-in-time access?
options: Network security groups
Azure Firewall
DDoS Network Protection
Just-in-time (JIT) VM access
explain: JIT VM access locks down management ports and opens them only for approved, time-bound requests with auditing. NSGs and Firewall filter traffic but do not provide the approval workflow; DDoS Protection mitigates volumetric attacks.

q: A CISO enables Microsoft Defender for Cloud and wants active threat protection for servers — not just security posture recommendations. What must the organization do?
options: Nothing — the free tier includes full threat protection
Enable a Defender plan (such as Defender for Servers) — the free tier covers posture management; workload protection plans are paid
Deploy Microsoft Sentinel instead
Create an Azure Policy
explain: Defender for Cloud's free tier provides cloud security posture management (CSPM) and Secure Score; threat protection for workloads requires enabling paid Defender plans per resource type. Sentinel is the separate SIEM/SOAR, and Policy enforces configuration rather than detecting threats.

q: A security analyst wants to hunt for threats across collected logs using a query language, and automatically isolate compromised virtual machines through a response workflow. Which Microsoft Sentinel capabilities support this?
options: ARM templates
Cost analysis views
KQL queries for hunting plus automation rules and playbooks (built on Logic Apps)
Update Manager
explain: Sentinel analysts hunt with KQL and automate response through playbooks powered by Logic Apps — the SOAR half of the solution. ARM templates deploy infrastructure, cost analysis tracks spending, and Update Manager patches machines.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A developer can see a key vault in the portal but gets 'access denied' when code tries to read a secret. The vault is configured to use Azure RBAC for authorization. Which role grants read access to secret values?
options: Reader
Contributor
Key Vault Secrets User
Owner
explain: Key Vault has data-plane roles: Key Vault Secrets User reads secret values, while Reader and Contributor are management-plane roles that cannot see secret contents. Owner is excessive — least privilege points to the purpose-built data role.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A customer wants to read Microsoft's general statements on cloud security, privacy, and compliance principles — not download audit certificates. Where should they go?
options: The Microsoft Trust Center
The Service Trust Portal
The Azure status page
The Azure pricing calculator
explain: The Trust Center is the public information site covering Microsoft's security, privacy, and compliance approach. The Service Trust Portal hosts downloadable audit reports and certifications; the status page shows service health; the calculator estimates costs.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A compliance officer wants to track the organization's compliance posture against standards like ISO 27001 and GDPR, with a score and prioritized improvement actions. Which tool is built for this?
options: Azure Advisor
Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager
Microsoft Defender for Cloud
Microsoft Cost Management
explain: Compliance Manager assesses and tracks compliance against regulatory templates with improvement actions and scoring. Advisor optimizes Azure resources, Defender for Cloud covers security posture, and Cost Management tracks spending.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Which statement about customer data in Azure reflects Microsoft's privacy commitments?
options: Microsoft mines customer data to serve advertising
Microsoft takes ownership of customer data stored in Azure
Customer data remains the customer's — Microsoft does not use it for advertising and processes it only to provide the service
Customer data is shared publicly by default
explain: Microsoft's privacy commitments state that customers own their data: it is not used for advertising or shared without instruction, and processing follows the customer's direction. The distractors describe the opposite of the documented commitments.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A CFO is nervous about cloud costs swinging wildly month to month and about performance varying under load. Which combination of cloud capabilities BEST delivers the predictability the CFO wants?
options: Buying the largest virtual machines available in every region
Autoscaling to absorb demand spikes plus budgets and cost alerts to keep spending stable
Running all workloads on a single virtual machine
Disabling all monitoring to reduce service charges
explain: Predictability comes from elasticity handling demand automatically and governance tools (budgets, alerts, policies) keeping cost and configuration stable. Oversized VMs waste money without guaranteeing stability, a single VM is a single point of failure, and disabling monitoring removes the visibility predictability depends on.

q: An architect is choosing where to host a critical ordering system. One option is a single on-premises server; the other is an Azure service backed by a published SLA with built-in redundancy. The Azure option's ability to recover from failures and keep functioning demonstrates which cloud benefit?
options: Reliability — the system keeps working through failures thanks to redundancy and SLA-backed design
Agility — the system can be rebuilt from scratch in minutes
Geo-distribution — the system runs on every continent
Consumption pricing — the system costs nothing when idle
explain: Reliability is the ability of a system to recover from failures and continue to function, supported by redundancy and SLAs. Agility is speed of change, geo-distribution is about location, and consumption pricing is a billing model — none describe failure recovery.

q: A company runs 800 virtual machines. Instead of logging into each one, administrators manage them all from a single portal, automate tasks with templates, and monitor everything centrally. This reflects which cloud benefit?
options: Fault tolerance
Multitenancy
Manageability — centralized, automated control of resources at scale
Data sovereignty
explain: Manageability means administering cloud resources centrally — one portal, APIs, and infrastructure-as-code instead of per-server manual work. Fault tolerance is about surviving failures, multitenancy is shared infrastructure, and data sovereignty is about data location.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A bank's regulators require that every database be encrypted and every virtual machine carry an owner tag. The bank wants these rules enforced automatically on every deployment, with violations flagged. Which cloud benefit or capability delivers this?
options: Elasticity
High availability
Consumption-based pricing
Governance — using tools like Azure Policy and templates to enforce organizational standards automatically
explain: Governance is about enforcing standards — Azure Policy can require encryption and tags, blocking or flagging non-compliant resources. Elasticity scales capacity, high availability keeps systems running, and pricing models don't enforce configuration rules.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A small fintech startup must prove to enterprise customers that its infrastructure meets strict security standards. By hosting on Azure, it can point to Microsoft's published certifications and audited datacenter controls. This illustrates which cloud benefit?
options: Security — customers inherit the provider's massive security investments and compliance certifications
Serverless computing
Vertical scaling
Community cloud
explain: A major cloud benefit is leveraging the provider's security scale — dedicated teams, audited controls, and certifications no small company could build alone. Serverless and vertical scaling are architecture choices, and community cloud is a deployment model, not a security benefit.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company with steady, unchanging workloads compares five years of cloud bills against buying servers. The analysis shows the cloud total is higher over five years. Which statement BEST explains this outcome?
options: Cloud bills are always a bad deal
The company should never use the cloud for anything
OpEx trades large upfront CapEx for ongoing payments — for flat, predictable workloads, owning hardware can cost less over time
Consumption pricing charges for resources that are turned off
explain: OpEx eliminates upfront commitment but the meter never stops — steady 24/7 workloads can be cheaper to own outright, which is why reservations exist to close the gap. Blanket statements like 'always a bad deal' are not analysis, and consumption pricing stops billing deallocated compute.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company wants a custom-built customer portal where its developers write all the business logic, but nobody will manage servers, operating systems, or runtime patching. Which service model fits BEST?
options: Infrastructure as a Service
Platform as a Service — developers own the code while the provider manages servers, OS, and runtime
Software as a Service
On-premises virtualization
explain: PaaS is the model where you bring custom code and the provider manages everything underneath. IaaS would leave OS patching to the team, SaaS provides finished software you can't customize at the code level, and on-premises keeps all management in-house.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company rolls out a SaaS CRM to 200 salespeople. IT installs nothing; users sign in through a browser, and new features appear automatically each month. Which SaaS characteristic makes the zero-install rollout possible?
options: Each laptop needs a perpetual license key
The company must patch the application servers monthly
Users need VPN access to the vendor's datacenter
The software runs in the provider's cloud and is delivered over the internet — no local installation or server patching
explain: SaaS is centrally hosted by the provider and consumed over the internet, so there is nothing to install or patch on the customer side. Perpetual license keys and self-patching describe traditional software, and SaaS needs no VPN into the vendor's datacenter.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A photo-sharing app uses a serverless function to generate thumbnails. On a normal day it runs a few hundred times; after a viral post it runs two million times in an hour — with no configuration change and no idle servers in between. Which serverless characteristic does this demonstrate?
options: Reserved capacity planning
Manual server provisioning
Automatic scaling from zero to massive throughput with pay-per-execution billing
Fixed monthly pricing regardless of usage
explain: Serverless platforms scale executions automatically — from zero when idle to enormous concurrency under load — and bill per execution. Reserved capacity and manual provisioning are the opposite of serverless, and fixed monthly pricing contradicts pay-per-use.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company is migrating virtual machines to Azure but must keep its existing OS-level backup agents, monitoring agents, and custom kernel modules. Which service model supports this?
options: Infrastructure as a Service — full OS control lets the company keep its agents and kernel modules
Software as a Service
Platform as a Service
Serverless computing
explain: Only IaaS gives OS-level access for custom agents and kernel modules. PaaS and serverless hide the OS entirely, and SaaS offers no place to run custom infrastructure agents.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs SQL Server on Azure virtual machines (IaaS) and configures an Always On availability group between two VMs. Who is responsible for configuring and maintaining this database-level high availability?
options: Microsoft, because the VMs run in Azure
The customer — in IaaS, everything from the OS upward, including application-level clustering, is the customer's job
The virtual network
Nobody; Azure configures it automatically
explain: IaaS draws the responsibility line at the virtualization layer: Microsoft provides the VMs and network, but OS-level clustering and application configuration belong to the customer. Azure doesn't auto-configure guest-level clustering, and the network is just connectivity.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A team deploys a custom web app to Azure App Service (PaaS). A vulnerability is found in the team's own application code. Who must fix it?
options: Microsoft, because App Service is a managed platform
The internet service provider
Nobody — PaaS apps can't have vulnerabilities
The customer — the provider secures the platform, but the customer's code is the customer's responsibility
explain: PaaS splits responsibility cleanly: Microsoft patches the OS and runtime, but application code — including its vulnerabilities — is always the customer's. The 'nobody' option tests the myth that managed platforms eliminate all customer security duties.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company uses a SaaS email service. An employee leaves, but IT forgets to disable the ex-employee's mailbox for a month. Who is responsible for managing user access to the SaaS application?
options: The customer — identities and access management are always the customer's responsibility, in every service model
The SaaS provider
The email protocol designers
The domain registrar
explain: Under the shared responsibility model, data and identity/access are always the customer's — even in SaaS where the provider manages the application. The provider secures the service itself; who may use it is the customer's decision and duty.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's relational database is struggling, and the database cannot easily be split across multiple servers. The architect adds CPU and memory to the existing database server. This approach is:
options: Horizontal scaling
Elasticity
Vertical scaling (scaling up) — the right call for stateful workloads that can't be distributed
Geo-distribution
explain: Adding resources to one instance is vertical scaling, often the practical choice for stateful systems like databases that resist distribution. Horizontal scaling adds instances, elasticity is the automatic aspect, and geo-distribution is about location.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A stateless web application scales out to 12 identical instances. Users must be spread evenly across them, and traffic must avoid any instance that fails. What must sit in front of the instances?
options: A larger database
A load balancer — scaling out only works when traffic is distributed and unhealthy instances are removed
A longer backup retention policy
A second cloud provider
explain: Scale-out requires a load balancer to distribute requests and health-probe instances so failures don't receive traffic. A bigger database doesn't distribute web traffic, backups don't route requests, and a second provider adds complexity without solving distribution.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's internal reporting portal is heavily used 8 AM–6 PM on weekdays and idle nights and weekends. The architect configures the system to run extra instances on weekday mornings and remove them each evening on a schedule. This is an example of:
options: Vertical scaling
Disaster recovery
High availability
Elasticity — capacity expanding and contracting to match demand, here driven by a schedule rather than live metrics
explain: Elasticity is resources growing and shrinking with demand — it can be triggered by schedules as well as live metrics. Vertical scaling resizes one instance, disaster recovery restores after outages, and high availability is about surviving failures.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An architect explains two designs: Design X keeps the checkout service running with zero interruption when a single server fails. Design Y restores the whole datacenter's workloads in another region after a regional disaster. These designs respectively demonstrate:
options: Fault tolerance (surviving component failure without interruption) and disaster recovery (restoring operations after a major outage)
Disaster recovery and fault tolerance, in that order
Elasticity and scalability
Two unrelated concepts with no formal names
explain: Fault tolerance = no single component failure interrupts service; disaster recovery = a plan to restore operations after a large-scale outage. The reversed order is the trap, elasticity/scalability are about capacity, and both concepts are formally named.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company backs up its databases nightly and assumes it is protected against a regional outage. Its architect says backups alone are not a disaster recovery plan. What ELSE does a real DR plan require?
options: More backups of the same database
A faster internet connection
A secondary location to recover into, documented recovery procedures, assigned roles, and regular testing
Cheaper storage
explain: Backups are only data copies — DR needs a recovery target (like a paired region), written runbooks, clear ownership, and tested rehearsals. More copies of the same backup don't create a recovery site, and bandwidth or cheaper storage don't substitute for a plan.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company demands near-zero data loss (RPO of minutes) and recovery within an hour (RTO) for its trading system, but accepts 24-hour RPO/RTO for its internal wiki. What does this difference reflect?
options: The wiki is more important than the trading system
Tighter RPO/RTO targets cost more — aggressive recovery objectives require expensive replication and automation, so they are set per workload criticality
RPO and RTO are only defined for wikis
Recovery objectives are free regardless of target
explain: Lower RPO (less data loss) and RTO (faster recovery) demand costly mechanisms like synchronous replication and hot standbys — so targets are matched to each workload's business criticality. Trading justifies the spend; the wiki doesn't. Recovery objectives are never free.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A retailer runs its storefront in two Azure regions simultaneously, with traffic split between both. When one region has problems, the other is already serving customers. This is an example of:
options: Active-passive disaster recovery
A single point of failure
Vertical scaling
An active-active design — both regions serve traffic, giving better utilization and faster failover than a standby region
explain: Active-active means all regions handle live traffic, so failover is near-instant and no capacity sits idle. Active-passive keeps one region on standby; this isn't a single point of failure or a scaling technique.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Microsoft states that Azure operates in more datacenter regions than any other cloud provider. For a company launching a product on five continents, what is the practical value of this footprint?
options: More regions mean more choices to place workloads near users for low latency and to meet data-residency rules
It guarantees the lowest price
It means servers never fail
It eliminates the need for any network design
explain: A large region footprint gives placement flexibility: low latency by running near users, and compliance by keeping data in required geographies. Region count doesn't set prices, prevent failures, or remove the need for network architecture.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A mining company operates a remote site with unreliable internet and strict rules that sensor data must be processed locally. It still wants Azure services and the same management tools as its cloud workloads. Which offering fits?
options: A second public cloud provider
More on-premises virtual machines with no cloud connection
Azure Stack — Azure services running in the company's own datacenter for disconnected or regulated scenarios
A content delivery network
explain: Azure Stack brings Azure services into your own datacenter for scenarios needing local processing or disconnected operation. Another public cloud doesn't solve local processing, plain VMs lack Azure services, and a CDN only caches content.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company keeps all production servers on-premises but replicates backups to Azure and can restore workloads there if its datacenter is lost. This architecture is an example of:
options: A purely private cloud
A hybrid cloud — on-premises infrastructure combined with public cloud services for backup and recovery
A multicloud strategy
Serverless computing
explain: Using public cloud as the recovery target for on-premises workloads mixes both models — the definition of hybrid. It's not purely private since Azure is involved, not multicloud (only one public provider), and backup replication isn't serverless.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company adopts a multicloud strategy to avoid vendor lock-in. Six months later, its engineers complain about duplicated tooling, inconsistent security controls, and skill gaps across platforms. What does this illustrate?
options: Multicloud has no downsides
The company should abandon the cloud entirely
Vendor lock-in is legally required
A real tradeoff of multicloud — resilience and choice come at the cost of operational complexity
explain: Multicloud reduces dependence on one provider but multiplies operational surface: more tools, more skills, harder consistent governance. 'No downsides' ignores reality, abandoning cloud isn't the lesson, and lock-in is a business risk to manage, not a legal requirement.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company moves from its own datacenter to the public cloud. Which statement honestly describes a tradeoff of this move?
options: The company gains elasticity and freedom from hardware management but gives up direct control over the physical infrastructure
The company keeps full physical control of all servers
Security becomes the provider's problem entirely
There are no tradeoffs in cloud adoption
explain: Public cloud trades direct infrastructure control for elasticity and freedom from hardware — that's the core bargain. You don't keep physical control, security remains shared (never 'entirely' the provider's), and every architecture has tradeoffs.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Several neighboring city governments build a shared cloud platform that meets municipal record-keeping regulations, separate from the provider's commercial customers. This deployment model is:
options: Public cloud
Private cloud
Community cloud — infrastructure shared by organizations with common compliance and policy concerns
Hybrid cloud
explain: A community cloud serves organizations with shared concerns — here, municipal regulations — on infrastructure separate from the general public. Public cloud is open to all, private is one organization, and hybrid mixes models rather than sharing one.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A CIO believes moving to a private cloud will eliminate hardware refresh costs and give public-cloud-like elasticity. What should the architect tell the CIO?
options: The CIO is entirely correct
Private cloud still requires buying and refreshing hardware, and capacity is limited to what was purchased — elasticity is constrained
Private clouds are free to operate
Private cloud automatically includes a second public provider
explain: Private cloud keeps the hardware ownership burden — you buy, house, and refresh the servers, and you can only scale to what you bought. The honest tradeoff is control and isolation, not cost elimination or unlimited elasticity.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Which of the following is a capital expenditure (CapEx)?
options: A monthly cloud subscription bill
Hourly virtual machine charges
Electricity for a rented office
Purchasing $150,000 of physical servers for the company datacenter
explain: CapEx is upfront investment in physical assets owned by the company — servers you buy and depreciate. Monthly bills and hourly charges are OpEx, and office electricity is an operating cost, not a capital asset.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: In a public cloud, many customers' virtual machines run on the same physical servers. What keeps one customer's workloads isolated from another's?
options: The hypervisor and platform-level isolation enforce strict boundaries between tenants
Customers can see each other's data by default
Physical servers are never shared between customers
Isolation is impossible in a shared cloud
explain: Multitenancy relies on the hypervisor and platform controls to isolate tenants sharing physical hardware — that isolation is a core provider responsibility. Customers never see each other's data, and sharing hardware is the whole point of the model.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A developer says, 'With serverless, there are no servers, so it must be more secure automatically.' What is wrong with this statement?
options: Nothing — the statement is fully correct
Servers still exist and are managed by the provider — 'serverless' means no server management, not no servers, and security still requires proper code and configuration
Serverless is slower than all alternatives
Serverless cannot run in production
explain: Serverless abstracts server management; the servers are real and run by the provider. Security is never automatic — your code, permissions, and configuration are still your responsibility in every model.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Which service model gives the customer the MOST control over the computing environment, and what is the cost of that control?
options: SaaS — most control, least management
Serverless — most control
PaaS — most control
IaaS — most control, but the customer takes on the most management responsibility (OS, patching, middleware)
explain: Control and management move together: IaaS gives the most control because you manage the OS upward. SaaS and serverless minimize management precisely by removing control; PaaS sits in the middle.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs a VM for exactly 6 hours and 23 minutes, then deletes it. Its bill reflects precisely that usage. This granularity illustrates:
options: Flat-rate pricing
Perpetual licensing
Measured service — usage is metered and billed with fine granularity
Capital expenditure
explain: Measured service means the provider meters exactly what you consume and bills accordingly — down to minutes or seconds. Flat-rate and perpetual licensing charge regardless of use, and CapEx is about asset ownership.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's Azure SQL Database automatically adds compute capacity during month-end reporting and scales back down afterward, with no administrator action. This demonstrates:
options: Elasticity applied to a PaaS database — automatic scaling with demand, not just for virtual machines
Manual vertical scaling
Disaster recovery
Geo-distribution
explain: Elasticity isn't limited to VMs — PaaS services like Azure SQL Database can scale compute automatically with demand. Manual scaling requires administrator action, disaster recovery is about outages, and geo-distribution is about location.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A startup has an idea on Monday, provisions a global test environment on Tuesday, runs a pilot with real users on Friday, and shuts it all down the next week after learning the idea won't work — spending almost nothing. Which cloud benefit made this possible?
options: Fault tolerance
Agility — rapid provisioning and deprovisioning lets the business experiment fast and cheaply
Data sovereignty
Reserved capacity
explain: Agility is the business benefit of provisioning speed: try ideas in days, kill failures cheaply, keep winners. Fault tolerance is about surviving failures, data sovereignty about location, and reserved capacity is a pricing commitment — the opposite of this flexibility.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An architect designs a solution using a new Azure service, then discovers it isn't offered in the company's preferred region. What is the correct takeaway?
options: All Azure services are available in all regions
The architect should deploy anyway and hope it appears
Regions are only about latency
Not every service is available in every region — service availability must be verified during region selection, alongside latency and compliance
explain: New and specialized services roll out to regions gradually, so region selection must check service availability plus latency and data-residency needs. Assuming universal availability is a classic design mistake.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company deploys a zone-redundant Azure SQL Database. What does 'zone-redundant' mean here?
options: Azure automatically replicates the database across availability zones, so a datacenter failure doesn't cause data loss or extended downtime
The database runs in only one datacenter
The company must manually copy data between zones
Zone-redundant means the database is paused
explain: Zone-redundant services spread replicas across a region's availability zones automatically — the platform handles replication and failover. Single-datacenter deployment is zonal, manual copying defeats the purpose, and redundancy has nothing to do with pausing.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants its disaster-recovery region to be a specific region of its choosing, paired with its primary. What should it know about Azure region pairs?
options: Customers can pair any two regions freely
Region pairs change every month
Each Azure region has a fixed, pre-defined pair within the same geography — the pairing cannot be customized
Region pairs are only for storage accounts
explain: Region pairs are static and defined by Microsoft, generally within the same geography for data-residency purposes. You choose which regions to deploy to, but you can't redefine the pairings — and pairs benefit platform updates and DR for many services, not just storage.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A commercial gaming company wants to deploy in Azure Government regions to get extra security. What will it discover?
options: Anyone can deploy there
Azure Government is restricted to US government entities and partners serving them — commercial customers use the global Azure cloud
It is cheaper than global Azure
It has no compliance certifications
explain: Sovereign clouds like Azure Government require eligibility validation — they're isolated environments for government workloads, not premium tiers anyone can buy. Commercial customers get the same security tooling in the global cloud.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A global enterprise designs its management group hierarchy: root, then geography, then country, then business unit, then environment — five levels deep. Is this allowed?
options: No — only one level is allowed
No — subscriptions can't sit under management groups
Yes, but policies can't be assigned above subscriptions
Yes — management groups support up to six levels of depth, and policies assigned high up inherit downward
explain: Management group trees support up to six levels, and assignments (Policy, RBAC) inherit down to every subscription below. Subscriptions sit under management groups by design — that's the whole point of the hierarchy.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team's deployment fails with an error that the subscription has reached its limit of virtual machine cores in a region. What is the right response?
options: Request a quota increase for the subscription — quotas are adjustable limits, not hard technical ceilings
Delete the subscription
Quotas can never be changed
Move to a different cloud provider immediately
explain: Subscription quotas (cores, resources per region) are guardrails you can raise via a support request. Deleting the subscription or switching providers over an adjustable limit is drastic and unnecessary.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company reorganizes and wants to move a virtual machine from the 'Dev' resource group to the 'Prod' resource group in the same subscription, with no downtime. What should it know?
options: Resources can never move between resource groups
Moving requires rebuilding the VM
Most Azure resources can be moved between resource groups and subscriptions, though some services have limitations to check first
The VM must be deleted first
explain: Azure supports moving most resources across resource groups and subscriptions without rebuilds — but a few services restrict moves, so checking limitations first is the professional step. 'Never' and 'must delete' are both wrong.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An administrator deploys an ARM template in Complete mode to a resource group containing extra resources from old experiments. What happens to those extra resources?
options: They are left untouched
Complete mode deletes resources in the group that aren't defined in the template — unlike Incremental mode, which leaves them
They are automatically upgraded
The deployment fails
explain: Complete mode makes the resource group match the template exactly, deleting anything extra — powerful but dangerous in shared groups. Incremental (the default) only adds or updates. Knowing the difference is a must before touching production.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Before deploying a template that modifies production networking, an engineer wants to preview exactly what will change without changing anything. Which ARM feature does this?
options: Complete mode
Template specs
Bicep decompile
The what-if operation — it previews changes without applying them
explain: The what-if operation shows the create/modify/delete/ignore outcome of a deployment before it runs — the safe way to review production changes. Complete mode is a deployment behavior, template specs store templates, and decompile converts formats.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team inherits verbose ARM JSON templates and wants the conciseness of Bicep going forward. What is the most practical path?
options: Use Bicep's decompile capability to convert the existing ARM JSON into Bicep files, then maintain the Bicep
Rewrite everything from memory
Bicep cannot work with existing templates
Delete all templates and start over
explain: Bicep can decompile ARM JSON into Bicep files, giving a clean migration path from legacy templates. Rewriting from memory risks errors, and deleting working infrastructure code is never the practical answer.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company runs a database on an Azure VM. The architect places the database files on a separate data disk rather than the OS disk. Why?
options: OS disks are free
Data disks are slower
Separating OS and data disks allows independent sizing, performance tuning, and backup policies — the OS disk holds the operating system, data disks hold application data
Azure requires exactly one disk per VM
explain: Every VM has one OS disk; data disks are separate managed disks for application data, letting you size, tune, and back them up independently. VMs can attach many data disks, and neither disk type is free.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An older deployment guide references 'unmanaged disks' stored in a storage account the team manages. What should a new architect know?
options: Unmanaged disks are the recommended modern approach
Managed disks — where Azure handles the underlying storage accounts — are the modern standard; unmanaged disks are legacy
Disks no longer exist in Azure
Unmanaged disks perform better
explain: Managed disks abstract away storage account management (no more manual account juggling or limits), and are the current standard. Unmanaged disks are the legacy model — still functional, but not what new designs should use.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A developer needs a cheap VM for a test environment that idles most of the day but occasionally bursts. Which VM series fits, and why?
options: Memory-optimized E-series
GPU N-series
Storage-optimized L-series
B-series burstable VMs — they accumulate credits while idle and burst when needed, ideal for variable dev/test workloads
explain: B-series VMs bank CPU credits during idle periods and spend them on bursts — the economical choice for spiky, low-average workloads. E-series is for memory-heavy apps, N-series for GPUs, and L-series for storage throughput.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team needs a VM preconfigured with a hardened, benchmarked Linux image instead of building hardening themselves. Where should they look?
options: Azure Marketplace — certified, preconfigured VM images and solutions from Microsoft and partners
The Azure status page
The billing portal
The compliance dashboard
explain: Azure Marketplace offers ready-made, often certified VM images and solutions — saving the team from building hardening from scratch. The status page shows outages, and billing/compliance portals serve entirely different purposes.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An engineer tries to peer two virtual networks but the peering fails validation. Both VNets use the address space 10.1.0.0/16. What is the problem?
options: Peering is not supported
The regions are too close
VNet peering requires non-overlapping IP address spaces — the VNets must be re-addressed so ranges don't collide
Peering requires ExpressRoute
explain: Peered VNets must have non-overlapping address spaces, or routing between them is ambiguous — one VNet needs re-addressing. Peering works across regions without ExpressRoute, and proximity isn't a factor.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company needs encrypted connectivity between virtual networks in two regions and doesn't want to use peering. Which alternative works?
options: Azure Bastion
VNet-to-VNet VPN using VPN gateways — encrypted tunnels between the VNets over the Microsoft backbone
Azure DNS
A storage account
explain: VNet-to-VNet connections use VPN gateways to build encrypted IPsec tunnels between VNets, including across regions. Bastion is for admin RDP/SSH, DNS resolves names, and storage doesn't connect networks.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company uses ExpressRoute for its Azure workloads and also wants its Microsoft 365 traffic to travel over the ExpressRoute circuit instead of the public internet. Which ExpressRoute peering enables this?
options: Azure private peering
A site-to-site VPN
A virtual network gateway
Microsoft peering — routes Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, and other Microsoft public services over ExpressRoute
explain: Microsoft peering carries traffic to Microsoft's public services (Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365) over the private circuit; private peering is for the company's own VNets. VPNs and gateways are separate connectivity methods, not peering types.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A retailer has 200 branch stores and wants simple, automated branch-to-branch and branch-to-Azure connectivity without managing dozens of VPN devices manually. Which service is designed for this?
options: Azure Virtual WAN — a managed hub-and-spoke networking service that simplifies large-scale branch connectivity
Azure Bastion
Azure Firewall
A single virtual network
explain: Virtual WAN provides managed hubs that automate branch and Azure connectivity at scale. Bastion is for admin VM access, Firewall filters traffic, and a single VNet can't natively interconnect hundreds of branches.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company uses Traffic Manager with the Performance routing method. A user in Tokyo is directed to the Southeast Asia endpoint while a user in London goes to North Europe. This demonstrates:
options: Priority failover
Weighted round-robin
Performance routing — Traffic Manager directs each user to the lowest-latency endpoint
Geographic routing based on location policies
explain: Performance routing measures network latency and sends each user to the fastest endpoint. Priority is active-passive failover order, weighted distributes by assigned weights, and geographic routing pins regions to endpoints by policy.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An architect must choose between Azure Front Door and Traffic Manager for global routing. Which distinction is CORRECT?
options: They are identical services
Front Door is a global Layer 7 reverse proxy with instant failover; Traffic Manager is DNS-based routing with DNS-TTL-dependent failover
Traffic Manager inspects HTTP content
Front Door only works in one region
explain: Front Door proxies HTTP/S traffic at the edge with instant failover; Traffic Manager answers DNS queries, so failover waits on DNS TTL caching. Traffic Manager never inspects content, and Front Door is global by design.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company runs a three-tier app: the web tier takes internet traffic, while the app tier only talks to the web tier internally. Which load balancer types fit?
options: Two public load balancers
No load balancer is needed
Two application gateways
A public load balancer for the web tier and an internal load balancer (private IPs) for the app tier
explain: Public load balancers front internet-facing tiers; internal load balancers distribute traffic privately within the VNet for back-end tiers. Two public LBs would expose the app tier unnecessarily, and skipping load balancing removes distribution and health checks.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An NSG rule must allow traffic from Azure's load balancer health probes, whose source IPs change. What's the best approach?
options: Use the AzureLoadBalancer service tag — it automatically represents the current probe IP ranges without manual updates
Allow all internet traffic
Hard-code today's probe IP addresses
Remove the NSG
explain: Service tags represent groups of Azure IP prefixes that Microsoft keeps current — AzureLoadBalancer covers the probe sources automatically. Allowing all internet traffic is insecure, hard-coded IPs go stale, and removing the NSG abandons filtering.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company has 50 web servers whose IP addresses change frequently. Writing NSG rules with individual IPs is unmanageable. What should it use?
options: A larger subnet
A public IP on every server
Application security groups — group the VMs logically and reference the group in NSG rules instead of individual IPs
Delete the NSG
explain: Application security groups let you label VMs by role (e.g., 'web-servers') and write NSG rules against the label, so IP churn doesn't break rules. Bigger subnets and public IPs don't solve rule maintenance, and deleting the NSG removes protection.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants all outbound internet traffic from a subnet inspected by Azure Firewall before leaving. How is this enforced?
options: An NSG allow rule
A user-defined route (UDR) sending 0.0.0.0/0 to the firewall as the next hop
A private DNS zone
Disabling the subnet
explain: A user-defined route overrides default routing, steering the default route (0.0.0.0/0) through the firewall for inspection. NSGs filter but don't steer traffic, DNS resolves names, and disabling the subnet breaks everything.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A SaaS provider wants its customers to reach its service privately from their own VNets, without traffic crossing the public internet. Which Azure feature lets the provider expose its service this way?
options: VNet peering
A public load balancer
Azure DNS
Private Link service — publish the service so consumers connect via private endpoints in their own VNets
explain: Private Link service lets a provider expose its service privately; each customer creates a private endpoint in their VNet. Peering would require network-level trust between companies, a public LB keeps traffic public, and DNS doesn't carry traffic.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A developer tries to create a storage account named 'My_Storage!2024' and it fails validation. Which naming rule was violated?
options: Storage account names must be 3–24 characters, lowercase letters and numbers only
Names must be over 50 characters
Names must include symbols
Names must be all uppercase
explain: Storage account names are globally unique DNS-style names: 3–24 characters, lowercase letters and numbers only — no uppercase, underscores, or symbols. The other options describe the opposite of the actual rules.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A latency-sensitive database needs consistently low storage latency, while archival blobs just need cheap capacity. Which performance tiers fit?
options: Standard for both
Premium for both
Premium (SSD-based, low latency) for the database; Standard (HDD-based, cost-effective) for archival blobs
Archive tier for the database
explain: Premium storage uses SSDs for consistent low latency — right for databases — while Standard HDD-based storage is the economical choice for cold data. Using one tier for both either overpays or underperforms, and Archive has hours-long retrieval.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An administrator accidentally deletes a container of important blobs. The storage account had soft delete enabled with a 14-day retention. What happens?
options: The data is permanently lost
The deleted blobs can be recovered within the 14-day retention period
Only Microsoft can recover them, for a fee
Soft delete only works for virtual machines
explain: Soft delete retains deleted blobs in a recoverable state for the configured retention period — the safety net for exactly this mistake. Without it the data would be gone; Microsoft doesn't sell recovery, and VM backup is a separate feature.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A developer needs (1) a durable message queue between an order API and a fulfillment worker, and (2) a cheap NoSQL store for millions of small user-preference records. Which Azure Storage services fit?
options: Blob and Files
Two SQL Databases
Event Hubs only
Queue storage for the messaging and Table storage for the key-attribute NoSQL data
explain: Queue storage provides durable messaging between application components, and Table storage is a cheap NoSQL key-attribute store — both part of the storage account family. Blob/Files are for objects and files, SQL Database is overkill for both needs, and Event Hubs is for streaming ingestion.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team has a simple static marketing site (HTML/CSS/JS) and wants to host it as cheaply as possible with no servers. Which Azure option fits?
options: Static website hosting on Azure Blob Storage — serve static content directly from a storage account
Azure Virtual Machines
Azure SQL Database
ExpressRoute
explain: Blob Storage can serve static websites directly — no compute to pay for or manage. VMs add unnecessary cost and management, SQL Database stores relational data, and ExpressRoute is private network connectivity.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company migrates file shares to Azure Files and wants users to access shares with their Microsoft Entra identities instead of storage account keys. What enables this?
options: Shared key rotation
Anonymous access
Identity-based authentication — Azure Files supports Microsoft Entra ID authentication for SMB shares
A VPN gateway
explain: Azure Files supports identity-based authentication with Entra ID, so users sign in with their own identities and storage keys stay secret. Shared keys are the less-secure alternative, anonymous access removes control, and a VPN doesn't provide identity.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company's reporting database is queried heavily for two hours each morning and sits idle the rest of the day. Which Azure SQL Database compute tier fits best?
options: Provisioned at peak capacity 24/7
The serverless compute tier — it auto-scales with demand and auto-pauses during inactivity, billing per second used
SQL Server on a virtual machine
Cosmos DB
explain: The serverless tier scales compute with workload and pauses when idle — ideal for intermittent use, billed per second. Provisioned 24/7 wastes money on idle hours, SQL on a VM adds management, and Cosmos DB is a different (NoSQL) database.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An architect compares Azure SQL Database purchasing models. Which statement about DTU vs vCore is TRUE?
options: DTU lets you scale compute and storage independently
vCore is only for on-premises servers
They are the same model with different names
DTU bundles compute, storage, and IO into one measure for simple workloads; vCore lets you choose compute, storage, and hardware independently
explain: The DTU model bundles resources into simple tiers; the vCore model lets you independently select compute, storage, and hardware generation. Independent scaling is the vCore advantage, and the models are genuinely different.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A new company signs up for Microsoft 365 and gets its own contoso.onmicrosoft.com directory. What is this dedicated instance called?
options: A Microsoft Entra tenant — a dedicated, isolated instance of Entra ID for the organization
A subscription
A resource group
A management group
explain: An Entra tenant is the organization's dedicated identity boundary — its own users, apps, and policies, isolated from other tenants. Subscriptions, resource groups, and management groups organize Azure resources, not identities.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company currently enables MFA per user in the Entra admin center but wants richer policies (for example, MFA only for risky sign-ins or unmanaged devices). What should it do?
options: Keep per-user MFA; it supports conditional policies
Disable all MFA
Enforce MFA through Conditional Access policies, which evaluate signals and apply granular controls
Buy more licenses to unlock conditions in per-user MFA
explain: Conditional Access is the policy engine for MFA — it evaluates user, device, location, and risk signals and enforces controls granularly. Per-user MFA is a blunt on/off switch with no conditions, and disabling MFA weakens security.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An administrator is 'eligible' for the Owner role through Privileged Identity Management but doesn't currently have it. What does this mean in practice?
options: They are permanently an Owner
They hold no standing access — they must activate the role (with approval, MFA, and a time limit) before acting as Owner
Eligible means read-only access
PIM grants the role to everyone automatically
explain: PIM eligibility means zero standing privilege: the admin activates the role just-in-time, with MFA, approval, and automatic expiry. That's the opposite of permanent access, and eligibility is not a read-only state.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A hybrid company uses Microsoft Entra Connect sync. Users reset passwords via self-service in the cloud, but the new password must also work on on-premises systems. Which feature makes this possible?
options: Conditional Access
Private DNS
Seamless single sign-on only
Password writeback — syncs cloud password changes back to on-premises Active Directory
explain: Password writeback flows SSPR password changes from Entra ID back to on-premises AD, keeping both in sync. Conditional Access controls access, DNS resolves names, and SSO handles sign-in — none synchronize passwords.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A user is granted the Reader role at the subscription scope. What access do they have to resource groups inside that subscription?
options: Reader access to all resource groups — role assignments inherit down the hierarchy unless explicitly overridden
No access at all
Owner access to all resource groups
Access only if re-granted on each group
explain: RBAC assignments inherit downward: subscription-level Reader means read access to everything beneath it. Inheritance is the default — you don't re-grant per group, and Reader never escalates to Owner.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A user has the Contributor role on a resource group, but a deny assignment blocks virtual machine deletion. The user tries to delete a VM. What happens?
options: The allow wins; the VM is deleted
Deny assignments don't exist in Azure
The deny wins — explicit deny always overrides allow, and the deletion is blocked
The user is promoted to Owner
explain: Deny assignments take precedence over any allow — that's how resource locks and similar protections hold even against Owners. 'Allow wins' reverses the actual precedence, and deny assignments are a real RBAC mechanism.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A finance analyst needs to view invoices and billing data but must not manage any resources. Which built-in role fits?
options: Contributor
Billing Reader — view billing information without resource management rights
Owner
User Access Administrator
explain: Billing Reader is the least-privilege fit: billing visibility with no resource control. Contributor can modify resources, Owner can do everything, and User Access Administrator manages access — all far broader than needed.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: No built-in role matches 'restart VMs but not delete them or manage access.' The company creates a custom RBAC role. How is a custom role defined?
options: Through a storage account
By emailing Microsoft support
Custom roles are impossible in Azure
As a JSON definition listing allowed Actions and denied NotActions, then assigned like any role
explain: Custom roles are JSON definitions specifying permitted Actions (and exclusions via NotActions), created at a scope and assigned like built-in roles. They're a standard RBAC feature — not something requiring Microsoft intervention.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A ReadOnly lock is applied to a production resource group. An engineer runs an ARM template deployment that would add a new VM to the group. What happens?
options: The deployment is blocked — ReadOnly prevents creating, updating, or deleting resources (reads still work)
The deployment succeeds — ReadOnly only blocks deletions
Locks don't affect template deployments
The lock is automatically removed by the deployment
explain: ReadOnly locks freeze the resource group against any modification — creates, updates, and deletes all fail, while reads continue. 'Only blocks deletions' confuses ReadOnly with CanNotDelete, and locks are never auto-removed by deployments.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants non-compliant resources reported in the compliance dashboard without blocking deployments yet. Later it will switch to blocking. Which two policy effects map to these phases?
options: DeployIfNotExists then Disabled
Modify then Append
Audit (report only) now, then Deny (block) later
Deny then Audit
explain: Audit flags non-compliance without blocking — the safe starting phase; Deny blocks non-compliant requests once teams are ready. Starting with Deny risks breaking deployments, DeployIfNotExists remediates rather than reports, and Disabled turns the policy off.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A compliance team must verify that every Windows VM has a specific password policy and disk encryption enabled inside the guest OS. Which Azure Policy capability audits these in-guest settings?
options: NSG rules
Guest Configuration — audits and can remediate settings inside virtual machines
Azure Firewall
Azure Bastion
explain: Guest Configuration extends Policy inside the VM's operating system — checking password policies, encryption, and similar OS-level settings. NSGs and Firewall handle network traffic, and Bastion provides admin access — none audit guest OS configuration.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A holding company must apply 20 related policies across 30 subscriptions. What is the most efficient approach?
options: Assign each policy to each subscription manually
Use resource locks instead of policies
Email the requirements to each team
Create an initiative (policy set) and assign it once at the management group scope — it inherits to all subscriptions
explain: An initiative bundles related policies into one assignable package, and assigning it at the management group flows down to every subscription. Manual per-subscription assignment doesn't scale, locks prevent changes rather than enforcing configuration, and email isn't enforcement.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company requires every resource to carry CostCenter and Environment tags. New resources keep arriving untagged. Which governance approach enforces this?
options: An Azure Policy that denies (or appends) resources missing required tags
A resource lock
An RBAC role
A budget alert
explain: Policy can require tags — denying untagged deployments or appending default values automatically. Locks prevent modification, RBAC controls who acts, and budget alerts warn about spending — none enforce tagging.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A manager wants to know, mid-month, whether the department is on track to exceed its cloud budget by month-end. Which Cost Management view helps?
options: The invoice download
The SLA dashboard
Cost analysis with forecasting — projects month-end spend based on the current burn rate
Azure Advisor security recommendations
explain: Cost analysis forecasting extrapolates current spending to predict month-end totals — the early warning the manager needs. Invoices show the past, SLAs cover availability, and Advisor security recommendations don't predict spend.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company owns SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance and wants to run Azure SQL Managed Instance without paying full license-included rates. Which benefit applies?
options: Spot pricing
Azure Hybrid Benefit for SQL Server — apply existing licenses to PaaS SQL services for reduced cost
The Azure free account
The Dev/Test offer
explain: Azure Hybrid Benefit for SQL Server lets you bring existing licensed SQL Server to Azure SQL PaaS services (including Managed Instance) instead of paying license-included rates. Spot pricing is for interruptible VMs, and free/Dev-Test offers don't cover production PaaS SQL.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A university student with no credit card wants to learn Azure hands-on. Which offer fits?
options: A production enterprise agreement
Reserved instances
Spot virtual machines
Azure for Students — free credit and free services for verified students, no credit card required
explain: Azure for Students gives verified students free credit plus free services without requiring a credit card — built exactly for learning. Enterprise agreements and reservations are commercial commitments, and Spot VMs still bill usage.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An application depends on two Azure services: one with a 99.95% SLA and one with a 99.99% SLA. What is the application's composite SLA?
