options: 99.94% — composite SLAs multiply: 99.95% x 99.99% = 99.94%, lower than either individual SLA
99.99% — the higher one wins
99.95% — the lower one wins
explain: Composite SLA is the product of the component SLAs — every dependency multiplies the chance of downtime, so the composite is always lower than any single SLA. Picking the higher or lower value ignores the math, and 100% is never offered.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An architect can deploy a workload with a 99.9% SLA design or add redundancy for 99.99%. The 99.99% design costs significantly more. What principle does this illustrate?
options: SLAs are free
Higher availability always costs less
Higher SLA tiers demand more redundancy, which costs more — availability is a business decision balancing cost against downtime tolerance
Microsoft sets prices randomly
explain: Each extra 'nine' of availability requires more redundancy (zones, replicas, failover), which costs more — so SLA targets are cost/benefit decisions per workload. SLAs aren't free, higher availability never costs less, and pricing follows the redundancy required.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Where does an administrator look to see upcoming planned Azure maintenance that might affect their region?
options: The Azure Marketplace
Azure Service Health — includes planned maintenance, health advisories, and security advisories alongside outage tracking
The pricing calculator
A code repository
explain: Service Health is the personalized Azure status hub: current issues, planned maintenance, and advisories for your subscriptions and regions. Marketplace lists solutions, the pricing calculator estimates cost, and repos hold code — none track platform health.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company has data scattered across databases, data lakes, and SaaS apps, and governance needs a map of what sensitive data lives where. Which service provides unified data discovery and classification?
options: Azure Bastion
Traffic Manager
Azure Data Box
Microsoft Purview — scans data sources, classifies sensitive data, and maps the data estate for governance
explain: Microsoft Purview is the unified data governance service: it scans sources, classifies sensitive data, and builds a map of the data estate. Bastion is admin VM access, Traffic Manager routes DNS, and Data Box moves data offline.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A bank's policy states that no Microsoft engineer may access its Azure data without the bank's explicit approval. Which feature enforces this approval workflow?
options: Customer Lockbox — Microsoft requests access and the customer approves or denies it
A VPN gateway
A network security group
A resource lock
explain: Customer Lockbox puts the customer in control: when Microsoft support needs data access, an approval request goes to the customer first. VPNs, NSGs, and resource locks protect infrastructure — they don't govern Microsoft's own support access.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A CISO enables Microsoft Defender for Cloud. Basic posture management and Secure Score appear at no extra cost, but protecting servers with threat detection requires enabling paid plans. This reflects which distinction?
options: Defender for Cloud is entirely free
Defender for Cloud is entirely paid
Cloud Security Posture Management (foundational, included) vs. Cloud Workload Protection (paid Defender plans per workload type)
Secure Score requires a paid plan
explain: Defender for Cloud has two halves: free CSPM (posture assessment, Secure Score, recommendations) and paid workload protections (Defender plans for servers, SQL, storage, etc.). It's neither all-free nor all-paid, and Secure Score comes with the free tier.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A compliance officer wants to see how Azure resources map against ISO 27001 controls, with failed controls highlighted. Where in Defender for Cloud is this?
options: The billing dashboard
The regulatory compliance dashboard — maps assessments to standards like ISO 27001, SOC, and PCI with pass/fail status
The MFA report
The backup vault
explain: The regulatory compliance dashboard translates technical assessments into control mappings for standards like ISO 27001, SOC, and PCI. Billing shows cost, MFA reports cover identity, and backup vaults hold recovery points — none map compliance controls.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A security team wants compromised accounts disabled automatically when Sentinel detects a high-severity incident, without waiting for an analyst. Which Sentinel capability does this?
options: Workbooks
Hunting queries
Data connectors
Automation rules with playbooks (Logic Apps) — the SOAR side of Sentinel that triggers automated responses
explain: Sentinel's SOAR capability uses automation rules and Logic Apps playbooks to respond without human delay — disabling accounts, isolating VMs, opening tickets. Workbooks visualize, hunting queries investigate manually, and connectors only ingest data.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants firewall logs, Entra sign-in logs, and Microsoft 365 alerts all analyzed together in Sentinel, with visual dashboards for the SOC. Which two Sentinel components deliver this?
options: Data connectors ingest the logs; workbooks visualize them in dashboards
Playbooks and hunting queries
Policies and resource locks
Virtual machines and storage accounts
explain: Data connectors bring diverse sources into Sentinel's workspace, and workbooks turn that data into SOC dashboards. Playbooks automate response and hunting queries investigate — neither ingests or visualizes; policies/locks and VMs/storage are unrelated.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A bank needs FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware protection for its encryption keys, with single-tenant control. Which Azure Key Vault offering fits?
options: Standard vault software-protected keys
A storage account
Azure Managed HSM — dedicated, single-tenant HSMs meeting FIPS 140-2 Level 3
A network security group
explain: Managed HSM provides dedicated, single-tenant hardware security modules validated to FIPS 140-2 Level 3 — the highest-assurance key protection Azure offers. Standard vaults use software or shared HSM backing, and storage/NSGs don't protect keys.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company runs five Azure Firewalls and wants one central place to define network and application rules applied consistently to all of them. What should it use?
options: Five separate local rule sets
Azure Firewall Policy — centrally managed rule collections that multiple firewalls inherit
A network security group
A route table
explain: Firewall Policy centralizes rule management: define once, inherit across firewalls, with hierarchical overrides. Separate rule sets drift apart, NSGs are per-subnet packet filters, and route tables steer traffic rather than filter it.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An architect compares options for administrators to reach VMs: Azure Bastion vs. a point-to-site VPN. Which statement is TRUE?
options: They are the same service
A VPN is browser-based with no client software
Bastion requires VMs to have public IPs
Bastion gives browser-based RDP/SSH through the portal with no public IPs on VMs; a VPN gives network-level access requiring a client
explain: Bastion is fully browser-based RDP/SSH with no public IPs exposed; point-to-site VPN installs a client and joins the admin's machine to the network. They're different tools — Bastion for session access, VPN for network access.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Following the 'assume breach' principle, a company divides its network into small isolated segments so an attacker who compromises one workload can't move laterally. This practice is called:
options: Micro-segmentation — limiting blast radius by isolating workloads, a core Zero Trust practice
Perimeter security
Single sign-on
Data encryption
explain: Micro-segmentation implements 'assume breach' by containing attackers within small segments — the opposite of perimeter security's trusted-inside model. SSO handles identity and encryption protects data, but neither stops lateral movement.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Azure Advisor recommends resizing an underused VM, but the team knows a seasonal peak starts next month. What can they do with the recommendation?
options: Nothing — recommendations are mandatory
Delete the virtual machine
Postpone or dismiss the recommendation — Advisor suggestions are advisory, and can be snoozed or dismissed with a reason
Disable Advisor permanently for the subscription
explain: Advisor recommendations are guidance, not mandates — they can be postponed or dismissed with justification when context (like a coming peak) makes them wrong. Deleting the VM or disabling Advisor throws away useful signal.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company must encrypt VM disks so that even if a disk file were stolen, its contents would be unreadable. Which Azure capabilities address OS and data disk encryption?
options: NSG rules
Azure Disk Encryption (BitLocker for Windows, DM-Crypt for Linux) and encryption-at-host options
A VPN gateway
Blob soft delete
explain: Azure Disk Encryption encrypts OS and data disks at the OS level (BitLocker/DM-Crypt), with encryption-at-host as an additional option — unreadable without the keys. NSGs filter network traffic, VPNs encrypt transit, and soft delete recovers deleted blobs.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A security review asks: 'Is data encrypted when moving between Azure services and when stored?' Which statement is TRUE?
options: Azure never encrypts anything by default
Only storage accounts are encrypted
Encryption is optional and off by default
Azure encrypts data in transit with TLS and encrypts stored data at rest by default with Microsoft-managed keys
explain: Azure encrypts data in transit (TLS) and at rest by default using Microsoft-managed keys — customers can bring their own keys via Key Vault for extra control. 'Never' and 'off by default' are flatly wrong; encryption covers far more than storage.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Which statement BEST summarizes the customer's security responsibilities across all Azure service models?
options: Customers are always responsible for their data, identities, and access management — plus everything above the provider's boundary in their chosen service model
Microsoft handles all security in every model
Customers handle physical datacenter security
There are no customer responsibilities in PaaS and SaaS
explain: The shared responsibility model is constant at its core: data, identities, and access are always yours, and your zone grows as you move from SaaS toward IaaS. Microsoft never handles 'all' security, physical security is always the provider's, and PaaS/SaaS still leave you data and identity duties.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company keeps a scaled-down copy of its production environment running in a paired Azure region at all times. During a regional outage, it scales that copy up to full capacity within an hour. This disaster recovery approach is called:
options: Backup-only recovery
A warm standby — a scaled-down live copy ready to scale up quickly
A cold standby with no running resources
An active-active deployment
explain: Warm standby keeps a minimal live copy running so recovery means scaling up, not rebuilding — faster than cold standby (nothing running) but cheaper than active-active (full capacity in both regions). Backup-only recovery has no running infrastructure to scale, and active-active serves live traffic from both regions.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's video-conference calls suffer from noticeable delays even though its internet plan advertises very high speeds. The high speed didn't fix the delay because:
options: Speed and delay are the same thing
The company needs more virtual machines
The provider throttles video traffic
Bandwidth (capacity) and latency (delay) are different — the plan increased capacity, but the delay comes from distance and routing
explain: Bandwidth is how much data moves at once; latency is how long each bit takes to travel. A bigger pipe doesn't shorten the trip — distance and network hops cause the lag. More VMs or throttling theories miss the actual distinction the exam tests.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A serverless function that hasn't run for an hour takes noticeably longer to respond on its first invocation, then runs fast again. This is an example of:
options: A cold start — the platform must provision resources for the first execution after idle
A billing error
Network latency between regions
A misconfigured load balancer
explain: Cold start is the initialization delay when serverless platforms spin up execution resources after idle periods. It's a normal platform behavior, not a billing problem, a network issue, or a load-balancer misconfiguration — and it's why latency-sensitive apps sometimes use pre-warmed (Premium) plans.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company shuts down its aging on-premises email servers entirely and moves all mailboxes to Microsoft 365, with no servers left to manage. In cloud migration terms, this strategy is called:
options: Rehosting
Refactoring
Replace — retiring the old application and substituting a SaaS product
Rearchitecting
explain: Replace means discarding the legacy application in favor of a SaaS equivalent — the fastest path when a SaaS product fits. Rehosting moves servers as-is, refactoring tweaks code for PaaS, and rearchitecting redesigns the application — none describe abandoning the app for SaaS.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A team moves its application to Azure with only minimal code changes — mainly switching to a managed PaaS database instead of a self-managed one. This migration strategy is:
options: Rebuilding from scratch
Refactor (replatform) — small adjustments to take advantage of cloud platform services without redesigning the app
Replacing with SaaS
Retiring the workload
explain: Refactor/replatform makes targeted changes (like adopting a PaaS database) while keeping the application architecture intact. Rebuilding rewrites the app, replacing swaps it for SaaS, and retiring eliminates it — all much bigger changes than described.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company redesigns its monolithic application as independent microservices running in containers with automatic scaling, built specifically to exploit cloud elasticity. This strategy is:
options: Lift and shift
A backup strategy
A hybrid deployment
Rearchitect — redesigning the application to be cloud-native
explain: Rearchitecting fundamentally redesigns the application around cloud capabilities — microservices, containers, elastic scaling. Lift and shift moves the monolith unchanged, and backup or hybrid describe data protection and deployment models, not application redesign.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A bank's trading system requires an RPO of zero — not a single transaction may be lost, even in a regional failure. What does this requirement demand technically?
options: Synchronous replication — every write must be confirmed at the secondary site before it is acknowledged
Nightly backups
Weekly backup testing
A faster internet connection
explain: Zero RPO means zero data loss, which only synchronous replication guarantees: the primary waits for the secondary to confirm each write. Nightly backups allow up to a day of loss, testing doesn't change the RPO, and bandwidth alone doesn't create a zero-loss guarantee.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Which BEST describes a cloud-native application?
options: Any application installed on a virtual machine in the cloud
A traditional application moved to the cloud without changes
An application designed for the cloud from the start — using microservices, containers, and elastic scaling
An application that only runs on-premises
explain: Cloud-native means architected for cloud: loosely coupled services, containers, dynamic orchestration, and design for failure and elasticity. Simply hosting a legacy app on a cloud VM is lift-and-shift, not cloud-native — the exam loves that distinction.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A CIO believes that moving to a private cloud will transfer operating-system patching and hardware maintenance to the cloud provider. What is wrong with this belief?
options: Nothing — private cloud includes full provider management
In a private cloud the organization retains the infrastructure — patching, hardware, and maintenance stay with the organization, not a provider
Private clouds cannot be patched
Only public clouds require patching
explain: Private cloud is single-tenant infrastructure the organization owns or dedicates — there is no provider absorbing the operational work. The management burden stays in-house; that's the core tradeoff versus public cloud, where the provider handles the physical and virtualization layers.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs full disaster-recovery failover drills twice a year. In its old datacenter, each drill risked disrupting production. In the cloud, the team tests failover into an isolated copy of the environment. This illustrates which cloud benefit?
options: Serverless computing
Geo-distribution
Measured service
Agility — the cloud makes it fast and safe to spin up isolated copies for testing without touching production
explain: Agility is rapid, low-risk change: isolated test environments can be provisioned in minutes and torn down afterward, so DR drills no longer threaten production. Serverless, geo-distribution, and measured service don't describe safe, fast test-environment provisioning.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company wants to heavily customize its SaaS CRM — rewriting core workflows in custom code the way it did with on-premises software. What should it understand about SaaS?
options: SaaS offers configuration options, not code-level customization — deep custom logic belongs in a PaaS or IaaS solution, not SaaS
SaaS allows unlimited rewriting of the vendor's code
Customization requires buying the vendor's datacenter
SaaS and on-premises software are customized identically
explain: SaaS trades control for convenience: you configure settings and integrations, but you don't rewrite the vendor's application. Teams needing deep custom code should build on PaaS or IaaS. Expecting on-premises-style code access in SaaS is a classic misconception.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs a background data processor 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, at constant utilization. An architect warns that moving it to serverless functions could INCREASE costs. Why?
options: Serverless is always free
Virtual machines cannot run 24/7
The cloud charges extra for background work
Serverless bills per execution — a constant 24/7 workload can cost more per month than a right-sized VM billed at a flat hourly rate
explain: Serverless shines for spiky or idle-heavy workloads; a flat-out 24/7 workload pays per execution around the clock, which can exceed a VM's steady hourly rate. Matching the pricing model to the workload pattern — not assuming serverless is always cheaper — is the real skill being tested.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An SLA improves from 99.9% to 99.99%. What does that extra 'nine' mean for allowed monthly downtime?
options: It roughly doubles the allowed downtime
It cuts allowed downtime by roughly 10x — from about 43 minutes to about 4 minutes per month
Downtime stays exactly the same
It guarantees zero downtime
explain: Each additional nine reduces allowed downtime by roughly a factor of ten: 99.9% allows ~43 minutes monthly, 99.99% allows ~4.4 minutes. No SLA guarantees zero downtime, and the improvement is dramatic — which is also why each nine costs significantly more in redundancy.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An Azure cost review finds virtual machines consistently running at 12% CPU utilization. The recommended practice of matching resource sizes to actual workload demand is called:
options: Overprovisioning
Geo-distribution
Fault tolerance
Right-sizing — and it is an ongoing process, not a one-time task, as workloads change
explain: Right-sizing aligns VM sizes (and other resources) with real utilization, eliminating waste from oversized deployments. Overprovisioning is the problem, not the fix; geo-distribution and fault tolerance address location and resilience, not cost efficiency.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's IT team spends every month patching on-premises Exchange servers. After migrating mailboxes to Microsoft 365, that patching work disappears. This illustrates which SaaS benefit?
options: The provider absorbs application maintenance — patching, updates, and infrastructure — so the customer team can focus on higher-value work
Email becomes free
The company no longer needs any IT staff
SaaS eliminates the need for user training
explain: SaaS shifts the entire application stack — patching, upgrades, infrastructure — to the provider. The benefit is reclaimed staff time, not free email or zero IT staff; administration, identity, and user support remain customer responsibilities.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A team debates lift-and-shift versus rearchitecting for its cloud migration. Which statement honestly captures the tradeoff?
options: Lift-and-shift is always better
Rearchitecting is always faster
Lift-and-shift moves fast but carries existing technical debt into the cloud; rearchitecting takes longer but unlocks elasticity and managed services
There is no difference between the approaches
explain: Lift-and-shift (rehost) prioritizes speed — you migrate as-is, inefficiencies included. Rearchitecting costs more time upfront but produces a cloud-native design that scales and uses PaaS/serverless. Neither is universally better; the tradeoff is speed versus long-term fit.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A startup decides to rewrite its prototype as a set of serverless functions and managed services, discarding the old codebase entirely, to maximize scalability. This migration strategy is:
options: Rehosting
Rebuild — discarding the existing application and rewriting it cloud-native
Replacing with SaaS
A backup strategy
explain: Rebuild means starting over with a cloud-native design — the highest effort, highest long-term payoff option. Rehosting moves the old code as-is, replacing substitutes a SaaS product, and backup is data protection, not a migration strategy.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A CFO asks whether moving to the cloud will eliminate the need for IT operations staff. What is the honest answer?
options: Yes — the cloud runs itself completely
No — the cloud shifts operations work from hardware management to higher-value work like automation, architecture, and governance
Yes — Microsoft hires your IT staff automatically
No — cloud requires more datacenter technicians than on-premises
explain: Cloud eliminates hardware-centric roles but creates demand for cloud architecture, automation, cost governance, and security skills. 'Runs itself' ignores the customer's ongoing responsibilities for data, identity, and application operations.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A software company moves its CI/CD build agents to the cloud. During release week, 50 builds run in parallel; the rest of the month, almost none run. Which cloud characteristics make this economical?
options: Fault tolerance and disaster recovery
Elasticity plus consumption-based pricing — capacity scales out for release week and shrinks to near-zero after, with billing following actual use
Geo-distribution and data sovereignty
Reserved capacity and fixed pricing
explain: Elastic build capacity that appears for release week and disappears after — billed only for what runs — is the elasticity plus pay-as-you-go combination. Reserved/fixed pricing would waste money on idle agents, and the scenario isn't about failure recovery or data location.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company is comparing a 3-year server purchase against cloud hosting for a workload that will be decommissioned in 18 months. Which financial argument favors the cloud here?
options: The cloud is always cheaper regardless of timeframe
Servers can be resold at full price after 18 months
With an 18-month lifespan, OpEx avoids paying for 18 months of unused server life — the workload's cost ends when the workload ends
Capital purchases are illegal for short projects
explain: OpEx matches cost to the workload's actual life: when the workload dies at 18 months, so does the bill. A 3-year server purchase strands 18 months of capital. The cloud isn't universally cheaper — the advantage here is specifically about avoiding stranded investment in short-lived work.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company keeps production systems on-premises but runs all development and test environments in the public cloud, tearing them down after each release. This is an example of:
options: A purely private cloud
Hybrid cloud — combining on-premises production with public cloud dev/test in one strategy
Multicloud
Serverless computing
explain: Mixing on-premises and public cloud resources as one coordinated environment is hybrid cloud — even when the split is by environment (prod vs. dev/test) rather than by application. It's not purely private (public cloud is involved), not multicloud (one provider), and not a compute model.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An architect warns that a multicloud design will replicate large datasets between two public cloud providers nightly. What cost concern should the team plan for?
options: Compute costs are always free between providers
Storage is free when shared between clouds
Providers charge nothing for cross-cloud traffic
Data egress charges — each provider bills for data leaving its cloud, so cross-provider replication incurs bandwidth costs on the sending side
explain: Outbound data transfer (egress) is metered by every major provider, so multicloud architectures pay each time data crosses provider boundaries. Inbound is typically free, but nothing about cross-cloud traffic is free — a real and often underestimated multicloud cost.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A research team needs GPU-powered virtual machines for two weeks of model training, then nothing for months. Buying GPU servers is unjustifiable. Which cloud benefit solves this?
options: On-demand access to specialized hardware — rent GPUs by the hour with no purchase, then release them
Free GPU servers for researchers
Permanent GPU reservations at no cost
GPUs are only available on-premises
explain: The cloud's resource pool includes specialized hardware (GPUs, high-memory, HPC) available on demand — you rent for the two weeks and stop paying. Nothing is free or permanent, and specialized hardware is a flagship cloud scenario, not an on-premises-only one.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs its application on Azure SQL Database (PaaS). The team assumes Microsoft will also tune its slow queries and classify its sensitive data. Where does the responsibility actually lie?
options: Microsoft tunes queries and classifies data in PaaS
The internet provider handles database performance
Data-level concerns — query tuning, data classification, and access to the data — remain the customer's responsibility in PaaS
Nobody needs to tune queries in the cloud
explain: PaaS draws the line at the platform: Microsoft manages the engine, patching, and availability, but data and application logic — including query performance and data classification — stay with the customer. Assuming the provider owns data-level work is a common PaaS misconception.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company is evaluating a SaaS application and asks the vendor, 'If we leave in two years, how do we get our data out?' What is the company wisely investigating?
options: The vendor's office locations
Data portability and exit strategy — ensuring the company's data can be exported in a usable format before committing to SaaS
The color scheme of the application
The vendor's stock price
explain: Data portability is a key SaaS evaluation criterion: your data must remain extractable in usable formats so you're never held hostage. It's a business-continuity question, not a cosmetic or financial one — and a mature sign the company understands SaaS tradeoffs.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company lifts its virtual machines to Azure (IaaS) and assumes backups are now Microsoft's job. After an accidental database deletion, it discovers no backups exist. What went wrong?
options: Azure deleted the backups
The virtual network blocked the backup
IaaS includes automatic backups of all data
In IaaS, data protection is the customer's responsibility — the company needed to configure Azure Backup itself
explain: IaaS gives you virtualized hardware, not managed data protection: the customer must configure backups, just as on-premises. Azure Backup exists for exactly this, but it must be set up. Assuming the provider backs up your IaaS data by default is a costly misconception.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Two designs are proposed: Design X fails over to a standby server with a 2-minute interruption. Design Y keeps running with zero interruption when a server fails. Which statement about cost is TRUE?
options: Design Y (fault tolerance, zero interruption) typically costs more than Design X (high availability with brief failover)
Design X always costs more
Both designs cost exactly the same
Fault tolerance is free in the cloud
explain: Fault tolerance (zero interruption) demands fully redundant, lockstep systems — more expensive than high availability's brief-failover design. The business question is whether those extra nines of continuity justify the cost; for most workloads, HA's short failover is the economical choice.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A news website's article pages are read millions of times but change rarely. Instead of adding web servers, the team caches pages at edge locations worldwide. This scaling approach demonstrates:
options: Vertical scaling
Disaster recovery
Scaling through caching and content distribution — serving repeated reads from cache instead of adding origin servers
Fault tolerance
explain: Caching is a scaling strategy: absorb read traffic at the edge so origin servers don't have to grow. It's often cheaper and faster than adding compute. Vertical scaling enlarges servers, disaster recovery handles outages, and fault tolerance handles failures — none describe cache-based scaling.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company hosts product images and videos that customers download worldwide. It stores the files once in Azure and uses a content delivery network to serve them from edge locations near each customer. This combines:
options: Fault tolerance and elasticity
Geo-distribution with caching — content placed close to users for fast delivery and reduced origin load
Vertical scaling and backups
Multicloud and hybrid cloud
explain: This is geo-distribution in action: a CDN caches content at global edge points so users download from nearby, cutting latency and origin traffic. It's not about failure survival (fault tolerance), bigger servers (vertical scaling), or multiple clouds.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company backs up its databases once every 24 hours. What is the company's Recovery Point Objective (RPO)?
options: Zero — backups guarantee no data loss
24 days
It cannot be determined from backup frequency
Up to 24 hours of data loss — RPO is determined by how frequently recoverable copies are made
explain: RPO (maximum tolerable data loss) follows directly from backup frequency: daily backups mean up to a day of transactions could be lost. Backups never guarantee zero loss — only synchronous replication does — and the RPO is absolutely determinable from the backup cadence.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A CFO notes that cloud spending rises and falls with customer usage, unlike the fixed cost of owned servers. This alignment of IT cost with business activity is an advantage of:
options: Operational expenditure — costs scale with revenue-generating usage instead of sitting fixed regardless of demand
Capital expenditure
Perpetual licensing
Hardware depreciation
explain: OpEx ties spending to actual consumption: quiet months cost less, busy months cost more — costs move with the business. CapEx and depreciation lock in fixed costs regardless of demand, and perpetual licensing is a software purchasing model, not a cost-alignment benefit.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's cloud bill jumps 40% in one month. Investigation finds dozens of forgotten test virtual machines still running from a project that ended months ago. This illustrates:
options: A provider billing error
That consumption pricing is unpredictable by nature
The need for cloud hygiene — governance, tagging, and lifecycle policies to find and remove idle resources
That virtual machines should never be used for testing
explain: Bill shock from zombie resources is a governance failure, not a pricing-model flaw: untagged, unmonitored test environments run forever because nobody owns their lifecycle. Tags, budgets with alerts, and automation prevent it. Consumption pricing is predictable when resources are actually managed.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company builds its application in containers orchestrated by Kubernetes — open standards that run on any cloud — specifically so it could move providers later with minimal rewrites. Which concern is the company addressing?
options: High availability
Vendor lock-in — portable container standards reduce dependence on any single provider's proprietary services
Consumption-based pricing
Data sovereignty
explain: Vendor lock-in is dependence on one provider's proprietary services; building on portable open standards (containers, Kubernetes) keeps future moves feasible. High availability is about uptime, consumption pricing is about billing, and data sovereignty is about data location — none describe portability strategy.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs a weekend hackathon with 200 developers, each needing an isolated environment with databases and test data for 48 hours. What makes the cloud ideal for this?
options: Hackathons are only possible on-premises
The cloud requires 6-week procurement for environments
Developers must share one laptop
Agility plus consumption pricing — 200 identical environments provisioned in minutes, used for two days, then deleted with billing stopping
explain: Ephemeral, large-scale environments are the cloud's home turf: infrastructure-as-code spins up 200 identical setups fast, and consumption billing means you pay for 48 hours, not permanent hardware. Procurement delays and shared laptops belong to the world the cloud replaced.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An engineer is configuring a VPN gateway and is told it must be deployed into a subnet with a specific name. What is that subnet name?
options: GatewayNet
VPN-Subnet
GatewaySubnet — the VPN gateway requires a subnet with this exact name
Any name works
explain: Azure requires the gateway subnet to be named exactly 'GatewaySubnet' — the platform looks for this name when deploying VPN or ExpressRoute gateways. A custom name fails validation. It's one of those exact-name facts the exam loves.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A new network security group is created with no custom rules. Which statement about its default behavior is TRUE?
options: Default rules allow traffic within the virtual network and from the Azure load balancer, but deny all inbound traffic from the internet
All traffic is blocked in every direction
All traffic is allowed in every direction
Default rules cannot be overridden
explain: Every NSG ships with default rules: allow VNet-to-VNet and Azure Load Balancer inbound, deny all other inbound; allow VNet and internet outbound. Custom rules with lower priority numbers override defaults. 'Blocks everything' and 'allows everything' both misstate the defaults.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team deploys Azure Bastion and is told it needs its own dedicated subnet of at least /26. Why do some Azure services require dedicated subnets?
options: To increase the Azure bill
Dedicated subnets are optional for all services
To slow down deployments
Certain services (Bastion, VPN gateways, App Service) need delegated subnets so the platform can manage their networking without conflicting with customer resources
explain: Subnet delegation hands control of a subnet to an Azure service, letting the platform inject and manage its resources there safely. Mixing customer VMs into those subnets would cause conflicts — hence the dedicated-subnet requirement. It's a platform safety mechanism, not a billing tactic.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An engineer adds a user-defined route (UDR) sending all traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to a firewall appliance. What happens to Azure's built-in system routes?
options: System routes are deleted permanently
The UDR overrides the matching system routes — user-defined routes take precedence where they overlap
UDRs are ignored when system routes exist
The virtual network stops working
explain: Azure provides default system routes (VNet-local, internet, etc.), and user-defined routes override them where address prefixes overlap — that's how forced tunneling through a firewall works. System routes aren't deleted; they're simply superseded for the overlapping prefixes.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company uses ExpressRoute but is frustrated by the extra latency of traffic passing through the ExpressRoute gateway to reach its VMs. Which feature lets traffic bypass the gateway?
options: A VPN gateway
VNet peering
ExpressRoute FastPath — sends network traffic directly to virtual machines, bypassing the gateway for lower latency
Azure DNS
explain: FastPath improves ExpressRoute performance by sending traffic straight to the VMs instead of hairpinning through the gateway. A VPN gateway is a different (internet-based) connection, VNet peering connects VNets, and DNS resolves names — none bypass the ExpressRoute gateway.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A global retailer wants web application firewall protection applied at the edge, close to users worldwide, in front of its multi-region web app. Where should it deploy Azure WAF?
options: On Azure Front Door — WAF policies at the global edge protect all regional backends with one configuration
On each virtual machine
On Azure DNS
WAF can only protect one region
explain: Azure WAF integrates with Front Door to inspect traffic at the global edge — one policy protects every backend region. Per-VM WAFs don't scale globally, DNS doesn't inspect HTTP, and WAF is explicitly designed for multi-region protection.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company hosts an internal web server with only a private IP, but partners need to reach it from the internet. The security team will not assign it a public IP. Which Azure Firewall capability publishes it safely?
options: An NSG allow rule
A VPN gateway
Azure Bastion
DNAT rules — translate a public firewall IP/port to the internal server's private address
explain: Firewall DNAT (destination NAT) rules publish internal servers: the firewall's public IP receives traffic and forwards it to the private server. An NSG alone can't translate addresses, a VPN is for private connectivity (not public publishing), and Bastion provides admin RDP/SSH — not application publishing.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company must retain compliance logs for 7 years. The logs are almost never read, but when auditors request them, access must be immediate. Which blob access tier is the MOST cost-effective fit?
options: Hot
Cold — the low-cost tier for rarely accessed data that still needs instant retrieval, unlike Archive which takes hours
Archive
Premium
explain: The Cold tier sits between Cool and Archive: cheaper than Cool for long-retained, rarely read data, with millisecond retrieval unlike Archive's hours-long rehydration. Archive would break the 'immediate access' requirement, and Hot/Premium overpay for data nobody reads.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A hospital needs its patient-images storage to survive a datacenter failure within its region AND a full regional outage. Which redundancy option covers both?
options: Locally redundant storage (LRS)
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS)
Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) — synchronous copies across zones plus asynchronous replication to a secondary region
Premium storage
explain: GZRS combines ZRS (survives zone/datacenter loss) with GRS (survives regional loss) — the highest durability option. LRS survives only drive/rack failure, ZRS only datacenter failure, and Premium is a performance tier, not a redundancy option.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A developer overwrites a critical blob and needs the previous version back. The storage account had blob versioning enabled. What happens?
options: Versioning automatically kept the prior version — the developer can restore it
The old data is permanently lost
Only Microsoft support can recover it
Versioning only works for virtual machines
explain: Blob versioning automatically preserves previous versions whenever a blob is modified or deleted, making point-in-time restore self-service. Without versioning the overwrite would be final; Microsoft doesn't need to intervene, and versioning is a storage feature, not a VM one.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company has 50 TB of files on an on-premises file server. It wants infrequently used files to automatically tier to Azure while keeping the full namespace visible locally. Which service does this?
options: Azure Data Box
Azure Migrate
AzCopy
Azure File Sync — tiers cold files to Azure Files while the on-premises server keeps the complete file namespace
explain: Azure File Sync cloud-tiers aging files to Azure Files, recalling them on access, while users still see the full directory tree locally. Data Box is offline bulk transfer, Migrate moves servers/workloads, and AzCopy is a manual copy tool — none provide ongoing transparent tiering.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A research institute must move roughly 800 TB of genomic data to Azure over a private, offline shipment. Which Data Box option fits?
options: Data Box Disk — ruggedized SSDs for smaller transfers
Data Box Heavy — the high-capacity appliance holding around a petabyte, for the largest offline transfers
AzCopy over the internet
A VPN gateway
explain: Data Box Heavy handles ~1 PB for massive offline migrations; the standard Data Box holds ~100 TB (too small here), and Data Box Disk suits terabyte-scale jobs. AzCopy over the internet would take impractical amounts of time for 800 TB, and a VPN is connectivity, not bulk transfer.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company runs a critical Azure SQL Database in its primary region and needs automatic failover to a readable secondary in the paired region during an outage, with no manual steps. Which feature provides this?
options: Manual backups
An availability zone
Auto-failover groups — automatically fail over databases to the secondary region, which can also serve read traffic
A VPN gateway
explain: Auto-failover groups provide policy-driven automatic failover of SQL databases to the paired region, with the secondary available for read scale-out. Manual backups require human restore steps, availability zones protect within one region, and VPNs are network connectivity.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Data analysts need to run T-SQL queries directly against CSV and Parquet files in the company's data lake, with no infrastructure to provision and paying only per query. Which Synapse capability fits?
options: The serverless SQL pool — query data lake files on demand with T-SQL, no provisioning, pay per data processed
A dedicated SQL pool
Azure Cosmos DB
SQL Server on a virtual machine
explain: The serverless SQL pool is built for exactly this: ad-hoc T-SQL over data lake files with zero provisioning and per-query billing. Dedicated SQL pools require provisioned capacity, Cosmos DB is an operational NoSQL database, and SQL on a VM adds full management overhead.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A logistics company needs to analyze its delivery-truck telemetry stream in real time — flagging late trucks within seconds — using familiar SQL-like queries. Which service fits?
options: Azure Data Factory
Azure Synapse Analytics
Azure Blob storage
Azure Stream Analytics — real-time stream processing with a SQL-like query language
explain: Stream Analytics processes event streams in real time using SQL-like queries — the purpose-built tool for 'analyze now, alert now' scenarios. Data Factory runs batch ETL pipelines, Synapse is for large-scale batch analytics, and Blob storage just stores data.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A data-science team needs a collaborative Apache Spark environment for large-scale data processing and machine learning, without managing Spark clusters itself. Which Azure service fits?
options: Azure Functions
Azure Databricks — a managed Apache Spark analytics platform for data engineering and machine learning
Azure App Service
Azure DNS
explain: Azure Databricks is the first-party managed Spark platform: collaborative notebooks, optimized Spark runtime, and ML workflows without cluster management. Functions runs event-driven code, App Service hosts web apps, and DNS resolves names — none is a Spark analytics platform.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An insurance company needs to extract text, tables, and key-value pairs from thousands of scanned claim forms automatically. Which Azure AI service is purpose-built for this?
options: Azure OpenAI Service
Azure AI Speech
Azure AI Document Intelligence — extracts text and structured data from documents and forms
Azure Machine Learning
explain: Document Intelligence (formerly Form Recognizer) is the prebuilt AI service for OCR plus layout and key-value extraction from documents. OpenAI Service provides language models, Speech handles audio, and Machine Learning is for training custom models — none is the document-extraction specialist.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A social platform needs to automatically detect and filter hate speech, violent imagery, and self-harm content from user uploads. Which Azure AI service provides content moderation?
options: Azure AI Content Safety — detects harmful content in text and images
Azure AI Search
Azure Data Factory
Azure Key Vault
explain: Content Safety is the moderation API: it scores text and images for hate, violence, sexual, and self-harm content. AI Search builds search indexes, Data Factory moves data, and Key Vault stores secrets — none moderate content.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A factory wants to run quality-inspection AI directly on cameras at the production line, continuing to work even when internet connectivity drops. Which Azure IoT service runs cloud workloads on edge devices?
options: Azure IoT Hub
Azure IoT Central
Azure Sphere
Azure IoT Edge — deploys containerized workloads to edge devices for local, offline-capable processing
explain: IoT Edge pushes cloud logic (containers, AI models) down to edge devices so processing happens locally and survives connectivity loss. IoT Hub is the cloud connectivity PaaS, IoT Central is the SaaS app, and Sphere secures the devices themselves — none run workloads on the edge.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A building-management company wants a live digital replica of its office towers — modeling floors, HVAC systems, and sensors — to simulate energy optimizations. Which Azure service builds these virtual models of physical environments?
options: Azure Maps
Azure Digital Twins — creates digital models of physical environments for simulation and monitoring
Azure IoT Central
Azure Monitor
explain: Digital Twins builds graph-based virtual replicas of physical spaces and systems, fed by live sensor data, for simulation and insight. IoT Central is a ready-made device app, Monitor tracks resource telemetry, and Maps handles geospatial data — none models whole physical environments.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A medical-device maker needs its connected devices secured from chip to cloud — hardened hardware, a secured OS, and cloud security monitoring together. Which Azure offering provides this?
options: Azure Firewall
Azure Bastion
Azure Sphere — secured microcontrollers, a secured OS, and cloud security service as one solution
Azure DDoS Protection
explain: Azure Sphere is the end-to-end IoT security solution: certified chips, the Azure Sphere OS, and cloud-based security monitoring. Firewall and DDoS Protection guard networks, Bastion secures admin VM access — none secures the device hardware and OS itself.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A film studio needs to render 10,000 animation frames in parallel, using hundreds of VMs for a few hours, then release them all. Which Azure service orchestrates this kind of large-scale parallel batch computing?
options: Azure Batch — schedules and scales large parallel and HPC batch workloads across VM pools
Azure Functions
Azure App Service
Azure Virtual Desktop
explain: Azure Batch is purpose-built for parallel batch/HPC: it provisions VM pools, schedules thousands of tasks, and tears everything down after. Functions suits event-driven code (not 10,000-way rendering), App Service hosts web apps, and Virtual Desktop delivers desktops.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A bank must run its web apps on fully isolated, single-tenant App Service infrastructure to meet regulatory requirements — no sharing with other customers. Which option provides this?
options: The Free tier
The Shared tier
The Standard tier
An App Service Environment (ASE) — dedicated, isolated App Service infrastructure in the customer's virtual network
explain: An App Service Environment deploys App Service onto dedicated, single-tenant infrastructure inside your VNet — the isolation story. Free/Shared tiers are explicitly multi-tenant shared infrastructure, and Standard is still multi-tenant; only ASE removes the shared tenancy.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team loves Azure Functions' event-driven model but needs two things the Consumption plan lacks: connectivity into its virtual network and no cold starts. Which hosting plan should it choose?
options: The Consumption plan
The Premium plan — adds VNet integration, pre-warmed instances (no cold starts), and longer execution times
Static website hosting
A storage account
explain: The Functions Premium plan keeps the serverless model while adding VNet connectivity, always-ready pre-warmed instances, and extended timeouts. The Consumption plan is the scale-to-zero option that has cold starts and no VNet access; static hosting and storage accounts don't run functions.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company deploys Azure Virtual Desktop for 300 call-center agents who need identical, non-persistent desktops that reset after logoff. Which host pool type fits?
options: A personal host pool
A dedicated physical PC per agent
A pooled host pool — users share session hosts and get a fresh desktop each session, ideal for task workers
Azure Bastion
explain: Pooled host pools serve non-persistent, multi-session desktops — perfect for call centers where agents need identical, resettable sessions. Personal host pools give each user a dedicated persistent desktop (for power users), physical PCs defeat the VDI purpose, and Bastion is admin RDP/SSH, not desktop delivery.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A high-frequency trading firm needs the lowest possible network latency between its Azure VMs. Which feature lets it request that VMs be physically co-located as closely as possible?
options: Proximity placement groups — co-locate VMs on nearby physical hardware to minimize network latency
Availability zones
A VPN gateway
Azure DNS
explain: Proximity placement groups instruct Azure to place VMs on physically adjacent hardware, shaving microseconds off inter-VM latency. Availability zones do the opposite (spread VMs across datacenters for resilience), VPNs connect networks, and DNS resolves names.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company runs Kubernetes clusters on-premises and in another cloud, and wants to manage them all with Azure Policy and Azure Monitor from one place. Which Azure Arc capability enables this?
options: Azure Arc-enabled servers
Azure Stack Hub
Azure Migrate
Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes — projects Azure management, policy, and monitoring onto Kubernetes clusters anywhere
explain: Arc-enabled Kubernetes extends the Azure control plane to clusters on-premises or in other clouds — Policy, Monitor, and Defender apply uniformly. Arc-enabled servers covers VMs (not clusters), Stack Hub runs Azure services on-premises, and Migrate moves workloads rather than managing them in place.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants to modernize its on-premises datacenter with hyperconverged infrastructure that it manages with familiar Windows Admin Center and Azure tools, keeping everything on-site. Which Azure Stack offering fits?
options: Azure Stack Hub
Azure Stack HCI — hyperconverged infrastructure for on-premises virtualized workloads, managed with Azure tooling
Azure Arc
Azure Migrate
explain: Azure Stack HCI is the hyperconverged (compute+storage+networking) on-premises solution for running virtualized workloads locally with Azure management. Stack Hub runs Azure cloud services on-premises, Arc manages existing infrastructure, and Migrate moves workloads to Azure.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A platform team maintains 40 approved ARM templates and wants developers across the company to deploy them from a central, versioned library inside Azure — not from scattered files. What should it use?
options: Email the templates to developers
A storage account with public access
Template Specs — store and version ARM templates as Azure resources for centralized, governed reuse
The Azure status page
explain: Template Specs store ARM templates as versioned Azure resources with RBAC control — a governed template library. Email and public storage lack versioning and access control, and the status page reports service health, not templates.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: During an Azure Migrate assessment of on-premises servers, the tool maps which servers talk to each other and recommends right-sized Azure VM SKUs. These capabilities are called:
options: Dependency mapping and right-sizing recommendations — understanding application topology and matching workloads to appropriately sized Azure resources
A lift-and-shift deployment
DNS resolution
Backup and restore
explain: Assessment isn't just inventory: dependency mapping reveals which servers form an application (so nothing is left behind), and right-sizing uses actual utilization to recommend VM sizes. Lift-and-shift is the migration action, DNS resolves names, and backup is data protection — not assessment.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An operations team wants an email and an automated runbook to trigger whenever a VM's CPU exceeds 85% for 10 minutes. Which Azure Monitor components deliver this?
options: Log Analytics only
Application Insights only
Network Watcher
Metric alerts with action groups — alerts fire on threshold breaches and action groups notify or trigger automation
explain: Azure Monitor metric alerts evaluate conditions (CPU > 85% for 10 min) and invoke action groups, which send emails, SMS, or trigger runbooks/webhooks. Log Analytics queries logs, Application Insights monitors app code, and Network Watcher diagnoses networks — none is the alerting engine.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A junior engineer asks when to use Azure Monitor metrics versus logs. Which explanation is CORRECT?
options: They are the same thing
Metrics are lightweight numeric time-series values (CPU %, request counts) for near-real-time alerting; logs are detailed records of events for deep investigation with KQL
Logs are for billing; metrics are for security
Metrics require Sentinel; logs require a VPN
explain: Metrics = numbers over time, cheap and fast, ideal for dashboards and alerts. Logs = rich event records, queried with KQL for root-cause analysis. They're complementary data types in Monitor — not identical, and neither is billing/security-specific or requires other services.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A virtual machine suddenly becomes unreachable. The engineer needs to know: is this a problem with the VM itself, or is the Azure platform having issues? Which service answers this per-resource question?
options: Azure Service Health
Azure Advisor
Azure Resource Health — reports the health of individual resources and whether issues stem from the platform or the resource
The pricing calculator
explain: Resource Health diagnoses YOUR specific resources ('this VM is unavailable due to a platform event' vs. a guest OS issue). Service Health reports region-wide platform status, Advisor gives optimization recommendations, and the pricing calculator estimates cost — none diagnose an individual VM.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A managed service provider (MSP) supports 30 different customer tenants and wants to manage all of them from its own Azure portal, with customer approval and full audit trails. Which service enables this cross-tenant management?
options: Azure Policy
A single shared subscription
Resource groups
Azure Lighthouse — delegated cross-tenant management with customer-controlled access
explain: Azure Lighthouse lets service providers manage customer tenants from their own tenant, with the customer defining exactly what's delegated — all actions logged in both tenants. A shared subscription would mix billing and boundaries, and Policy/resource groups don't span tenants.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants to enforce Conditional Access policies (for example, requiring MFA for risky sign-ins). What is the licensing prerequisite?
options: Microsoft Entra ID P1 (or P2) — Conditional Access is a premium identity feature, not included in the free tier
Any Microsoft 365 license automatically includes it
No license is required
An Azure storage account
explain: Conditional Access requires Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 licensing — it's the key reason organizations buy P1. The free Entra tier covers basic SSO and per-user MFA but not policy-driven conditional controls. Storage accounts are irrelevant to identity licensing.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Employees on domain-joined office PCs are frustrated by password prompts when opening Microsoft 365 apps, even though they're already signed into Windows. Which feature removes these prompts on the corporate network?
options: Multifactor authentication
Seamless single sign-on — domain-joined devices on the corporate network sign in automatically without re-entering passwords
Azure Bastion
A VPN gateway
explain: Seamless SSO uses Kerberos tickets from the on-premises domain so signed-in Windows users aren't re-prompted for cloud apps. MFA adds verification steps (the opposite of removing prompts), Bastion is VM admin access, and VPNs provide network connectivity.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants every user in the 'Engineering' department automatically added to the 'VPN-Users' group based on their department attribute, with membership updating as people join or leave. What should it use?
options: Manual group management
A spreadsheet of members
Dynamic groups — rule-based membership that updates automatically from user attributes
A resource lock
explain: Dynamic groups evaluate membership rules (department = Engineering) continuously, so joins, moves, and departures update access automatically. Manual management and spreadsheets don't scale and go stale; resource locks protect Azure resources, not group membership.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A custom application needs to authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID and read calendar data via Microsoft Graph, without any user signing in. What identity construct should the developers create?
options: A guest user account
A shared mailbox
A resource group
An app registration — which creates a service principal the application uses to authenticate as itself
explain: App registrations create service principals: identities for applications (not people) that authenticate with secrets or certificates. Guest accounts are for external users, mailboxes are for email, and resource groups organize Azure resources — none gives an app its own identity.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants to stop users from setting easily guessed passwords like 'Spring2026!' across the organization. Which Microsoft Entra feature enforces this?
options: Password protection — blocks known-weak passwords using Microsoft's global banned list plus a custom banned list
Single sign-on
Self-service password reset
Azure Policy
explain: Entra password protection screens new passwords against a global banned-password list (plus org-specific additions), blocking common and breached passwords. SSO simplifies sign-in, SSPR helps locked-out users, and Azure Policy governs Azure resources — not password strength.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An administrator deletes a key vault containing production certificates by mistake. The company had enabled soft delete and purge protection on the vault. What is the outcome?
options: The vault and certificates are permanently lost
Only Microsoft can recover them for a fee
Soft delete retains the deleted vault for 90 days for recovery; purge protection additionally blocks permanent deletion during that period
Purge protection makes deletion impossible, so the delete failed
explain: Soft delete keeps deleted vaults recoverable for 90 days; purge protection prevents anyone (including admins) from permanently purging during retention — guarding against malicious or catastrophic deletion. Recovery is self-service, not a paid Microsoft intervention, and the initial delete still succeeds.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants Azure to automatically add a required 'DataClassification' tag to every storage account at creation time, rather than just flagging missing tags. Which policy effect does this?
options: Audit
Deny
Modify — updates resource properties (like adding tags) during creation or afterward via remediation
Disabled
explain: The Modify effect changes resource properties — here, injecting the tag — instead of merely reporting (Audit) or blocking (Deny). Audit would only flag, Deny would block creation, and Disabled turns the policy off; only Modify actively fixes the configuration.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An enterprise architect is designing a management group hierarchy and asks about limits. Which statement is TRUE?
options: Only one management group is allowed per tenant
Management groups cannot contain subscriptions
Policies cannot be assigned at the management group level
A tenant supports up to 10,000 management groups with up to six levels of depth, and assignments inherit downward
explain: Management groups scale to 10,000 per directory with six levels of depth, and Policy/RBAC assignments inherit to everything below — the whole point of the hierarchy. Single-group limits, subscription exclusion, and assignment restrictions all misstate the design.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A service advertises a 99.99% monthly SLA. Approximately how much downtime does that allow per month?
options: About 4.4 minutes
About 43 minutes
About 7 hours
Zero — 99.99% means no downtime
explain: 0.01% of a ~30-day month is roughly 4.4 minutes of allowed downtime — ten times less than the ~43 minutes a 99.9% SLA allows. Seven hours would be near a 99% SLA, and no SLA promises zero downtime.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A team builds a proof of concept on an Azure service's free tier and asks about its SLA. What should they understand?
options: Free tiers carry the highest SLAs
Free (and preview) services are typically excluded from SLAs — there is no uptime commitment
Free tiers have the same SLA as paid tiers
SLAs double for free tiers
explain: SLAs back paid, generally available services; free tiers and previews are provided as-is with no uptime commitment. Proof-of-concept work is fine, but production workloads should never depend on a tier with no SLA.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A manager wants a single number showing how well the company's Azure environment follows best practices — and whether it's improving month over month. Which Azure Advisor feature provides this?
options: The Azure status page
Cost analysis
The Advisor Score — an aggregated 0-100 rating across Advisor's recommendation categories, tracked over time
Service Health
explain: Advisor Score consolidates recommendation posture into one trackable number across cost, security, reliability, operational excellence, and performance. Cost analysis tracks spending, Service Health tracks platform issues, and the status page shows outages — none score best-practice adherence.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company needs to keep 200 Azure VMs patched on a schedule, with reports showing which machines are missing updates. Which service provides centralized update management?
options: Azure Policy
Microsoft Sentinel
Azure Bastion
Azure Update Manager — schedules patching and reports update compliance across machines
explain: Update Manager (part of Azure's management tooling) orchestrates OS patching schedules and reports compliance across VMs. Policy enforces configuration rules, Sentinel is security analytics, and Bastion provides admin VM access — none schedules or reports on patching.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company runs workloads on Azure but also has servers in AWS. Its CISO wants one security posture dashboard covering both clouds. Which Microsoft Defender for Cloud capability enables this?
options: Defender for Cloud's multicloud protection — connectors extend posture management and threat protection to AWS and GCP
Azure Policy
Microsoft Sentinel
Azure Arc
explain: Defender for Cloud isn't Azure-only: cloud connectors onboard AWS and GCP accounts for unified posture management and workload protection. Policy governs Azure resources, Sentinel is the SIEM/SOAR, and Arc manages servers — none natively unifies multicloud security posture.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A SOC analyst opens a Microsoft Sentinel incident and sees it mapped to tactics like 'Initial Access' and 'Lateral Movement.' What framework is Sentinel using to organize the attack story?
options: The Azure pricing model
MITRE ATT&CK — incidents are mapped to adversary tactics and techniques so analysts understand the attack's stage and methods
The OSI network model
Agile sprint planning
explain: Sentinel maps incidents to the MITRE ATT&CK framework, showing which adversary tactics (initial access, persistence, lateral movement, exfiltration) were observed. The OSI model describes network layers, and pricing/agile frameworks have nothing to do with threat analysis.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A junior engineer asks: 'We have both Azure WAF and DDoS Protection — don't they do the same thing?' What is the CORRECT distinction?
options: They are identical services
DDoS Protection inspects SQL injection; WAF absorbs volumetric floods
WAF protects at Layer 7 against application attacks (SQL injection, cross-site scripting); DDoS Protection absorbs Layer 3/4 volumetric floods — they defend different layers
Only one can be enabled at a time
explain: WAF is the application-layer shield (bad requests, injection, XSS); DDoS Protection is the network-layer shield (massive traffic floods). They complement each other in a defense-in-depth design — the reversed descriptions are the trap, and both can and should run together.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company connects to Azure SQL Database through a private endpoint, but applications can't resolve the database's name to the private IP. What is missing?
options: A VPN gateway
A larger virtual machine
An NSG rule
Private DNS integration — a private DNS zone linked to the VNet so the service name resolves to the private endpoint IP
explain: Private Link gives the service a private IP, but name resolution still needs a private DNS zone linked to the VNet — otherwise apps resolve the public name. VPNs, bigger VMs, and NSG rules don't fix DNS resolution.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A Zero Trust rollout declares: 'The corporate network is no longer the security boundary — identity is.' What does this mean in practice?
options: Identity becomes the primary security perimeter — every access decision is based on verified user and device identity, not network location
Passwords are no longer needed
The company disconnects from the internet
Firewalls are removed
explain: Zero Trust shifts the perimeter from the network to identity: 'never trust, always verify' means access depends on who and what is requesting, with strong authentication and device health — regardless of where the request comes from. It strengthens controls; it doesn't remove passwords, firewalls, or connectivity.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: As part of defense in depth, a team adds strict input validation to its web application so attackers can't inject malicious commands through form fields. Which defense-in-depth layer does this strengthen?
options: The physical security layer
The application layer — validating input blocks injection attacks before they reach deeper layers
The perimeter network layer
The datacenter power supply
explain: Defense in depth spans layers — physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application, data. Input validation is an application-layer control against injection. Physical security, network perimeter, and power are different layers addressing different threats.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants developers to create and manage resources in the 'Dev' resource group, but only view resources in the 'Prod' resource group. How should access be assigned?
options: Assign the Owner role at the subscription scope
Assign the Contributor role at the subscription scope
Assign Contributor scoped to the Dev resource group and Reader scoped to the Prod resource group — RBAC roles apply at the scope where they are assigned
Create a separate Azure subscription for each developer
explain: RBAC assignments are scoped: Contributor on the Dev group grants management there, while Reader on the Prod group grants view-only there — precise least privilege. Subscription-wide Owner or Contributor would over-grant access to production, and per-developer subscriptions are unmanageable.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company enforces strict Conditional Access policies, but keeps two 'break-glass' emergency administrator accounts. How should these accounts be configured?
options: Delete them — emergency accounts are unsafe
Give them to every administrator
Use them for daily administration
Exclude them from Conditional Access policies, monitor their use with alerts, and store credentials securely offline
explain: Break-glass accounts are the last resort if Conditional Access or MFA systems fail — so they're excluded from those policies, heavily monitored, and their credentials kept offline. Deleting them removes the safety net, sharing them destroys accountability, and daily use defeats their purpose.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A security team wants sign-in methods that resist phishing — where stolen passwords alone can't be reused by attackers. Which authentication methods meet this bar?
options: Phishing-resistant methods like FIDO2 security keys and Windows Hello for Business, which use cryptographic proof instead of shareable secrets
SMS codes sent to personal phones
Security questions about childhood pets
Writing passwords on sticky notes
explain: FIDO2 keys and Windows Hello use public-key cryptography bound to the device — there's no password for a phisher to steal and replay. SMS codes can be intercepted, security questions are guessable, and sticky notes are the canonical bad practice.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company buys a one-year reservation for 10 VMs but only uses 6 of them for most of the year. What happens to the unused reservation capacity?
options: Microsoft refunds the unused portion automatically
Unused reservation hours are simply lost — reservations are a use-it-or-lose-it commitment with no rollover or refund
The reservation extends itself by six months
Unused hours convert to Spot VM credit
explain: Reservations trade commitment for discount: you pay for the capacity whether you use it or not, with no rollover, refund, or conversion. That's why reservations suit steady, predictable workloads — overcommitting on spiky usage wastes the discount.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants to apply Azure Hybrid Benefit to its Azure VMs. What is required for the Windows Server licenses it plans to bring?
options: Any old Windows license works
No license is needed at all
The licenses must have active Software Assurance (or equivalent subscription rights) to be eligible
Only retail licenses qualify
explain: Hybrid Benefit requires eligible licenses with active Software Assurance — that's the license-mobility right that makes bring-your-own-license legal. Random old or retail licenses without SA don't qualify, and the benefit is specifically about reusing properly licensed entitlements.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A finance team sets a monthly budget and wants to be warned not only when spending crosses 90% of the budget, but also when the current burn rate is FORECAST to exceed it by month-end. Which budget alert type covers the second case?
options: Actual-cost alerts only
Reservation utilization alerts
Quota alerts
Forecasted-cost alerts — budgets can trigger on projected month-end spend, giving early warning before the money is actually spent
explain: Azure budgets support both actual and forecasted alerts: forecasted alerts fire when the projected month-end total will breach the threshold — the early warning. Actual-cost alerts only fire after spending crosses the line, which is too late for prevention.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A CIO using the TCO calculator is surprised it asks about datacenter power, cooling, and IT administrator salaries — not just server prices. Why?
options: The TCO calculator compares total cost of ownership — facilities, power, and staffing are real on-premises costs the cloud eliminates or reduces
The calculator is malfunctioning
Power costs don't matter
Only hardware prices count in TCO
explain: Total cost of ownership means ALL costs: hardware plus the building, electricity, cooling, network gear, and people to run it. Server sticker price alone wildly understates on-premises cost — capturing the full picture is the TCO calculator's entire purpose.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An architect presents pricing-calculator estimates to the CFO as guaranteed final costs. What important caveat should the architect have included?
options: The calculator is always wrong
Estimates are not quotes — actual costs depend on real usage, and Azure prices can change, so estimates guide planning but don't guarantee the bill
The CFO should never see estimates
Calculator estimates are legally binding contracts
explain: The pricing calculator produces estimates from assumed usage — real bills follow metered consumption, and prices are subject to change. Treating an estimate as a binding quote sets false expectations; honest framing is 'planning guidance, not a guaranteed invoice.'
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A team tries to create a resource tag named 'azure-costcenter' and it fails. What is the likely reason?
options: Tags cannot contain hyphens
Tags are limited to 5 characters
Tag names cannot use reserved prefixes like 'azure', 'microsoft', or 'windows' — these are reserved for Azure's own use
Tags can only be applied on Tuesdays
explain: Azure reserves the 'azure', 'microsoft', and 'windows' tag-name prefixes for platform use — customer tags with those prefixes are rejected. Hyphens are fine, tags allow far more than 5 characters, and there's no day-of-week restriction.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A team wants to prevent developers from deploying expensive VM sizes, while still allowing all other changes. Which approach is correct, and why?
options: Apply a CanNotDelete lock to the subscription — it blocks expensive VM deployments
Apply a ReadOnly lock — it still allows deploying cheap VMs
Azure Policy cannot restrict VM sizes
Assign an Azure Policy with a Deny effect on disallowed VM SKUs — policies evaluate each request against rules, while locks can only freeze resources wholesale
explain: A Deny policy on VM SKUs blocks exactly the expensive sizes and allows everything else — the precise tool.
