CanNotDelete only blocks deletions (not creations), ReadOnly blocks all changes (too blunt), and Policy absolutely can restrict SKUs. Policies judge requests against rules; locks freeze resources.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: In Azure Resource Health, a VM shows as 'Degraded' rather than 'Unavailable.' What does this distinction tell the engineer?
options: Degraded means the VM is running but performing below expected levels — a partial issue — while Unavailable means it cannot be reached at all
They mean exactly the same thing
Degraded is worse than Unavailable
Resource Health only reports billing issues
explain: Resource Health states are precise: Available (healthy), Degraded (running but impaired), Unavailable (down), Unknown (no telemetry). 'Degraded' points toward performance investigation rather than outage response — the distinction shapes the troubleshooting path.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A European company wants assurance that its Azure customer data stays within the EU for storage and processing. Which Microsoft commitment addresses this?
options: The Azure free account
The EU Data Boundary — Microsoft's commitment to store and process EU customer data within the EU
A VPN gateway
Spot virtual machines
explain: The EU Data Boundary is Microsoft's public commitment that in-scope customer data for EU customers stays in the EU. Region selection controls where resources deploy, but the Data Boundary is the overarching data-residency commitment. VPNs, free accounts, and Spot VMs are unrelated.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants to automatically block employees from emailing spreadsheets containing credit-card numbers to external addresses. Which Microsoft Purview capability provides this data-loss protection?
options: Purview Data Map
Azure Firewall
Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) — policies that detect sensitive data and block or warn on risky sharing
Azure Bastion
explain: Purview DLP defines policies that detect sensitive information types (credit cards, SSNs) and block or warn when users try to share them externally. The Data Map catalogs data, Firewall filters network traffic, and Bastion secures VM admin access — none inspects email content for sensitive data.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company runs Azure Stack Hub in its own datacenter. A physical intruder steals a server from the rack. Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for the physical security failure?
options: Microsoft, because it's Azure software
The internet service provider
The hardware vendor
The customer — with Azure Stack Hub on-premises, the customer owns the datacenter facility and its physical security
explain: Shared responsibility follows the deployment: in the public cloud Microsoft secures the facilities, but Azure Stack Hub runs in YOUR datacenter — so physical security, power, and cooling are yours. The software being Microsoft's doesn't transfer responsibility for your building.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company moves its on-premises SQL Server database to Azure SQL Database. It keeps the same schema and queries, changing only the connection strings in its application. Which migration strategy is this?
options: Replatform — moving to a managed cloud platform with minor adjustments
Rehost — lifting the workload as-is onto virtual machines
Repurchase — replacing the workload with a different product
Retain — keeping the workload on-premises
explain: Replatform means moving to a managed platform (PaaS) with small optimizations — here, swapping SQL Server for Azure SQL Database with only connection-string changes. Rehost would mean moving the database as-is onto Azure VMs; repurchase means buying a different product entirely; retain means leaving it on-premises.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A retailer shuts down its aging on-premises CRM and moves users to Dynamics 365, a SaaS product. Users learn new software rather than using a moved copy of the old system. Which migration strategy is this?
options: Rehost
Repurchase — replacing the workload with a different, usually SaaS, product
Replatform
Refactor
explain: Repurchase means dropping the old application and buying or subscribing to a different product — typically SaaS. Rehost moves the existing app as-is; replatform makes minor cloud optimizations; refactor means significantly rewriting the application architecture.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: During migration planning, a company discovers twelve applications that nobody has opened in over two years. What is the most cost-effective cloud strategy for these applications?
options: Rehost them onto Azure virtual machines
Replatform them to managed PaaS services
Retire — decommission them instead of migrating anything
Retain them on-premises indefinitely
explain: Retire means identifying workloads that are no longer needed and shutting them down rather than paying to migrate and run them. Rehosting or replatforming unused apps wastes migration effort and ongoing cloud spend; retaining them keeps the on-premises burden alive for no benefit.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A factory's production-line control system cannot leave the on-premises datacenter yet because the vendor's support contract requires it. The migration plan leaves that system in place while everything else moves to Azure. Which strategy is this?
options: Rehost
Replatform
Refactor
Retain — deliberately keeping a workload on-premises for now
explain: Retain means consciously keeping a workload on-premises (for contractual, compliance, or technical reasons) while migrating the rest. Rehost, replatform, and refactor all describe ways of moving a workload to the cloud, which is the opposite of what's happening here.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company keeps only backups and documented rebuild procedures in a secondary region — no running servers there. After a disaster it would rebuild everything from scratch, accepting many hours of downtime. This disaster-recovery design is called a:
options: Cold site — minimal cost, longest recovery time
Hot site
Warm site
Active-active deployment
explain: A cold site keeps no running infrastructure — just backups and runbooks — so it is the cheapest option but takes the longest to bring online. A hot site runs a full synchronized duplicate; a warm site keeps a scaled-down running copy; active-active serves traffic from both sites continuously.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A bank runs a full duplicate of its trading platform in a paired Azure region, continuously synchronized with production and ready to take traffic instantly if the primary region fails. This disaster-recovery design is called a:
options: Cold site
Hot site — fully running duplicate with near-zero recovery time
Backup vault
Development environment
explain: A hot site is a fully provisioned, continuously synchronized duplicate that can take over almost immediately — the most expensive DR design but with the shortest recovery time. A cold site has no running servers; a backup vault only stores backup data; a dev environment is not a DR strategy.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An architect explains availability sets: 'Fault domains protect your VMs against unplanned hardware failures. Update domains protect them against:'
options: DDoS attacks
Entire region failures
Planned maintenance, such as host operating-system patching
Accidental deletion by administrators
explain: Update domains ensure VMs are not rebooted simultaneously during planned Azure maintenance like host patching. Fault domains guard against unplanned hardware faults (a failed rack); neither protects against region-wide outages, DDoS, or admin mistakes.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An administrator shuts down an Azure virtual machine from inside the guest operating system (Start > Shut down). In the portal the VM shows 'Stopped' — not 'Stopped (deallocated)'. What happens to compute billing?
options: Compute billing stops immediately
The VM is automatically deleted after 24 hours
Storage billing also stops
Compute billing continues until the VM is deallocated
explain: Shutting down from inside the guest OS leaves the VM allocated on an Azure host, so compute charges continue — only deallocating (via the portal, CLI, or API) releases the hardware and stops compute billing. Storage charges continue either way while the disks exist; nothing is auto-deleted.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Which of the following is an operational expenditure (OpEx)?
options: The monthly Azure bill for resources actually consumed
Purchasing a server rack for the company datacenter
Buying a datacenter building
A perpetual software license paid upfront
explain: OpEx is ongoing spending on consumed services — like the monthly cloud bill. Buying servers, buildings, or perpetual licenses are capital expenditures: large upfront investments in assets the company owns and depreciates.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs 40 virtual machines at steady 70% utilization, 24 hours a day, with no expected change for two years. Which purchasing approach minimizes its compute cost?
options: Pay-as-you-go pricing for all 40 VMs
Committing to one- or three-year reservations for the steady baseline
Running everything on Spot VMs
Rebuilding every VM from scratch each month
explain: Reservations give deep discounts in exchange for a one- or three-year commitment — ideal for steady, predictable baselines. Pay-as-you-go costs more per hour; Spot VMs can be evicted and don't suit constant production workloads; rebuilding monthly adds work without lowering the hourly rate.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An Azure Function executes for about 200 milliseconds per run, a few hundred times a day, and scales to zero between runs. Why is this far cheaper than running the same code on an always-on virtual machine?
options: Microsoft subsidizes every function execution
Virtual machines cannot run event-driven code
The customer pays only for the milliseconds of execution time, and nothing while scaled to zero
Functions include a free virtual machine
explain: Serverless billing is purely consumption-based: you pay for execution time (measured in milliseconds) and pay nothing when the function scales to zero. An always-on VM bills for every hour it exists whether code runs or not; Microsoft does not subsidize executions.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A health insurer's enrollment portal is quiet for eleven months, then receives fifty times its normal traffic during a three-week open-enrollment window. Which approach fits best?
options: Buying servers sized for the three-week peak and letting them idle the rest of the year
Throttling users with a waiting room during enrollment
Rewriting the portal from scratch every year
Using elastic auto-scaling so peak capacity exists only during enrollment
explain: Elasticity automatically adds capacity for the enrollment surge and removes it afterward, so the insurer pays for peak resources only while they are needed. Sizing for peak wastes eleven months of idle hardware; throttling hurts customers; annual rewrites don't address capacity at all.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An accounting firm's tax application sees ten times its normal usage from January through April, then drops back to a trickle. With cloud elasticity, the firm's infrastructure spending will:
options: Rise only during the January–April surge and fall back afterward
Stay flat because elasticity requires annual contracts
Be impossible to predict
Require buying permanent peak-capacity licenses
explain: Elasticity scales resources with demand in both directions, so costs follow the seasonal curve — up during tax season, down after. There is no requirement for annual contracts or permanent peak licenses; and because scaling is automatic and metered, the pattern is predictable, not random.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A competitor launches a new feature. A cloud-native retailer prototypes, tests, and deploys its response in nine days using on-demand environments — no hardware procurement. This primarily demonstrates which cloud benefit?
options: Elasticity
Agility — the ability to develop, test, and deploy quickly
Geo-distribution
Fault tolerance
explain: Agility is speed of change: provisioning environments in minutes lets the retailer respond in days instead of waiting months for hardware. Elasticity is about scaling capacity with demand; geo-distribution is about placing resources near users; fault tolerance is about surviving failures.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A startup tests a risky product idea using cloud resources for three weeks, then shuts everything down when the idea flops. Its total infrastructure loss is three weeks of usage. This illustrates which cloud benefit?
options: Capital preservation through asset ownership
Vendor lock-in
Low-cost experimentation — a failed idea costs only what was consumed
Guaranteed product success
explain: Because cloud resources need no upfront purchase and billing stops on deletion, experiments are cheap to run and cheap to abandon. This is the opposite of capital preservation through ownership (CapEx); it doesn't involve lock-in, and nothing about the cloud guarantees an idea succeeds.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company backs up its database every 6 hours and can restore service within 2 hours of an outage. What are its Recovery Point Objective (RPO) and Recovery Time Objective (RTO)?
options: RPO 2 hours, RTO 6 hours
RPO 8 hours, RTO 4 hours
RPO and RTO are both 6 hours
RPO 6 hours, RTO 2 hours
explain: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss — set by backup frequency (6 hours). RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime — set by restore speed (2 hours). Swapping them is the classic trap: frequency determines RPO, restore speed determines RTO.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A trading firm requires an RPO of 15 minutes — it cannot afford to lose more than 15 minutes of transactions. Why are nightly backups insufficient for this requirement?
options: Nightly backups can only achieve a 24-hour RPO, so the firm needs near-continuous replication
Backups cannot be encrypted
RPO measures restore speed, not data loss
15 minutes is longer than 24 hours
explain: RPO is bounded by how often data is captured: a backup taken once a day means up to 24 hours of data could be lost. Meeting a 15-minute RPO requires replication or backups every 15 minutes or less. RPO measures data loss (not restore speed), and encryption is unrelated.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs its application live in one Azure region and keeps a standby copy in a paired region that receives replicated data but serves no traffic until a failover occurs. This is an example of:
options: Active-active
Active-passive — the standby serves traffic only after failover
Multicloud
Serverless computing
explain: In active-passive, one site is live while the standby stays synchronized and idle until failover. Active-active serves traffic from both sites simultaneously; multicloud means using multiple providers; serverless is a compute model, not a DR topology.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A vendor advertises a 99.9% SLA. A customer assumes this means the service will never go down. What is wrong with this assumption?
options: SLAs apply only to free service tiers
99.9% is mathematically equal to 100%
An SLA is a financially backed commitment, not a promise that outages never happen
SLAs are not legally enforceable
explain: A 99.9% SLA allows roughly 43.8 minutes of downtime per month and backs the target with service credits — it does not promise zero outages. The 'never goes down' reading confuses a commercial commitment with a technical guarantee; SLAs apply to paid tiers and are enforceable per their terms.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A CIO believes moving to a private cloud will eliminate hardware purchasing and maintenance costs. What is the flaw in this thinking?
options: Private clouds are free to operate
Private cloud hardware never fails
The organization still funds, houses, and maintains the underlying hardware
Private clouds require no IT staff at all
explain: A private cloud is still dedicated infrastructure the organization owns or leases — someone buys the servers, powers and cools them, and replaces them. The cloud operating model doesn't remove the hardware burden; only a public cloud shifts it to the provider. The other options describe fantasies, not private cloud.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company is migrating 200 applications over 18 months. During the transition, some applications run on-premises while others already run in Azure, all managed together. This phased approach is an example of:
options: Hybrid cloud supporting a gradual, phased migration
Public cloud only
Multicloud
Pure SaaS adoption
explain: Hybrid cloud deliberately combines on-premises and public cloud resources in one coordinated environment — exactly what a phased migration looks like. It isn't public-only (some workloads stay on-prem), isn't multicloud (one public provider plus on-prem), and isn't pure SaaS.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company adopts a multicloud strategy to avoid vendor lock-in, but finds data-transfer fees between providers and duplicated tooling are erasing the expected savings. This illustrates that multicloud:
options: Is always cheaper than single-cloud
Introduces data-egress charges and duplicated operational complexity that must be weighed against lock-in concerns
Makes egress within one provider expensive
Eliminates vendor lock-in entirely
explain: Moving data between providers incurs egress charges, and each platform needs its own skills, tooling, and security controls — real costs that offset lock-in benefits. Multicloud reduces single-vendor dependence but never eliminates switching costs, and it is not inherently cheaper.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company using a SaaS CRM wakes up to a redesigned interface after an overnight vendor upgrade it could not postpone. This demonstrates that with SaaS:
options: Customers approve every upgrade before it happens
SaaS applications never receive updates
The vendor controls the application, including when upgrades roll out
Upgrades require new customer hardware
explain: In SaaS the provider manages the entire application stack, so upgrade timing is the vendor's decision — the trade-off for never patching anything yourself. Customers don't approve each release, the software absolutely does change, and no customer hardware is involved.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A team deploys its web application to Azure App Service (PaaS) and assumes Microsoft will find and fix vulnerabilities in the team's own application code. What is the reality?
options: Microsoft reviews all customer application code
PaaS includes free penetration testing of customer code
Microsoft rewrites any insecure customer code it finds
The customer remains responsible for securing its own application code
explain: PaaS removes platform patching (OS, runtime) from the customer's plate, but application-layer security — secure coding, dependency updates, input validation — stays with the customer under the shared responsibility model. Microsoft never reviews or rewrites your code.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company closes its small, inefficient on-premises server closet and moves to Azure. Which environmental argument genuinely supports this move?
options: Hyperscale datacenters operate far more efficiently per workload than small server closets
Cloud servers consume no electricity
On-premises servers are carbon negative
Energy efficiency is unrelated to scale
explain: Large cloud datacenters use advanced cooling, higher utilization, and bulk power purchasing, making them far more energy-efficient per unit of compute than a half-empty server closet. They still consume electricity — just much less per workload — and scale is precisely what drives the efficiency.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An architect must design a virtual-machine-based application for a 99.99% SLA. A single Azure VM carries a lower SLA, so the design must:
options: Use one larger VM instead of two smaller ones
Add redundancy — for example, deploying VMs across availability zones behind a load balancer
Attach a faster disk to the single VM
Disable monitoring to reduce overhead
explain: Higher SLAs are earned through redundancy: distributing instances across fault-isolated zones means one failure doesn't stop the application. A bigger single VM is still a single point of failure; faster disks and disabled monitoring don't change availability math.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five essential characteristics of cloud computing defined by NIST?
options: On-demand self-service
Measured service
Customer ownership of the provider's physical datacenters
Rapid elasticity
explain: NIST's five characteristics are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service. Customers never own the provider's physical datacenters — that would defeat the entire cloud model of shared, provider-managed infrastructure.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An Australian company must keep customer data inside Australia for legal reasons, but its European customers complain about slow response times. This scenario illustrates the tension between:
options: CapEx and OpEx
Public cloud and private cloud pricing
SaaS and PaaS
Data residency requirements and the latency benefits of geo-distribution
explain: Data residency rules can pin data to one geography, while geo-distribution (placing resources near users) reduces latency — the two goals pull in opposite directions here. This has nothing to do with CapEx/OpEx accounting, cloud pricing models, or the SaaS/PaaS distinction.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Compared with virtual machines, containers are attractive for microservices architectures primarily because they:
options: Share the host operating-system kernel, so they start faster and consume fewer resources than VMs
Each include a full guest operating system
Are automatically more secure than virtual machines
Cannot be orchestrated at scale
explain: Containers share the host OS kernel instead of virtualizing hardware per workload, so they start in seconds and pack densely — ideal for many small microservices. They don't include a guest OS, aren't inherently more secure, and are routinely orchestrated by platforms like Kubernetes.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A ten-person company wants GPT-powered chat in its support portal but owns no GPUs and employs no machine-learning engineers. The cloud makes this feasible through:
options: Buying a supercomputer
Managed AI services consumed via API, with no ML infrastructure to build or maintain
Hiring fifty ML engineers
Training models on employee laptops
explain: Managed AI services (like Azure OpenAI) expose powerful models through simple APIs — the provider trains and hosts the models, so a small team gets advanced AI with zero ML infrastructure. Buying hardware or hiring a research team would defeat the economic advantage.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company closes three regional datacenters and moves everything to Azure. Beyond eliminating server purchases, it also eliminates:
options: Its entire IT staff
The need for any network connectivity
Power, cooling, physical security, and hardware-refresh burdens of owned facilities
All software licensing costs
explain: Owning datacenters means paying for electricity, cooling, guards, and replacing aging hardware — all of which disappear with the facilities. IT staff still manage cloud resources, network connectivity is still required, and software licenses are a separate concern.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: After acquiring a smaller firm, a company provisions cloud identities, virtual machines, and applications for 300 new employees in two weeks — with no hardware orders or datacenter build-out. This demonstrates cloud:
options: Vendor lock-in
Higher capital expenditure
Mandatory retraining
Agility — resources provision in days instead of months of procurement
explain: Agility is the ability to obtain and change IT resources at the speed of business: two weeks versus months of hardware procurement. This scenario shows speed and flexibility, not lock-in, higher CapEx (there is none), or retraining.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A service advertises a 99.95% monthly SLA. Approximately how much downtime per month does that SLA allow?
options: About 22 minutes per month
About 4 hours per month
About 43 minutes per day
Zero downtime
explain: 99.95% allows 0.05% downtime: 0.0005 × ~43,800 minutes in a month ≈ 22 minutes. Four hours would be roughly 99.4%, and no SLA below 100% promises zero downtime — each additional 'nine' cuts allowed downtime roughly tenfold.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A banking regulator requires that customer records remain restorable even if the company's primary datacenter is destroyed. The company replicates encrypted backups to a distant Azure region. This primarily addresses:
options: High availability
Disaster recovery through geographic redundancy
Elasticity
Agility
explain: Keeping a restorable copy in a distant region protects against site loss — the essence of disaster recovery via geographic redundancy. High availability is about minimizing downtime of the live system; elasticity and agility concern scaling and speed of change, not surviving datacenter destruction.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A team wants a workflow that runs with no code: when a support email arrives, create a Planner task and post a message to Teams. Which Azure service is built for this kind of automated workflow?
options: Azure Functions
Azure Batch
Azure Logic Apps — serverless, no-code workflow automation across apps and services
Azure Arc
explain: Logic Apps is the serverless integration platform for no-code workflows with hundreds of prebuilt connectors (email, Teams, Planner). Functions requires writing code; Batch is for large-scale parallel HPC jobs; Arc manages non-Azure resources.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company exposes its booking API to external travel partners and needs rate limiting, usage analytics, and a self-service developer portal. Which Azure service provides this?
options: Azure DNS
Traffic Manager
Azure Front Door
Azure API Management
explain: API Management publishes, secures, and governs APIs — with throttling/quotas, analytics, and a developer portal for partners. DNS resolves names, Traffic Manager routes DNS traffic, and Front Door is a global entry point — none provide API governance.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A web application stores shopping-cart session state in a fast in-memory store so that any web instance can serve any user. Which Azure service fits this need?
options: Azure Cache for Redis — an in-memory data store for low-latency scenarios like session state
Azure Blob storage
Azure Files
Azure Data Box
explain: Azure Cache for Redis is a managed in-memory store built for sub-millisecond reads like session state and caching. Blob storage and Files are persistent disk-based storage (too slow for this use); Data Box is for offline bulk data transfer.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An administrator stores a database's transaction logs on a VM's temporary disk. After Azure moves the VM to a different host for maintenance, the logs are gone. Why?
options: The disk was encrypted
Temporary disk data is not persisted when the VM moves to another host
Azure deleted the resource group
Temporary disks are read-only
explain: The temporary disk is local scratch space on the physical host — its contents survive reboots but are lost when the VM is moved, resized, or redeployed. Durable data belongs on OS or data disks (managed disks); encryption and resource-group deletion had nothing to do with it.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Two virtual machines are placed in an availability set. What does Azure guarantee about their placement?
options: They run in different Azure regions
They share a single physical host for lower latency
They are spread across fault domains so a single rack failure cannot stop both
They automatically replicate each other's data
explain: Availability sets distribute VMs across fault domains (separate racks with independent power/network) and update domains, so one hardware failure or maintenance event can't take down every instance. They stay in the same datacenter — not different regions — and provide placement isolation, not data replication.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants all DNS-based traffic sent to its primary Azure region, failing over to the secondary region only if the primary becomes unhealthy. Which Traffic Manager routing method does this?
options: Performance
Weighted
Geographic
Priority — all traffic goes to the primary endpoint until health checks fail
explain: Priority routing designates a primary endpoint that receives all traffic, with ordered backups taking over on health-check failure — the classic active-passive DR pattern. Performance routes by lowest latency, Weighted splits by ratio, and Geographic routes by user location.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A global application needs instant failover between regional deployments with continuous health probes, plus content cached at the edge near users. Which Azure service delivers both?
options: Azure Front Door — global entry point with instant failover, health probes, and edge caching
Azure Load Balancer
Azure Virtual WAN
Azure Bastion
explain: Front Door is Microsoft's global Layer-7 entry point: it health-probes backends for fast failover and caches content at edge locations. Load Balancer is regional; Virtual WAN connects networks; Bastion provides VM admin access — none combine global failover with edge caching.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company uses ExpressRoute. Traffic to its Azure virtual machines should flow over private peering, while its Microsoft 365 traffic should use:
options: The public internet only
Microsoft peering — the ExpressRoute peering type for Microsoft 365 and other public Microsoft services
A second VPN connection
Private peering for everything
explain: ExpressRoute offers private peering (for VNet/Azure compute traffic) and Microsoft peering (for Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, and other public Microsoft services). Routing M365 over private peering is incorrect, and Microsoft peering is precisely the supported path for it over the private circuit.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company has ExpressRoute circuits in New York and London. It wants the two on-premises sites to communicate privately through Microsoft's backbone instead of the public internet. Which feature enables this?
options: ExpressRoute Direct
VNet peering
ExpressRoute Global Reach — connects two ExpressRoute circuits via Microsoft's network
Point-to-site VPN
explain: Global Reach links two ExpressRoute circuits so on-premises sites communicate privately across Microsoft's backbone. ExpressRoute Direct is about higher-bandwidth circuit connectivity; VNet peering connects virtual networks (not on-prem sites); point-to-site VPN serves individual clients.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: VNet-A is peered with VNet-B, and VNet-B is peered with VNet-C. Can a virtual machine in VNet-A reach VNet-C through VNet-B?
options: Yes — peering is fully transitive
Yes, automatically after 24 hours
Only with ExpressRoute
No — VNet peering is non-transitive, so VNet-A needs its own direct peering to VNet-C
explain: VNet peering is non-transitive: each peering is an independent link, so A cannot ride B's peering to reach C. Connectivity requires a direct A–C peering or a hub-and-spoke design with routing through a hub appliance. There is no waiting period or ExpressRoute requirement involved.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An engineer tries to deploy a regular virtual machine into the GatewaySubnet alongside the VPN gateway. What happens?
options: The deployment is blocked because GatewaySubnet is reserved exclusively for gateway use
It succeeds but with higher latency
The VPN gateway automatically moves to another subnet
Nothing — subnets have no usage restrictions
explain: GatewaySubnet is reserved solely for VPN and ExpressRoute gateways; Azure blocks any other resource deployment there. The gateway doesn't relocate, latency is irrelevant, and this particular subnet absolutely has a usage restriction.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants to host DNS records for its public internet domain (contoso.com) in Azure for fast, resilient global resolution. Which service should it use?
options: Azure Private DNS
Azure DNS public hosting — authoritative DNS for internet-facing domains
Hosts files on each server
Azure Firewall
explain: Azure DNS public zones authoritatively host internet-facing domains on Microsoft's global anycast network. Private DNS zones resolve names only inside virtual networks; hosts files don't scale; Firewall filters traffic rather than serving DNS.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A network security group allows inbound HTTPS to a web VM. Must the administrator also create an outbound rule so the VM's HTTPS responses can return to clients?
options: Yes, always
Only on weekends
No — NSGs are stateful, so return traffic for allowed connections is automatically permitted
Only for UDP traffic
explain: NSGs are stateful: once a connection is allowed in one direction, its return traffic is automatically allowed without a matching rule in the other direction. No extra outbound rule is needed for HTTPS responses, regardless of protocol or day of the week.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company hosts an internal web server with only a private IP address, but business partners must reach it from the internet through Azure Firewall. Which rule type publishes the server externally?
options: Application rule
Network rule
Threat intelligence alert
DNAT rule — translates the firewall's public IP to the server's private IP
explain: A DNAT (destination NAT) rule maps the firewall's public IP and port to the internal server's private address, publishing it safely. Application and network rules control outbound/allowed traffic flows rather than inbound publishing; threat intelligence only detects malicious destinations.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Azure Firewall raises an alert when a virtual machine attempts to contact a known malicious IP address. Which capability produces this detection?
options: Threat intelligence-based filtering — matching traffic against feeds of known malicious addresses
DNAT rules
TLS inspection
BGP route learning
explain: Threat intelligence-based filtering compares traffic against Microsoft's feeds of known malicious IPs and domains, alerting on or denying matches. DNAT publishes internal servers, TLS inspection decrypts traffic, and BGP handles routing — none identify known-bad destinations.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company reads its stored blobs many times every day. Which access tier minimizes its total cost, and why?
options: Archive — it is always the cheapest tier
Hot — higher per-GB storage cost but the lowest access and transaction costs, which suits frequent reads
Cool — designed for data read daily
Premium — required for all blob reads
explain: The Hot tier charges more per gigabyte stored but the least per access — the right trade-off for frequently read data. Cool and Archive slash storage prices but raise per-access fees, punishing daily reads; Premium tiers target low-latency workloads, not general cost savings.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Why must Azure virtual machine disks use page blobs rather than block blobs?
options: Block blobs cannot be encrypted
Page blobs are always cheaper
Page blobs support the random read/write operations that virtual disks require
Block blobs do not support redundancy
explain: Page blobs are optimized for random read/write I/O, which is exactly how virtual disks behave. Block blobs are optimized for sequential streaming uploads (documents, media). Both support encryption and redundancy; cost isn't the deciding factor.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An administrator needs an ad-hoc graphical tool to browse storage accounts, view blobs, and upload files — without writing scripts. Which tool fits?
options: AzCopy
Azure Data Box
ARM templates
Azure Storage Explorer — a free GUI for managing storage accounts
explain: Storage Explorer is the free graphical tool for browsing and managing storage accounts interactively. AzCopy is a command-line bulk-copy utility; Data Box is physical hardware for offline transfers; ARM templates deploy infrastructure rather than managing stored data.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A startup's application is built on MySQL, and the team does not want to manage database servers, patching, or backups. Which Azure PaaS option fits?
options: Azure Database for MySQL — a fully managed MySQL service
SQL Server on Azure virtual machines
Azure Cosmos DB Gremlin API
Azure Files
explain: Azure Database for MySQL (Flexible Server) is the managed PaaS offering: Microsoft handles patching, backups, and high availability. SQL Server on VMs is IaaS (self-managed); Cosmos DB's Gremlin API is a graph database; Azure Files is file storage, not a database.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Analysts need a petabyte-scale data warehouse with predictable performance for heavy nightly reporting. Within Azure Synapse Analytics, which compute option fits?
options: Serverless SQL pool
Dedicated SQL pool — provisioned resources delivering predictable data-warehouse performance
Azure Cosmos DB
Azure Data Factory
explain: Dedicated SQL pools provision reserved compute for consistent, predictable warehouse performance at scale. Serverless SQL pools are pay-per-query for ad-hoc exploration; Cosmos DB is a NoSQL operational database; Data Factory orchestrates data movement rather than serving queries.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Match each need to the right messaging service: (1) react instantly when a file lands in Blob storage, (2) ingest millions of telemetry events per second, (3) guaranteed ordered delivery of payment messages.
options: Service Bus, Event Grid, Event Hubs
Event Hubs, Service Bus, Event Grid
Event Grid, Event Hubs, Service Bus
Event Grid for all three
explain: Event Grid routes discrete events (like blob creation) to handlers; Event Hubs ingests massive telemetry streams; Service Bus provides enterprise messaging with ordering, transactions, and guaranteed delivery. Each is purpose-built — one service can't cover all three patterns well.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A retailer wants to score thousands of product reviews as positive, negative, or neutral through an API — without training any machine-learning models. Which Azure AI service does this?
options: Azure OpenAI
Azure AI Translator
Azure AI Content Safety
Azure AI Language — with prebuilt sentiment analysis
explain: Azure AI Language offers prebuilt sentiment analysis: send text, get a sentiment score, no model training required. OpenAI is for generative scenarios; Translator converts languages; Content Safety detects harmful content rather than sentiment.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A support portal must translate help articles into forty languages on demand. Which Azure AI service is purpose-built for this?
options: Azure AI Translator — real-time and document text translation
Azure AI Speech
Azure AI Vision
Azure AI Language
explain: Translator is the dedicated text-translation service covering 100+ languages. Speech handles audio, Vision handles images, and Language handles text analytics like sentiment — none translate documents between languages.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A call center wants customer voicemails automatically transcribed into text for its ticketing system. Which Azure AI service converts speech to text?
options: Azure AI Translator
Azure AI Speech — including speech-to-text transcription
Azure AI Content Safety
Azure AI Document Intelligence
explain: Azure AI Speech provides speech-to-text (plus text-to-speech and translation of spoken language). Translator works on written text, Content Safety moderates harmful content, and Document Intelligence extracts data from documents — not audio.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company adopts Azure OpenAI but worries its prompts and data will be used to train public models. What is Microsoft's published commitment?
options: All prompts are used to train the base models
Prompts are shared with advertisers
Customer prompts and data are not used to train foundation models
Training use cannot be avoided
explain: Microsoft states that data sent to Azure OpenAI — prompts, completions, and fine-tuning data — is not used to train foundation models, and data stays within the chosen boundary. The distractors describe practices Microsoft explicitly disavows for the service.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An IoT solution must track each device's reported firmware version and push desired configuration settings to individual devices. Which IoT Hub feature provides this per-device state?
options: Device Provisioning Service only
IoT Central
Event Grid
Device twins — JSON documents holding desired and reported properties per device
explain: Device twins are JSON documents per device with 'desired' properties (set by the solution) and 'reported' properties (sent by the device) — ideal for configuration and firmware tracking. Provisioning only onboards devices; IoT Central is the SaaS app platform; Event Grid routes events rather than storing device state.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A logistics application needs route optimization, geofencing, and map rendering APIs for its delivery fleet. Which Azure service provides geospatial capabilities?
options: Azure Maps — geospatial APIs for routes, geofencing, and maps
IoT Hub
Azure Batch
Azure Front Door
explain: Azure Maps is the geospatial service: routing, geofencing, and map rendering APIs. IoT Hub manages devices, Batch runs parallel compute jobs, and Front Door is a global traffic entry point — none provide mapping APIs.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A bank wants its own mobile app to send SMS one-time passcodes through an API, without building telecom infrastructure. Which Azure service adds messaging, voice, and video capabilities to applications?
options: Notification Hubs
Azure Communication Services — SMS, voice, video, and chat APIs
Azure Logic Apps
Event Grid
explain: Azure Communication Services exposes SMS, voice, video, and chat as APIs so apps gain telecom features without carrier infrastructure. Notification Hubs only push mobile notifications; Logic Apps orchestrates workflows; Event Grid routes events.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Two web apps share a single App Service plan. What does the plan determine for both apps?
options: The application code they run
The database engine they use
The region, operating system, pricing tier, and scaling shared by the apps in the plan
Only their custom domain names
explain: The App Service plan defines the compute foundation — region, OS, pricing tier (VM size), and instance count/scale — shared by every app in it. Apps keep their own code, databases, and domains; the plan is about the underlying compute, not the applications.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A design firm uses Azure Virtual Desktop and needs each engineer to keep installed tools, settings, and files between sessions — the same desktop every time. Which host-pool type fits?
options: Pooled — users get a random fresh VM each session
RemoteApp only
Host pools cannot persist user state
Personal — each user is assigned their own VM, so state persists
explain: Personal (persistent) host pools assign one VM per user, preserving everything between sessions. Pooled (non-persistent) pools give users any available VM with a fresh profile each time — cheaper for task workers but wrong for engineers needing persistent desktops.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants cloud PCs with zero infrastructure management — Microsoft handles everything behind a simple per-user monthly price. Which is the SaaS option?
options: Windows 365 — a SaaS Cloud PC fully managed by Microsoft
Azure Virtual Desktop
A virtual machine with RDP enabled
Azure Bastion
explain: Windows 365 is the SaaS Cloud PC: Microsoft manages the infrastructure and the customer just assigns licenses per user. Azure Virtual Desktop is a PaaS/IaaS-style service where the customer manages host pools and images; a plain VM or Bastion doesn't provide managed cloud PCs.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company runs Kubernetes clusters on-premises and in another public cloud. It wants to apply Azure Policy and Azure Monitor to those clusters from one place. Which Azure Arc capability does this?
options: Arc-enabled servers
Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes — projects non-Azure clusters into Azure for governance and monitoring
Azure Stack HCI
Azure Virtual Desktop
explain: Arc-enabled Kubernetes connects clusters running anywhere so Azure Policy, Monitor, and RBAC apply uniformly. Arc-enabled servers covers VMs (not Kubernetes); Stack HCI is on-premises hyperconverged infrastructure; Virtual Desktop delivers desktops.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An auditor asks: 'Who deleted the production virtual machine last Tuesday at 3 AM?' Which log answers who-did-what questions about control-plane operations?
options: Virtual machine metrics
Application Insights
The Activity Log — which records control-plane operations like creates, updates, and deletes
Packet captures
explain: The Activity Log records management-plane operations — who created, updated, or deleted each resource and when. Metrics show performance numbers, Application Insights tracks application behavior, and packet captures show network traffic — none answer 'who deleted this resource'.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A retailer builds a customer-facing mobile app and needs millions of shoppers to sign up with social or local accounts — separate from employee identities. Which Microsoft Entra offering is designed for customer-facing apps?
options: Microsoft Entra ID B2B collaboration
Microsoft Entra Domain Services
Privileged Identity Management
Microsoft Entra External ID (B2C) — identity for customer-facing applications
explain: External ID (B2C) provides sign-up/sign-in for external customers with social and local accounts at consumer scale. B2B is for partner employees, Domain Services provides managed domain join for VMs, and PIM governs privileged admin access — none serve millions of shoppers.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company lifts an old application to Azure VMs. The app requires LDAP binds and Group Policy, but the company refuses to deploy and manage domain controllers. Which service meets this need?
options: Microsoft Entra Domain Services — managed domain join with LDAP, Kerberos, and Group Policy
Microsoft Entra ID alone
Microsoft Entra External ID
Privileged Identity Management
explain: Entra Domain Services provides a managed domain — domain join, LDAP, Kerberos, and Group Policy — without deploying domain controllers. Entra ID alone doesn't speak LDAP or Group Policy; External ID serves customers; PIM manages admin elevation.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants users to sign in with the same password on-premises and in the cloud, but no password — not even a hash — may leave the on-premises network. Which Microsoft Entra Connect sign-in option meets this requirement?
options: Password hash synchronization
Pass-through authentication — an on-premises agent validates passwords without them leaving the network
Federation with smart cards
Self-service password reset
explain: Pass-through authentication validates credentials via an on-premises agent, so passwords never leave the corporate network in any form. Hash sync sends password hashes to the cloud; federation and SSPR are different mechanisms that don't satisfy the no-password-leaves constraint.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Attackers are password-spraying employee accounts through old IMAP email clients that cannot perform multifactor authentication. Which Conditional Access approach best stops this attack?
options: Requiring longer passwords
Disabling MFA for email
Blocking legacy authentication — old protocols that cannot satisfy MFA are denied
Raising account lockout thresholds
explain: Legacy protocols like IMAP bypass modern authentication, so MFA can't protect them — Conditional Access can block legacy auth outright. Longer passwords and lockout tweaks don't fix the protocol weakness, and disabling MFA would make things worse.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An administrator is eligible for the Owner role through Privileged Identity Management but currently has no active permissions. To perform an emergency change, they must:
options: Email Microsoft support
Reboot the virtual machine
Wait 24 hours for automatic activation
Activate the role — typically with MFA, a justification, and automatic expiry after a set time
explain: PIM eligibility means zero standing privilege; the admin activates the role just-in-time, usually completing MFA and providing a reason, with access expiring automatically. There is no waiting period, no support ticket, and rebooting is irrelevant to identity.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: In a hybrid environment, users reset their passwords through cloud self-service, and the new passwords must sync back down to on-premises Active Directory. What enables this write-back?
options: Password writeback through Microsoft Entra Connect
Longer password expiration
Multifactor authentication
Seamless single sign-on
explain: Password writeback (part of Entra Connect) syncs cloud-initiated password changes back to on-premises AD. Without it, a cloud reset wouldn't update the on-premises password. Expiration length, MFA, and seamless SSO don't synchronize passwords downward.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A virtual machine uses a system-assigned managed identity to read secrets from Azure Key Vault. The virtual machine is then deleted. What happens to the managed identity?
options: It converts to a user-assigned identity
It is automatically deleted along with the resource
It transfers to another virtual machine
It persists in the directory forever
explain: A system-assigned managed identity's lifecycle is tied to its resource — deleting the VM deletes the identity automatically. It doesn't convert, transfer, or linger; a user-assigned managed identity would be the choice for an identity shared across resources.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A background service running outside Azure needs to authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID. Why can't it use a managed identity?
options: Managed identities are only for human users
Service principals do not exist
Managed identities are available only to Azure resources, so external apps use app registrations with service principals
External applications cannot authenticate at all
explain: Managed identities are issued to Azure resources (VMs, Functions, etc.) and can't be used off-platform. An external service authenticates as an app registration's service principal, managing its own credentials. Managed identities aren't for users, and external apps authenticate routinely via service principals.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An external auditor must be able to grant and review user access across the subscription, but must never create, modify, or delete resources. Which built-in RBAC role fits?
options: Owner
Contributor
Reader
User Access Administrator — manages access assignments without managing resources
explain: User Access Administrator can manage role assignments (who can access what) but cannot manage resources themselves. Owner and Contributor can modify resources; Reader can only view — none match the grant-access-but-touch-nothing requirement.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A user holds the Contributor role on a resource group, but a deny assignment blocks virtual-machine deletion. The user attempts to delete a VM. What is the result?
options: Deny assignments take precedence over allow assignments, so the deletion is blocked
The allow permission wins and the VM is deleted
The user is prompted for MFA and then allowed
Deny assignments only apply to the Reader role
explain: In Azure RBAC, an explicit deny always overrides an allow — the deletion is blocked despite the Contributor role. MFA doesn't override authorization, and deny assignments apply regardless of which allow role granted the permission.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants a single role assignment giving its security team Reader access across all 40 of its Azure subscriptions. Where should it assign the role for least administrative effort?
options: On every virtual machine
At the management group — the assignment inherits down to every subscription beneath it
In each resource group individually
Only on the tenant root through a support ticket
explain: RBAC assignments inherit down the hierarchy, so one assignment at the management group covers all subscriptions underneath. Assigning per-VM or per-resource-group means 40+ times the work, and no support ticket is needed for standard RBAC assignments.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A policy requiring encrypted storage accounts is assigned. Existing unencrypted accounts show as non-compliant in the dashboard but are not changed. Why didn't the policy fix them?
options: Azure Policy never works on existing resources under any circumstance
The policy definition is corrupted
Audit and deny effects only evaluate — remediating existing resources requires deployIfNotExists or modify effects plus a remediation task
Exemptions were applied automatically
explain: Audit flags and deny blocks new non-compliant deployments, but neither modifies resources that already exist. Changing existing resources requires deployIfNotExists or modify effects combined with a remediation task. The policy is working as designed — no corruption or automatic exemptions involved.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A legacy application receives a 90-day Azure Policy exemption while it is being migrated. What happens when the 90 days expire?
options: The exemption renews automatically
The resource is deleted
The policy definition is deleted
The exemption expires and the policy enforces against the resource again
explain: Exemptions can carry an expiration date; once it passes, the resource falls back under the policy's enforcement. Nothing renews, deletes the resource, or removes the policy automatically — the exemption simply lapses.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An administrator creates an Azure Policy definition requiring encrypted storage, but deployments remain unchanged. What step is missing?
options: A policy definition has no effect until it is assigned to a scope
Definitions apply automatically to the whole tenant
The Azure portal is malfunctioning
RBAC must be replaced with Azure Policy
explain: A definition is just a rule template — it does nothing until assigned to a management group, subscription, or resource group scope. Definitions never auto-apply, the portal is fine, and RBAC (who can do what) is a separate control from Policy (what configurations are allowed).
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A CanNotDelete lock is placed on a subscription. An administrator then tries to delete a virtual machine inside a resource group under that subscription. What happens?
options: The deletion is allowed — locks do not inherit
The deletion is blocked — locks inherit to all child resources
The deletion is allowed after MFA
Only resource groups are protected by locks
explain: Locks inherit down the hierarchy: a lock on a subscription protects every resource group and resource beneath it. MFA doesn't bypass locks, and the protection covers all child resources — not just resource groups.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A department configures a $5,000 monthly budget with an alert at 80%. Spending reaches $6,000. Why didn't Azure stop the spending when the budget was exceeded?
options: Budgets need 24 hours to activate
The alert threshold was misconfigured
Budgets only notify — they never stop, cap, or deallocate resources
Alerts only work for forecasted spending
explain: Budgets are notification mechanisms, not spending caps: exceeding one triggers alerts but Azure keeps resources running. To actually halt spending you'd need automation (e.g., an action group shutting down VMs). The threshold worked — it alerted — but alerting was all it was ever going to do.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company purchases a virtual-machine reservation with shared scope in its billing account. Which virtual machines receive the discounted rate?
options: Only a single designated VM
Only VMs in one region
Only B-series VMs
Any matching VMs across subscriptions in the billing scope
explain: Shared scope lets the reservation discount float to any VM matching its terms (size, region, OS) across subscriptions in the billing scope, maximizing utilization. Single-subscription scope would pin it; the discount isn't limited to one VM, one region, or B-series.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company's compute usage shifts constantly between VMs, App Service, and Container Instances, but totals a steady $10 per hour. Which commitment-based discount best fits this variable mix of services?
options: A compute savings plan — commit to a $/hour spend and the discount applies across eligible compute services
Virtual-machine reservations only
Spot virtual machines
Pay-as-you-go with no commitment
explain: Savings plans commit to an hourly spend ($/hour) rather than specific VMs, so the discount follows usage across VMs, App Service, Container Instances, and Functions. VM reservations lock to specific VM types; Spot is evictable and unsuitable for steady production; pay-as-you-go forgoes the discount.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company owns SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance and runs Azure SQL Database (PaaS). How can it reduce the database cost using those licenses?
options: Spot pricing for databases
Azure Hybrid Benefit for SQL Server — apply existing licensed cores to Azure SQL services
Deleting the database every night
The Azure free account
explain: Azure Hybrid Benefit for SQL lets customers apply existing SQL Server licenses with active Software Assurance to Azure SQL Database, Managed Instance, or SQL on VMs, paying only the base compute rate. Spot pricing doesn't apply to PaaS databases, nightly deletion destroys the workload, and the free account doesn't cover production databases.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A student burns through the Azure free account's $200 credit on day 20. What happens to the student's running virtual machines?
options: They keep running free for the rest of the year
Microsoft automatically starts billing the card on file
Services are disabled unless the subscription is upgraded to pay-as-you-go
The entire account is deleted instantly
explain: When the credit is exhausted, services are disabled — they don't keep running and Microsoft doesn't auto-bill. Upgrading to pay-as-you-go re-enables them with standard billing. The account itself isn't deleted; it's simply suspended until upgraded.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Azure misses a service's SLA in a given month and owes the customer service credits. How is the credit amount determined?
options: A fixed $100 credit
A full refund of the entire Azure bill
Double the month's charges
A percentage of the affected service's monthly bill, as specified in the SLA terms
explain: SLA service credits are calculated as a percentage of the monthly bill for the affected service, with higher percentages for worse shortfalls — defined in each service's SLA document. There is no flat $100, no full-bill refund, and certainly no double-charge penalty.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company deploys a VM with a public IP and asks what DDoS protection it receives without purchasing anything extra. What is the answer?
options: Always-on basic network-layer DDoS protection is included by default at no extra cost
No DDoS protection exists without a paid plan
Protection requires a web application firewall
Protection is only available in paired regions
explain: Azure provides always-on, baseline network-layer DDoS protection automatically for public endpoints at no charge. Paid options (DDoS Network Protection, DDoS IP Protection) add telemetry, mitigation policies, and cost protection — a WAF defends the application layer instead.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A team confuses Microsoft Defender XDR with Microsoft Sentinel. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
options: They are identical products with different names
Microsoft Defender XDR correlates protection across endpoints, identities, email, and apps, while Microsoft Sentinel is the cloud-native SIEM/SOAR for analytics, hunting, and automation
Sentinel replaces all firewalls
Defender XDR manages Azure spending
explain: Defender XDR unifies extended detection and response across security domains (endpoints, identity, email, cloud apps). Sentinel is the SIEM + SOAR: it ingests data from many sources for detection, threat hunting, and automated response. Neither replaces firewalls nor manages costs.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A developer's application needs to read secrets from a key vault, and the company uses Azure RBAC (not vault access policies) for authorization. Which role grants secret-read access?
options: Owner
Contributor
Key Vault Secrets User — the data-plane role for reading secret values
Reader
explain: Key Vault Secrets User is the RBAC data-plane role permitting secret reads. Owner and Contributor grant management-plane control but not data-plane secret access; Reader only lets you see the vault exists. This split is why code can see the vault yet get 'access denied' on secrets.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company currently administers VMs through a jumpbox virtual machine with a public IP. Security wants to eliminate the exposed IP and the patching burden of the jumpbox. Which service replaces it?
options: A larger jumpbox VM
A VPN gateway
Just-in-time VM access
Azure Bastion — browser-based RDP/SSH with no public IPs and no jumpbox to patch
explain: Bastion provides RDP/SSH through the Azure portal over TLS with no public IPs on the VMs and no jumpbox VM to maintain. A bigger jumpbox keeps the exposure; a VPN gateway serves different connectivity needs; just-in-time access still assumes a reachable management path.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants files containing passport numbers to be automatically classified and labeled wherever they live across Microsoft 365. Which capability does this?
options: Sensitivity labels — classify, label, and protect data based on its content
Azure resource tags
Network security group rules
Azure Policy
explain: Sensitivity labels (Microsoft Purview Information Protection) classify and protect content by what it contains, applying labels and encryption across Microsoft 365. Resource tags organize Azure resources, NSGs filter network traffic, and Azure Policy governs resource configuration — none classify document content.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company has one critical public IP address fronting its payment portal and wants dedicated DDoS telemetry, mitigation policies, and alerting for just that IP. Which offering fits?
options: DDoS Network Protection
DDoS IP Protection — paid per-public-IP protection with dedicated telemetry
The default basic protection
Azure Firewall
explain: DDoS IP Protection is the per-public-IP paid SKU with dedicated telemetry, mitigation tuning, and alerts. Network Protection covers all public IPs in a VNet; basic protection is automatic but without the dedicated telemetry; Firewall filters traffic rather than mitigating volumetric DDoS.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A web application firewall must block OWASP Top 10 attacks like SQL injection, but the team doesn't want to write and maintain custom rules. Which WAF feature meets this need?
options: Custom data-loss-prevention rules
Rate limiting only
Managed rule sets — prebuilt, Microsoft-maintained protection against common web attacks
Geo-filtering only
explain: Managed rule sets (including the OWASP core rule set) provide prebuilt, continuously updated protection against common web attacks with no custom rule authoring. Rate limiting and geo-filtering are useful controls but don't cover SQL injection; custom DLP is a different problem entirely.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company operates five Azure Firewalls and wants shared baseline rules plus per-region customizations, managed from one place. How should it structure this?
options: Five independent firewall configurations
Network security group rules
ARM templates only
A Firewall Policy hierarchy — base policy with inherited rules, customized per firewall, managed in Firewall Manager
explain: Firewall Policies support parent-child hierarchies: a base policy holds shared rules while child policies add regional customization, all managed centrally in Firewall Manager. Independent configs drift apart; NSGs are a different control; ARM templates deploy but don't provide the governance hierarchy.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company reaches Azure SQL Database through a service endpoint, but learns traffic still targets the public endpoint with a VNet identity. It wants the database to have a private IP inside its VNet instead. What should it use?
options: Private Link — a private endpoint giving the PaaS service a private IP inside the VNet
Additional service endpoints
ExpressRoute
The public endpoint with a longer firewall rule
explain: Private Link (private endpoint) assigns the PaaS service a private IP in the VNet, so traffic never traverses the public endpoint. Service endpoints keep the public endpoint with VNet-based identity — the very limitation here. ExpressRoute is on-premises connectivity, not PaaS addressing.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A startup buys the Developer support plan for its production e-commerce site. During a 2 AM outage, what limitation will it hit?
options: The Developer plan has no portal access
The Developer plan targets non-production workloads and lacks 24/7 critical-issue response — production needs Standard or higher
The Developer plan is the most expensive tier
Azure support plans do not exist
explain: The Developer plan is designed for trial and non-production use with business-hours response times. Production workloads needing 24/7 support and sub-one-hour critical response require Standard or Professional Direct. Portal access exists on all plans; Developer is the cheapest, not the priciest.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Managers must periodically certify that contractors still need their PIM-eligible administrator roles, or the access is removed. Which feature automates this recurring recertification?
options: Conditional Access policies
PIM role activation
Access reviews — recurring certification campaigns confirming continued need for access
Resource locks
explain: Access reviews create recurring campaigns where reviewers confirm or revoke access — including PIM-eligible role assignments. Conditional Access controls sign-in conditions, PIM activation grants just-in-time elevation, and locks prevent deletion — none perform periodic recertification.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A security researcher discovers a vulnerability in an Azure service. Where should they report it to Microsoft?
options: A standard Azure support ticket
A social media post
The Azure status page
The Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC)
explain: The MSRC is Microsoft's official channel for reporting security vulnerabilities in its products and services. Support tickets handle operational issues, social media isn't a reporting channel, and the status page only communicates service health — none route to the security response team.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company uploads 40 TB of archival data into Azure Blob storage, and later downloads 5 TB of it back to its on-premises datacenter. Which of these data transfers incurs Azure data-transfer charges?
options: The upload into Azure, because inbound data always incurs transfer fees
Neither transfer, because all data movement in Azure is free
The download back to on-premises, because outbound (egress) transfers are billed while inbound transfers are free
Both transfers equally, because every gigabyte moved is metered the same way
explain: Data ingress into Azure (uploads) is free; data egress out of Azure to on-premises or the internet is billed per gigabyte. The 'both billed' option ignores this asymmetry, the 'inbound billed' option reverses it, and 'all free' ignores egress pricing entirely — egress is one of the standard cost factors in Azure.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An e-commerce checkout system runs on a single virtual machine. The architect adds a second VM in another availability zone and places a load balancer in front of both. Which design goal does this change primarily serve?
options: Eliminating the single point of failure so one VM's failure doesn't stop checkouts
Increasing the VM's CPU and memory
Encrypting the checkout data
Reducing the number of backups needed
explain: A single VM is a single point of failure; adding a redundant VM plus a load balancer removes it, so the system survives one VM failing. Bigger hardware (vertical scaling) doesn't remove the SPOF, encryption addresses confidentiality rather than availability, and backups aid recovery but don't prevent the outage.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's servers are four years old, and the vendor quotes $300,000 for a full hardware refresh. The CIO notes that moving the workloads to Azure would end this repeating expense. Which cloud financial benefit is the CIO describing?
options: Eliminating all IT staffing costs
Free unlimited cloud resources
Guaranteed zero downtime
Avoiding recurring capital-expenditure hardware refresh cycles
explain: On-premises hardware must be repurchased every few years as CapEx; in the cloud the provider owns the hardware, so refresh cycles disappear from the customer's budget. The cloud doesn't eliminate IT staff (roles shift), resources are metered rather than free, and no provider guarantees zero downtime.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's workloads run on Azure virtual machines. Microsoft releases a critical security patch for the physical host servers and hypervisor underneath those VMs. Who is responsible for applying it?
options: The customer, because they chose virtual machines
Microsoft, because the physical hosts and virtualization layer are below the customer's IaaS responsibility boundary
No one, because hypervisors patch themselves
The customer's internet service provider
explain: In IaaS the provider owns everything up to virtualization — physical security, hosts, hypervisor, and platform networking — while the customer owns the guest OS upward. The customer patches guest operating systems (never the ISP's job), and hypervisors don't self-patch.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A SaaS project-management application serves thousands of companies from a single shared application instance. What keeps one company's projects and data separate from another's?
options: Each customer gets dedicated physical servers
A VPN tunnel per customer
Logical tenant isolation built into the application, separating each customer's data
Customers encrypt everything themselves, so isolation is unnecessary
explain: SaaS multi-tenancy isolates customers logically within shared infrastructure — tenant boundaries in the application and data layers. Dedicated servers per customer would defeat the economics of SaaS, VPNs secure connections rather than separate tenants, and customer encryption complements but doesn't replace tenant isolation.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A developer starts a virtual machine to run a 90-second test, then deletes it. How is the compute time billed?
options: Per-second billing granularity, so the customer pays for roughly the 90 seconds used
A full hour minimum regardless of actual use
A full day minimum per VM start
A flat monthly fee per VM
explain: Azure bills VM compute per second, so short-lived VMs cost proportionally little — deleting quickly stops the meter. There is no full-hour or full-day minimum, and pay-as-you-go has no flat monthly fee per VM.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's finance team allocates cloud costs to each department based on precisely metered usage. Which NIST essential characteristic of cloud computing makes this chargeback possible?
options: Resource pooling
Broad network access
Rapid elasticity
Measured service — usage is metered, monitored, and reported
explain: Measured service means the provider meters storage, compute, and bandwidth and reports it, enabling pay-per-use and chargeback. Resource pooling is shared infrastructure, broad network access is device ubiquity, and rapid elasticity is scaling — none of them produce the usage metering that chargeback needs.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company keeps nightly backups and a written failover runbook, but has never assigned who declares a disaster, who talks to customers, or in what order systems return. An auditor flags the DR plan as incomplete. What is missing?
options: Faster backup storage
Clearly assigned roles, decision authority, and a communication plan — the people and process side of recovery
More frequent backups
A second cloud provider
explain: A real DR plan covers people and process — who declares the disaster, who executes each step, and how customers are informed — not just technology. Faster storage or more frequent backups don't fix unclear ownership, and a second provider adds complexity without addressing the gap.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A flood closes a company's headquarters for two weeks. Employees work from home on laptops, accessing email, files, and business apps hosted in the cloud with no loss of productivity. Which cloud benefit does this demonstrate?
options: Economies of scale
Resource pooling
Broad network access supporting business continuity — services reachable over the internet from anywhere
Measured service
explain: Broad network access means cloud services are available over the internet from any device and location, which is what lets work continue when the office is unavailable. Economies of scale and resource pooling concern provider efficiency, and measured service concerns metering — none explain location-independent access.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A web application stores each user's shopping cart in the memory of the specific web server handling them. When the team scales out to more servers, users randomly lose their carts. What is the correct fix?
options: Make the application stateless by storing session state externally (for example, in a cache), so any server can serve any user
Use a bigger virtual machine
Add more internet bandwidth
Put a content delivery network in front of the servers
explain: Scale-out requires stateless servers: session state must live outside individual instances (for example, Azure Cache for Redis) so requests can land on any instance. A bigger VM is vertical scaling that keeps the single point of failure, bandwidth doesn't fix session affinity, and a CDN caches static content rather than user sessions.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A software company's engineers spend weeks each quarter racking servers, replacing disks, and patching firmware instead of building product features. The CTO moves infrastructure to the cloud so engineers focus on the product. Which cloud value is the CTO pursuing?
options: Eliminating the need for software developers
Removing all security responsibilities
Guaranteed higher revenue
Shifting effort from undifferentiated heavy lifting to work that differentiates the business
explain: Undifferentiated heavy lifting — racking, cabling, firmware — doesn't differentiate the product; the cloud absorbs it so engineers build features customers pay for. Developers are still needed, security becomes shared rather than removed, and the cloud guarantees nothing about revenue.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A media team wants to run a three-hour video-encoding job inside Azure Functions on the Consumption plan. Why is this a poor fit?
options: Functions are always more expensive than VMs
The Consumption plan enforces maximum execution time limits, so long-running jobs get terminated; a batch or VM-based approach fits better
Functions cannot be triggered automatically
Functions cannot scale
explain: Consumption-plan functions have execution time limits measured in minutes, so a three-hour encode would be killed mid-run — Azure Batch or VMs suit long-running compute.
