Functions are typically cheaper for short bursts, support many triggers, and scale automatically; cost isn't the issue here.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A developer says, 'The app works on my laptop but crashes on the production server.' The team packages the app with its libraries and runtime into containers, and the problem disappears. What did containers solve?
options: They automatically fixed the code bugs
They replaced the need for testing
They packaged the application with its dependencies, so it runs identically on any host
They removed the operating system entirely
explain: Containers bundle code with its exact dependencies and runtime, eliminating 'works on my machine' environment drift. They don't fix bugs, replace testing, or remove the OS — containers share the host OS kernel.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A team chooses Azure App Service (PaaS) over virtual machines for its web API, accepting that it cannot pick the exact OS patch level or install custom kernel drivers. Which statement about PaaS is TRUE?
options: PaaS requires the customer to patch the operating system
PaaS trades fine-grained infrastructure control for reduced operational burden — the provider manages the OS and runtime
PaaS cannot scale automatically
PaaS is only for static websites
explain: PaaS abstracts servers and operating systems: Microsoft patches the OS and runtime while the customer focuses on code — the price is less control over the underlying platform. Customers never patch the PaaS OS, App Service scales automatically, and it hosts dynamic APIs, not just static sites.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company pays a monthly per-user fee for Microsoft 365. How is this spending classified?
options: Capital expenditure, because software is an asset
A one-time sunk cost
Depreciation
Operational expenditure — an ongoing subscription cost for a consumed service
explain: Subscription payments for consumed services are OpEx: ongoing operating costs, not upfront asset purchases. CapEx covers assets bought outright (servers), depreciation spreads CapEx over years, and a monthly subscription is by definition recurring, not one-time.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Before migrating anything, a company builds a baseline Azure environment: a management-group hierarchy, baseline policies, hub networking, and naming standards. In the Cloud Adoption Framework, this foundation is called a:
options: An availability set
A landing zone
A resource group
A subscription
explain: A landing zone is the pre-built, governed foundation — identity, networking, policies, management hierarchy — that workloads migrate into. Availability sets handle VM fault tolerance, resource groups organize resources, and subscriptions are billing boundaries; none describe the CAF foundation concept.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An architect explains that a globally distributed database cannot offer both instantaneous worldwide writes and instantaneous consistent reads. What fundamentally causes this tradeoff?
options: Insufficient internet bandwidth
Lack of encryption
The speed of light and network latency — synchronizing data across continents takes time, so stronger consistency means higher write latency
Too few datacenters
explain: Data can't travel faster than physics allows: synchronously confirming a write on another continent adds latency, so systems trade consistency against latency. Bandwidth, encryption, and datacenter count don't change the speed-of-light limit — this is why databases offer tunable consistency levels.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A defense contractor needs custom hypervisor settings and specific certified hardware for its workloads — configurations a public cloud won't allow. Which deployment model gives it this control?
options: Public cloud
Private cloud — dedicated infrastructure the organization controls and customizes
SaaS
Serverless
explain: A private cloud dedicates infrastructure to one organization, allowing custom hardware, hypervisor tuning, and strict control. Public clouds standardize configurations, while SaaS and serverless abstract infrastructure away entirely rather than exposing more control.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Five regional credit unions share a cloud platform built to satisfy common financial regulations, splitting the cost of compliance audits and security assessments. This arrangement primarily demonstrates which community-cloud advantage?
options: Unlimited free resources
No shared responsibility
Zero administrative effort
Shared compliance and governance costs among organizations with common requirements
explain: A community cloud serves organizations with shared concerns (here, financial regulation), letting them split audit, compliance, and security costs. Resources are metered rather than free, the shared responsibility model still applies, and joint governance requires administrative effort — the advantage is shared cost, not zero cost.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs its storefront on one cloud provider and its payment processing on another, so a full outage at either provider alone cannot take down the entire business. Which multicloud benefit does this show?
options: Reduced complexity
Resilience against a single provider's outage
A single unified bill
Identical tooling everywhere
explain: Spreading critical systems across providers means one provider's outage can't halt everything — resilience through diversification. Multicloud actually increases complexity, produces separate bills, and requires different tooling; resilience is the genuine benefit here.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A retailer enables autoscaling for its storefront but worries a traffic spike — or a misconfiguration — could scale to hundreds of instances and explode the bill. Which setting provides a hard cost guardrail?
options: A budget alert, which automatically stops all spending
Deleting the scale set
Setting a maximum instance count on the autoscale rule
Buying a reservation
explain: Autoscale maximum instance counts cap how far scaling can go, bounding cost even during extreme spikes. Budget alerts only notify (they never stop spending — a classic exam trap), deleting the scale set removes the workload, and reservations discount steady usage rather than capping scale.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company buys a one-year virtual-machine reservation, then deallocates the VM for two months during a quiet period. What happens to the reservation charges during those two months?
options: The reservation charges continue, because a reservation is a billing commitment that applies whether or not the VM runs
The reservation pauses and resumes automatically
The reservation converts to pay-as-you-go pricing
The unused portion is refunded automatically
explain: A reservation is a commitment to pay for capacity for one or three years — the discount applies when matching usage exists, but the charge continues even if the VM is deallocated. It doesn't pause, convert, or auto-refund; this is why reservations suit steady, predictable workloads.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A research team runs interruptible batch simulations on Spot VMs at a deep discount. What must the workload design account for?
options: Spot VMs can never be evicted
Spot VMs include free premium support
Eviction is automatic and harmless for any workload
Azure can evict Spot VMs when capacity is needed, so the job must checkpoint progress and tolerate interruptions
explain: Spot VMs use spare capacity at deep discounts precisely because Azure may evict them with short notice when capacity is needed — workloads must save progress (checkpointing) and resume. Eviction is real, support isn't bundled, and stateful or non-interruptible workloads are a poor fit.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company uses Azure Arc to manage its on-premises servers from the Azure portal. When Microsoft releases a Windows security update, who installs it on those Arc-enabled servers?
options: The customer, because Arc extends management to servers the customer still owns and operates — including OS patching
Microsoft, automatically
No one — Arc-enabled servers don't need patching
The hardware vendor
explain: Azure Arc brings Azure management tooling to servers outside Azure, but the shared responsibility boundary doesn't move: the customer still owns the on-premises servers and patches their guest operating systems. Arc doesn't transfer ownership or auto-patch, and the hardware vendor isn't involved.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A SaaS vendor suffers a breach exposing its customers' stored data. Regulators ask who is responsible for notifying affected individuals. Under the shared responsibility model, who bears this responsibility?
options: Microsoft, in all cases
The SaaS vendor's internet provider
The customer, because customer data remains the customer's responsibility even in SaaS
No one — breaches have no notification requirements
explain: Even in SaaS, the customer always owns its data — including classifying it, controlling access to it, and meeting breach-notification obligations. The vendor secures the application and infrastructure, but data ownership and regulatory accountability stay with the customer.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's backup policy follows the 3-2-1 rule: three copies of data, on two different media types, with one copy offsite. Which Azure role fits naturally into this strategy?
options: Azure provides the offsite copy — for example, replicated backups or a secondary region — satisfying the '1' in 3-2-1
Azure eliminates the need for any backups
Azure replaces the two media types with one
The rule requires three Azure regions
explain: The 3-2-1 rule demands an offsite copy so a local disaster can't destroy data and backups together; Azure's geographically separate storage is a natural offsite target. Azure doesn't eliminate backups, the rule still wants two media types, and it requires one offsite copy — not three regions.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company replicates its VMs to a secondary region but has never actually tested failover. During a real regional outage, the failover fails because DNS records and runbooks are outdated. What is the lesson?
options: Replication is useless
Buy faster storage
Add more regions
Disaster recovery must be tested regularly — untested plans fail when needed most
explain: Replication without tested runbooks is hope, not a plan: regular failover drills surface stale DNS, outdated scripts, and missing steps before a real outage. Replication itself works, storage speed wasn't the failure, and more regions wouldn't fix untested procedures.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A hospital sets a 15-minute RPO for patient records but a 24-hour RPO for its marketing site. What should drive these different objectives?
options: A business impact analysis — the cost of downtime and data loss per hour for each system
The IT team's personal preferences
Microsoft's default values
The cheapest available option
explain: RPO and RTO come from business impact analysis: how much data loss and downtime each system can tolerate, quantified in business cost. They're not set by IT whim, Microsoft doesn't dictate them, and 'cheapest' ignores the cost of an outage.

q: An architect notices the same virtual machine size costs different amounts per hour in different Azure regions. What is the correct takeaway?
options: Prices are identical in every region
The billing system is broken
Azure pricing varies by region, so region choice affects cost — though compliance and latency requirements must come first
Always deploy in the cheapest region regardless of other requirements
explain: Azure prices vary by region due to local costs, so region selection is a genuine cost lever. But the cheapest region isn't automatically right — data-residency laws and user latency often dictate the region, making 'cheapest always wins' a trap.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An architect designs a zone-redundant deployment, then learns the chosen Azure region has no availability zones. What must the architect do?
options: Deploy anyway — zones work in every region
Choose a region that supports availability zones, or redesign without zone redundancy
Create the zones manually
Use a paired region as a substitute for zones
explain: Availability zones exist only in regions built with physically separate datacenters — not every region has them. Zones can't be created manually, a paired region is a different (regional-failover) concept, and deploying 'anyway' yields no zone redundancy.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company replicates its database to another region asynchronously and asks why the provider can't offer zero data loss (RPO zero) with asynchronous replication. What is the correct explanation?
options: Asynchronous replication is always instant
Zero data loss is impossible in any design
Encryption prevents synchronous replication
Synchronous replication confirms every write remotely before acknowledging it, which adds latency — so RPO zero requires synchronous replication, practical only over shorter distances
explain: Asynchronous replication acknowledges writes locally before they're sent remotely, so in-flight data can be lost — RPO zero demands synchronous confirmation, whose latency only works over shorter distances. Async is never instant, RPO zero is achievable with sync replication, and encryption is unrelated.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An Azure Function runs for 200 milliseconds per execution, a few hundred times a day, scaling to zero between runs. How is it billed?
options: Per execution and memory-time (GB-seconds) consumed — with no charge while scaled to zero
Per virtual machine hour
A flat monthly fee per function app
Per deployment
explain: The Consumption plan meters executions plus GB-seconds of memory used, and scaled-to-zero means zero idle cost — the essence of serverless economics. There's no VM-hour or flat monthly charge on Consumption, and deployments aren't billed.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company calls an Azure AI vision API to analyze 50,000 product images. How is this usage billed?
options: Per transaction (for example, per 1,000 API calls) — consumption-based pricing for the API
Per GPU hour reserved
A flat annual license
It's free and unlimited
explain: Azure AI services use consumption-based pricing per transaction (for example, per 1,000 calls), so cost tracks actual usage with no infrastructure to provision. There's no GPU reservation or flat license involved, and it's metered — not unlimited free.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: During Azure platform maintenance, most virtual machines experience no downtime even though their physical hosts are being patched. What makes this possible?
options: Virtual machines are never moved
Azure uses live migration and memory-preserving updates to move VMs between hosts without rebooting them
Customers must manually migrate their VMs first
Maintenance only happens when VMs are deallocated
explain: Azure patches hosts using live migration — VMs move to another host with memory preserved, avoiding reboots for most maintenance. VMs do move, customers aren't required to act, and maintenance doesn't wait for deallocation; update domains additionally sequence any required reboots.

q: A company uses a hub-and-spoke network: one hub VNet with a VPN gateway to on-premises, peered to several spoke VNets. A spoke VNet needs to reach on-premises through the hub's gateway. What must be configured?
options: Nothing — peering is transitive, so spokes automatically use the hub gateway
A second VPN gateway in each spoke
Gateway transit: allow the hub's gateway to be shared by enabling gateway transit on the hub-to-spoke peering
A public IP on every spoke VM
explain: VNet peering is non-transitive, so spokes can't reach on-premises through the hub by default — gateway transit on the peering explicitly shares the hub's VPN gateway with spokes. Spoke gateways are unnecessary cost, and public IPs would bypass the private path entirely.

q: A bank needs 40 Gbps of private, consistent-latency connectivity to Azure for its trading platform. Which ExpressRoute option supports this bandwidth?
options: A standard ExpressRoute circuit (up to 10 Gbps)
A site-to-site VPN gateway
VNet peering
ExpressRoute Direct, which provides up to 100 Gbps via direct fiber connections
explain: ExpressRoute Direct offers up to 100 Gbps through direct connections to Microsoft's network, fitting the 40 Gbps need. Standard circuits top out around 10 Gbps, VPN gateways are internet-based with lower throughput, and VNet peering connects Azure VNets — not on-premises.

q: A company connects its datacenter to Azure with a single site-to-site VPN gateway and wants better availability for the connection. What should it deploy?
options: Active-active VPN gateways, which provide redundant gateway instances for higher connection availability
A bigger virtual machine
A second internet provider only
ExpressRoute, which is the only highly available option
explain: Active-active mode deploys two gateway instances so one can fail without dropping the tunnels. A bigger VM is unrelated, a second ISP helps only the internet leg, and while ExpressRoute is private, active-active VPN is the direct high-availability answer for VPN connectivity.

q: A company's on-premises servers need to resolve the private DNS names of Azure resources in a private DNS zone. Its on-premises DNS servers can't see the Azure private zone. Which service bridges this?
options: A public DNS forwarder
Azure DNS Private Resolver, which forwards DNS queries between on-premises and Azure private DNS zones
Editing hosts files on every server
Azure Firewall
explain: DNS Private Resolver provides inbound and outbound endpoints so on-premises DNS can resolve Azure private DNS zones and vice versa. Public forwarders can't see private zones, hosts files don't scale, and Firewall filters traffic rather than resolving names.

q: A three-tier application has a public web tier and a private application tier. The app-tier VMs must be load-balanced, but they must never be reachable directly from the internet. Which load balancer fits?
options: A public load balancer
Traffic Manager
An internal load balancer, which distributes traffic using private IP addresses inside the VNet
Azure Front Door
explain: An internal load balancer has only private frontend IPs, so it balances traffic between private-tier VMs without internet exposure. A public LB would expose the tier, Traffic Manager is DNS-based global routing, and Front Door is a global Layer 7 entry point — not for private-tier balancing.

q: An administrator creates a new network security group and tries to delete the built-in default rules so only custom rules remain. What happens?
options: The default rules are deleted and the NSG becomes empty
Deleting defaults automatically allows all traffic
The NSG is deleted along with its rules
Nothing — Azure's default rules cannot be deleted; custom rules with lower priority numbers override them
explain: NSG default rules (allow VNet traffic, deny internet inbound, and others) are platform-managed and can't be removed — you override them with custom rules at higher priority (lower number). The NSG keeps working; deleting the defaults simply isn't possible.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An NSG is applied to a subnet, and a second NSG is applied to a VM's network interface inside that subnet. An inbound packet arrives for the VM. Which statement is TRUE?
options: Both NSGs are evaluated — the packet must be allowed by the subnet-level and the NIC-level rules to reach the VM
Only the subnet-level NSG applies
Only the NIC-level NSG applies
Whichever NSG was created first takes precedence
explain: NSGs can be attached at both subnet and NIC levels, and both are evaluated — a deny at either layer blocks the traffic. Neither layer is skipped, there's no 'most permissive wins' logic, and creation order is irrelevant.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company secures Azure SQL Database two ways for two workloads: one uses a service endpoint, the other a private endpoint. The finance team asks about cost differences. What is TRUE?
options: Both options are free
Service endpoints are free; private endpoints incur an hourly charge
Private endpoints are free; service endpoints are billed
Both are billed per gigabyte
explain: Service endpoints extend the VNet identity to the service at no charge, while private endpoints (which inject a private NIC and IP into the VNet) carry an hourly fee. Neither is per-gigabyte billed for the endpoint itself.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An administrator learns that Azure's default outbound internet access for VMs is being retired. A VM has no public IP and no NAT gateway. What is the consequence?
options: The VM keeps outbound internet access automatically
An NSG rule restores it
The VM loses default outbound internet access and needs an explicit outbound method, such as a NAT gateway or public IP
Azure Firewall is deployed automatically
explain: With default outbound access retired, VMs without explicit outbound connectivity (public IP, NAT gateway, or load balancer outbound) can't reach the internet. NSG rules filter traffic but don't provide outbound paths, and no firewall appears automatically — explicit outbound design is required.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A security team must inspect encrypted outbound web traffic for malware and data exfiltration, decrypting TLS sessions at the perimeter. Which Azure Firewall capability does this?
options: Network rules
DNAT rules
Threat intelligence alerts
TLS inspection, available on Azure Firewall Premium
explain: Only Firewall Premium supports TLS inspection — decrypting, inspecting, and re-encrypting traffic. Network rules filter by IP and port, DNAT publishes inbound services, and threat-intel alerts detect known-bad destinations without decrypting content.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company runs Application Gateway with WAF in front of its web app and expects traffic to swing from hundreds to tens of thousands of requests per second. Which tier handles this elastically with zone redundancy?
options: WAF_v2 — autoscaling and zone-redundant, designed for variable high-throughput workloads
The legacy WAF (v1) tier
A single fixed-capacity instance
Traffic Manager
explain: Application Gateway v2 SKUs (including WAF_v2) autoscale with demand and support zone redundancy; v1 requires manual instance sizing. Traffic Manager is DNS-based global routing, not a regional Layer 7 gateway.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A global web app runs in three regions behind Azure Front Door. The team wants each region's health continuously probed, with traffic automatically failing over from an unhealthy region. Which Front Door construct provides this?
options: A single origin with no probes
Origin groups with health probes — Front Door routes to healthy origins and fails over automatically
Round-robin DNS records
An NSG
explain: Front Door origin groups combine backends with configurable health probes; unhealthy origins are removed from rotation automatically. A single origin has no failover, DNS round-robin lacks health awareness, and NSGs filter packets rather than routing global traffic.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company must give an external auditor read access to one blob container for 48 hours, without sharing the storage account key and without making the container public. What should it create?
options: Share the storage account key and rotate it afterward
Make the container publicly readable
A shared access signature (SAS) token scoped to the container, with read-only permission and a 48-hour expiry
Create a second storage account for the auditor
explain: A SAS token grants delegated, time-limited, permission-scoped access without exposing the account key — least privilege for the audit. Sharing the account key grants full control, public access exposes data to everyone, and a new account is unnecessary overhead.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A compliance policy requires that all access to a storage account use encryption in transit. Which storage account setting enforces HTTPS and rejects plain HTTP?
options: Soft delete
Versioning
Blob lifecycle management
Secure transfer required
explain: The 'secure transfer required' setting forces clients to use HTTPS, rejecting unencrypted HTTP requests. Soft delete aids recovery, versioning keeps prior versions, and lifecycle management tiers data — none enforce transport encryption.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A latency-sensitive trading application reads and writes small files over SMB with strict latency requirements. Which Azure Files performance option fits?
options: Premium file shares, which use SSD-backed storage for consistently low latency and high IOPS
Standard HDD file shares
Archive blob tier
Data Box
explain: Premium Azure Files runs on SSDs for low, consistent latency and high IOPS — built for latency-sensitive SMB and NFS workloads. Standard HDD shares are cheaper but higher-latency, Archive is for rarely accessed blobs with hours-long rehydration, and Data Box is offline bulk transfer.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A data-science team needs POSIX-like folder permissions on individual files and directories in its data lake, with different teams getting different access to different folders. Which Azure Storage capability enables this?
options: Standard blob containers with public access
Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2's hierarchical namespace, which supports fine-grained ACLs on files and folders
Shared access signatures alone
Storage account keys
explain: ADLS Gen2's hierarchical namespace brings true directories with POSIX-style ACLs, enabling folder-level permissions. Flat blob namespaces can't do per-folder ACLs, SAS tokens grant access without managing permissions, and account keys are all-or-nothing.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company must automatically maintain a copy of critical blobs in a second storage account in another region, with changes replicated asynchronously. Which feature does this?
options: Geo-redundant storage (GRS)
Blob lifecycle management
Blob object replication, which asynchronously copies blobs between storage accounts according to replication rules
Soft delete
explain: Object replication copies blobs between storage accounts (same or different regions) asynchronously per policy. GRS replicates within Microsoft-managed secondary regions rather than a second account you control, lifecycle management tiers or deletes data, and soft delete recovers deletions — none copy between accounts.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A branch office must move 8 TB of files to Azure but has a slow internet link. Which offline transfer option fits this smaller shipment?
options: Keep retrying AzCopy over the slow link
Order a full Data Box (designed for hundreds of terabytes)
Provision ExpressRoute for a one-time move
Data Box Disk — shippable SSDs for smaller offline transfers
explain: Data Box Disk handles smaller offline transfers (up to tens of terabytes per order) without saturating a slow link. A full Data Box targets petabyte-scale moves, ExpressRoute is a standing private circuit (overkill for one move), and AzCopy over a slow link would take impractically long.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company uses an Azure SQL auto-failover group with a primary in East US and a secondary in West US. Applications must keep working after failover without connection-string changes. What makes this possible?
options: The read-write listener endpoint — a single DNS name that always resolves to the current primary
Updating every connection string during failover
Traffic Manager in front of the databases
The secondary's separate server name
explain: Failover groups provide read-write and read-only listener endpoints — stable DNS names that automatically point to the current primary after failover, so apps need no changes. Manual connection-string updates defeat automatic failover, Traffic Manager isn't used for SQL listeners, and the secondary's own name doesn't follow the primary role.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Regulators require a bank to retain monthly database backups for seven years. Azure SQL Database's built-in short-term retention is insufficient. Which feature extends backup retention to years?
options: Geo-redundant storage
Long-term retention (LTR) policies, which keep full backups for up to 10 years
Soft delete
Manual exports to a laptop
explain: SQL Database long-term retention stores full backups in Azure Blob storage for up to 10 years, meeting multi-year compliance mandates. GRS is storage redundancy rather than backup retention, soft delete recovers deleted data short-term, and manual exports aren't a managed retention policy.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team runs Azure Cosmos DB and must choose a consistency level. Which statement is TRUE?
options: There are only two consistency levels
Eventual consistency is the default
Cosmos DB offers five consistency levels, from strong to eventual; session consistency is the default
Strong consistency gives the highest performance
explain: Cosmos DB provides five tunable consistency levels (strong, bounded staleness, session, consistent prefix, eventual), with session as the default — balancing consistency and performance. Strong consistency actually costs the most latency and throughput, and eventual is the weakest level, not the default.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A Cosmos DB container will hold 50 million customer orders and sustain 20,000 RU/s. Which partition-key choice is BEST?
options: A single fixed value so all data stays in one partition
The region name
A low-cardinality field like country
A high-cardinality field like order ID, which distributes requests and storage evenly across physical partitions
explain: A high-cardinality partition key spreads RU/s and storage across partitions, avoiding hot partitions that throttle throughput. A single value forces everything into one partition with hard limits, and low-cardinality fields like region or country create a few overloaded partitions.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: Analysts need near-real-time dashboards over data in Azure Cosmos DB, without ETL jobs copying it to a warehouse. Which capability enables this HTAP pattern?
options: Azure Synapse Link for Cosmos DB, which analyzes operational data in near real time with no ETL
Azure Data Factory pipelines
Manual CSV exports
Database backups
explain: Synapse Link creates a columnar analytical store synced from Cosmos DB in near real time, enabling hybrid transactional/analytical processing with zero ETL. Data Factory is batch ETL, manual exports are operationally heavy, and backups are for recovery — not analytics.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A nightly ETL pipeline must pull data from an on-premises SQL Server behind the corporate firewall into Azure. The Azure Data Factory's cloud integration runtime cannot reach the on-premises server. What solves this?
options: Open the firewall to the public internet
A self-hosted integration runtime installed on-premises, which securely connects outward to Data Factory
Move the database to a public IP
Use AzCopy manually each night
explain: A self-hosted integration runtime runs inside the corporate network and makes outbound connections to Data Factory — no inbound firewall holes needed. Opening the firewall or using public IPs exposes the database, and manual AzCopy isn't an orchestrated pipeline.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A developer builds an Azure Function that must run whenever a new image lands in Blob storage and then write a message to a queue. Which Functions concepts implement this?
options: Two separate virtual machines
A timer trigger only
A blob trigger to fire on new images and an output binding to write to the queue — triggers invoke, bindings connect to data
An NSG rule
explain: Triggers define what invokes a function (blob trigger on new blobs); bindings declaratively connect to data sources and sinks (output binding writes to the queue) without boilerplate SDK code. VMs are the antithesis of serverless, a timer wouldn't react to uploads, and NSGs filter network traffic.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An order-processing workflow must run steps in sequence, wait for human approval, then resume — maintaining state across hours. Which Azure Functions capability supports this stateful orchestration?
options: Consumption-plan timers
Blob storage alone
A second function app
Durable Functions, which extend Functions with stateful orchestrators for long-running workflows
explain: Durable Functions add orchestrator functions that maintain workflow state across steps, timers, and human-approval waits. Plain timers can't sequence dependent steps, blob storage is just data, and another function app doesn't add orchestration semantics.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team wants containerized APIs that scale to zero when idle and scale on events like queue depth, without managing Kubernetes clusters. Which service fits?
options: Azure Container Apps — serverless containers with event-driven (KEDA) scaling, including scale to zero
A single Container Instance
Virtual machines
App Service on Windows
explain: Container Apps provides serverless Kubernetes-based hosting with KEDA event-driven autoscaling down to zero — no cluster management. Container Instances run single containers without this autoscaling, VMs need full management, and App Service isn't container orchestration with KEDA.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An AKS cluster runs customer workloads alongside cluster system components. The team wants to upgrade workload nodes without risking the system components. Which AKS construct enables this separation?
options: A single node pool for everything
System and user node pools — system pools host core components, user pools host workloads, each upgraded independently
Deleting the cluster
Running everything on the control plane
explain: AKS best practice separates system node pools (CoreDNS, metrics) from user node pools (workloads), so workload node upgrades don't disturb system components. A single pool mixes them, deleting the cluster is destructive, and customer workloads never run on the managed control plane.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team deploys a new version of its web app to an Azure App Service staging slot, tests it, then makes it live. Users experience no downtime during the switch. What made the cutover seamless?
options: Deleting the production slot
Restarting all VMs
Swapping the staging and production slots — the swap exchanges the running instances atomically
Changing DNS records manually
explain: Deployment slot swap exchanges the staged and production instances (warming up the staging slot first), achieving zero-downtime releases with instant rollback. Deleting production destroys the live app, VM restarts cause downtime, and manual DNS changes are slow and error-prone.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company uses pooled Azure Virtual Desktop host pools (desktops reset at logoff) but engineers need their installed tools and settings to persist between sessions. Which technology provides persistent user profiles on non-persistent desktops?
options: Roaming profiles on USB drives
Reinstalling tools daily
Local profiles only
FSLogix profile containers, which attach the user's profile at sign-in and persist it across sessions
explain: FSLogix profile containers store user profiles in virtual disks attached at sign-in, so settings and tools persist even on non-persistent pooled desktops. USB drives don't roam to cloud desktops, reinstalling daily wastes hours, and local profiles are wiped at logoff.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company runs thousands of identical stateless web servers that are replaced frequently. It wants faster VM provisioning and lower storage cost for the OS disks. Which disk option fits?
options: Ephemeral OS disks — stored on the VM's local temp storage, faster to provision and free, ideal for stateless workloads
Premium SSD for every VM
Unmanaged disks
Archive tier disks
explain: Ephemeral OS disks live on local VM storage: no remote storage cost, faster provisioning, and well-suited to stateless servers that are rebuilt rather than repaired. Premium SSDs cost more, unmanaged disks are legacy, and there is no archive tier for OS disks.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team has verbose ARM JSON templates and wants to convert them to Bicep without rewriting by hand. What should it use?
options: Manual rewriting only
The Bicep decompile command, which converts ARM JSON templates into Bicep files
The Azure pricing calculator
A support ticket
explain: Bicep's decompile command translates existing ARM JSON into Bicep, giving teams a starting point for the more concise language. Manual rewriting wastes effort, the pricing calculator estimates cost, and support tickets don't convert templates.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A platform team deploys 40 resources as one unit and wants deleting the deployment to clean up exactly those resources — including any added later outside the deployment. Which ARM feature manages this lifecycle?
options: Resource groups
Tags
Deployment stacks — they manage a group of resources as a unit, removing out-of-band resources on delete
Locks
explain: Deployment stacks treat resources as a managed unit: updating or deleting the stack reconciles the actual resources, removing anything created outside the stack. Resource groups are just containers, tags are metadata, and locks prevent changes rather than managing lifecycle.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants risk-based sign-in protection, just-in-time admin access with approvals, and recurring access recertification. What is the licensing prerequisite for Identity Protection, PIM, and Access Reviews?
options: They work on the free tier
Microsoft 365 Basic
Azure free account
Microsoft Entra ID P2 (included in premium suites)
explain: Identity Protection, Privileged Identity Management, and Access Reviews are P2 features — they require Microsoft Entra ID P2 licensing. The free tier covers basic directory and single sign-on; P1 adds Conditional Access but not these identity-governance features.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants to block all sign-ins originating from countries where it has no employees or customers. Which Conditional Access construct defines these locations?
options: Named locations — defined IP ranges or countries used as conditions in Conditional Access policies
Resource groups
Availability zones
Management groups
explain: Named locations let administrators label IP ranges or countries and use them as conditions — such as blocking sign-ins from unexpected geographies. Resource groups, availability zones, and management groups organize Azure resources, not sign-in geography.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An administrator builds a Conditional Access policy requiring compliant devices but fears locking out legitimate users. How can they measure the policy's impact before enforcing it?
options: Delete the policy
Report-only mode — the policy evaluates sign-ins and logs what would happen without enforcing
Apply it to break-glass accounts first
Disable MFA
explain: Report-only mode runs the policy in audit mode, logging which sign-ins would be allowed or blocked — safe impact analysis. Deleting loses the work, testing on break-glass accounts risks emergency access, and disabling MFA weakens security rather than testing the policy.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A 20-person company has no Microsoft Entra ID P1 licenses but wants baseline protection: MFA for admins and blocking legacy authentication. Which option provides this without P1?
options: Per-user MFA only
Nothing is available without P1
Security defaults — a free baseline enforcing MFA for admins and blocking legacy auth
A support ticket
explain: Security defaults give small tenants without P1 a free baseline: MFA registration for all users (enforced for admins), blocking legacy authentication, and protecting privileged actions. Per-user MFA is manual and less flexible than policy, and 'nothing available' is wrong — security defaults exist precisely for this scenario.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company regularly invites external consultants who need access to a bundle of resources: a SharePoint site, an app, and a Teams team — with automatic removal after 90 days. Which Entra ID governance feature packages this?
options: Manual group assignments
Resource locks
Conditional Access
Entitlement management access packages — bundled resources with policies, requests, and expiring assignments
explain: Access packages bundle multiple resources with access policies (request, approval, expiration) and are designed for guest lifecycle management. Manual assignments don't expire automatically, locks prevent deletion rather than granting access, and Conditional Access controls sign-in conditions — not resource bundling.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Microsoft Entra ID Protection flags some sign-ins as risky (impossible travel, leaked credentials) and some user accounts as compromised. An admin wants different automated responses for each. Which distinction should they use?
options: Sign-in risk policies react to risky authentication attempts; user risk policies react to likely-compromised accounts
They are the same policy
Risk policies only send emails
Risk policies apply only to admins
explain: Identity Protection separates sign-in risk (risky individual authentications — block or require MFA step-up) from user risk (probably compromised accounts — force password reset). They're distinct policies with different remediations, they can enforce automatically rather than just emailing, and they apply per configured users, not admins-only.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company uses pass-through authentication so no password hashes leave its network. During an internet outage at headquarters, cloud sign-ins start failing. What does this reveal about the design?
options: Microsoft Entra ID was deleted
Pass-through authentication relies on on-premises agents, so those agents must be deployed for high availability across servers
The cloud password vault was unreachable
SSO tokens expired permanently
explain: Pass-through authentication validates passwords via lightweight agents on-premises — no hashes in the cloud — so if all agents are unreachable, cloud authentication fails. The fix is multiple agents for redundancy. Passwords aren't in the cloud by design, and MFA or Conditional Access weren't the failure point.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company's old runbooks reference the 'co-administrator' role for subscription access. The admin learns this model is being retired. What should they migrate to?
options: Shared account passwords
The root management group
Azure RBAC roles (such as Owner or Contributor) — classic subscription admins are deprecated in favor of RBAC
Storage account keys
explain: Classic subscription administrators (Account Admin, Service Admin, co-admins) are deprecated; Azure RBAC with fine-grained roles is the replacement. Shared passwords weaken security, the root management group organizes hierarchy, and storage keys aren't an access-management model.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A security team is assigned the Reader role at the management group containing all 40 company subscriptions. What access do they have?
options: No access, because role assignments can't span subscriptions
Contributor access everywhere
Reader only on the management group object itself
Reader access across all subscriptions, resource groups, and resources beneath — role assignments inherit down the hierarchy
explain: RBAC assignments inherit downward: a Reader assignment at the management group flows to every subscription, resource group, and resource below it. Assignments absolutely span subscriptions via management groups, Reader doesn't grant Contributor rights, and the access isn't limited to the management group object.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company needs a custom role that can do everything a Contributor can except deleting virtual machines and managing access. How are these exclusions expressed in the custom role definition?
options: With NotActions in the role definition — Actions grant permissions, NotActions subtract specific ones
By creating two separate roles
With a CanNotDelete lock on the subscription
It's impossible to subtract permissions in RBAC
explain: Custom roles define allowed operations in Actions and carve out exceptions in NotActions — the effective permissions are Actions minus NotActions. Two roles wouldn't combine correctly, locks block operations for everyone (not a role definition), and subtraction is precisely what NotActions is for.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A ReadOnly lock is applied to a resource group containing a stopped virtual machine. An engineer tries to start the VM. What happens?
options: The VM starts normally
The start is blocked — ReadOnly locks deny write operations, and starting a VM is a write (POST) action
The VM is deleted
The lock is automatically removed
explain: ReadOnly locks block all write, create, and delete operations; starting a stopped VM issues a POST (write) to the compute provider, so it's denied. The VM isn't deleted and locks are never auto-removed — only authorized users can remove them.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company assigns a 'deployIfNotExists' policy to auto-install the monitoring agent on VMs. The policy detects non-compliant VMs but remediation fails. What is the most likely missing piece?
options: The policy needs a higher priority number
More tags
The remediation task's managed identity needs a role assignment granting it permission to install the extension
A second policy
explain: DeployIfNotExists remediation runs under a managed identity created with the assignment — that identity needs RBAC permission (for example, Contributor on the scope) to actually deploy the extension. Priority numbers don't grant permissions, tags are unrelated, and a duplicate policy wouldn't fix authorization.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company assigns a new policy requiring encryption on storage accounts. An hour later, several existing accounts still show as compliant. When will Azure re-evaluate them?
options: Never — only new resources are evaluated
Immediately for all resources
Manually only
New resources are evaluated at deployment; existing resources are re-scanned within about 24 hours in the regular compliance cycle
explain: Policy evaluates new deployments in real time, while existing resources are picked up by the periodic compliance scan (typically within 24 hours). 'Never' and 'manual only' are wrong — evaluation is automatic — and an hour may simply precede the next scan cycle.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A compliance team must implement 60 related controls from NIST SP 800-53 across all subscriptions. Rather than building each policy from scratch, what should they start from?
options: Built-in policy initiatives, such as the NIST SP 800-53 initiative, which package related definitions for assignment
A blank ARM template
A resource group
A support ticket
explain: Microsoft publishes built-in initiatives mapping regulatory frameworks (NIST SP 800-53, ISO 27001, PCI DSS) to policy definitions — assignable as one unit. ARM templates deploy resources rather than govern them, resource groups don't package policies, and support tickets don't create governance.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company pays upfront for a one-year VM reservation. In Cost Management, the finance team wants the reservation cost spread across the months it covers rather than appearing as one lump sum. Which view does this?
options: Actual cost view
Amortized cost view — it distributes upfront reservation and savings-plan charges across the benefit period
The invoice PDF
The pricing calculator
explain: Amortized cost spreads upfront commitment charges across the months they benefit, showing true monthly run-rate; actual cost shows when the charge hit. The invoice lists transactions and the pricing calculator estimates future costs — neither re-allocates reservation spend.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company runs shared platform services (firewall, DNS, monitoring) in one subscription used by ten departments. Finance wants those shared costs distributed to each department's subscription. Which Cost Management feature does this?
options: Resource locks
Tags alone
Cost allocation rules, which redistribute shared costs from one scope to others by configurable rules
Budgets
explain: Cost allocation rules split costs from a shared scope across target scopes (subscriptions or resource groups) by percentage or formula — built for shared-platform chargeback. Tags label resources but don't move costs, locks prevent changes, and budgets only alert on thresholds.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company holds a reservation for D-series VMs in West Europe but is standardizing on E-series in North Europe. What can it do with the existing reservation?
options: Nothing — reservations are immutable
Abandon it and buy a new one
Use it for any VM worldwide
Exchange the reservation for the new VM family and region, subject to eligibility rules
explain: Reservations can be exchanged for different VM families, sizes, or regions (with some restrictions), preserving the commitment value. They're not immutable, abandoning wastes the commitment, and scope rules limit where the discount applies — exchange is the designed path.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A startup wants reservation discounts but can't pay a large upfront sum. Which payment option exists for reservations?
options: Monthly payments — reservations can be paid upfront or in monthly installments
Upfront payment is the only option
Pay with cryptocurrency
Bill to a personal credit card only
explain: Reservations offer upfront or monthly payment options, so cash-constrained teams can still get commitment discounts. Upfront-only is false, crypto isn't a payment method, and billing follows the normal billing account — not a personal card requirement.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company is migrating 200 VMs to Azure over six months and holds Windows Server licenses with Software Assurance. During the migration, some workloads run simultaneously on-premises and in Azure. Which benefit covers this overlap?
options: Spot VMs
Dual-use rights — Azure Hybrid Benefit allows using the same licenses on-premises and in Azure simultaneously for up to 180 days during migration
Free Azure support
The Azure free account
explain: Hybrid Benefit's dual-use rights permit running the same Windows Server or SQL Server licenses both on-premises and in Azure for up to 180 days while migrating. Spot VMs are discounted spare capacity, support plans don't license software, and the free account is for learning — not license mobility.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A large enterprise negotiates custom pricing and a three-year commitment with Microsoft, while a small startup pays standard rates month-to-month. Which agreements describe these two purchasing models?
options: Both use the Microsoft Customer Agreement
Both must use an Enterprise Agreement
The enterprise likely uses an Enterprise Agreement (EA); the startup uses the Microsoft Customer Agreement (MCA) pay-as-you-go model
Agreements don't affect pricing
explain: The Enterprise Agreement serves large organizations with negotiated commitments and custom pricing; the MCA is the standard modern pay-as-you-go agreement. A startup wouldn't hold an EA, and agreements absolutely affect pricing and terms.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A student on the Azure free account worries about accidentally incurring charges while learning. What protects them?
options: Nothing — charges accrue freely
Microsoft waives all overages automatically
The credit card is never required
A spending cap that disables paid resources before charges occur; it can only be removed by upgrading to pay-as-you-go
explain: The free account includes a spending limit: when the credit is exhausted, paid services are disabled rather than billed — the cap is only lifted by explicitly upgrading to pay-as-you-go. Charges don't accrue silently, overages aren't auto-waived, and a card is required for identity verification (not charged while capped).
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A vendor promises '99.99% uptime backed by our SLA' for its application, which runs entirely on an Azure service whose own SLA is 99.9%. What should the customer understand?
options: Azure SLAs apply per service — the application's achievable uptime can't exceed its weakest dependency's SLA, and Microsoft's SLA covers the Azure service, not the vendor's promise
Azure's 99.9% automatically becomes 99.99%
The vendor's SLA is guaranteed by Microsoft
SLAs cover the entire Azure account at once
explain: Each Azure service carries its own SLA; a workload built on a 99.9% service can't deliver 99.99% on that dependency alone, and Microsoft's SLA is between Microsoft and the Azure customer — not a guarantee of a third party's marketing claim. SLAs are per-service, never account-wide.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company's Azure bill looks wrong — a charge it doesn't recognize appears. It has only the free Basic support plan. Can it get help with this billing question?
options: No — billing support requires a paid plan
Yes — billing and subscription support is included free on all plans, including Basic
Only through the community forums
Only by upgrading first
explain: Billing and subscription support is free for every Azure customer on every plan, including Basic — paid plans add technical support with response-time SLAs. Billing questions never require an upgrade or forum-only help.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An administrator wants to know whether an Azure outage is affecting only their tenant's resources or is a broad regional incident. Which sources answer each part?
options: The Azure status page shows personalized tenant impact
Service Health shows only billing data
Azure Service Health shows personalized impact on your resources; the public status page shows broad regional service issues
Neither exists
explain: Service Health is personalized — it reports incidents affecting your subscriptions and resources, plus planned maintenance. The public status page shows overall regional health for everyone. The status page isn't personalized, Service Health isn't billing data, and both tools exist.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants to automatically label documents containing passport numbers as 'Highly Confidential' and to keep financial records for seven years before deletion. Which two Purview label types serve these needs?
options: Both are retention labels
Both are sensitivity labels
Labels only apply to emails
Sensitivity labels classify and protect content (encryption, watermarking); retention labels govern how long content is kept
explain: Sensitivity labels classify and protect (labeling, encryption, watermarks); retention labels control lifecycle (retain then delete). They're complementary: classify with sensitivity labels, govern lifespan with retention labels — and both span documents, emails, and more.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A security team wants vulnerability assessment of its Azure VMs without installing or managing agents on each machine. Which Defender for Cloud capability enables this?
options: Agentless VM scanning — platform-level assessment without deploying agents
Manual penetration testing
Disabling the VMs
NSG flow logs
explain: Defender for Cloud's agentless scanning assesses VMs from the platform side — no agent deployment or maintenance. Manual pentesting doesn't scale continuously, disabling VMs defeats the purpose, and NSG flow logs record network traffic rather than assessing vulnerabilities.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A CISO is comparing Defender for Servers plan options and also needs threat protection for container workloads. Which statement is TRUE?
options: There is only one Defender plan for everything
Defender for Servers offers P1 and P2 tiers with increasing protection depth, and Defender for Containers protects container environments including registries and Kubernetes
Defender plans only cover storage
Containers can't be protected
explain: Defender for Cloud has per-workload plans: Defender for Servers P1/P2 (P2 adds deeper threat detection) and Defender for Containers (registries, Kubernetes, running containers). It's not one-size-fits-all, covers far more than storage, and containers are explicitly covered.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A SOC wants Microsoft Sentinel to automatically isolate a compromised VM and open a ServiceNow ticket when a high-severity incident fires, with no analyst clicking anything. What implements this response?
options: Manual runbooks only
Sentinel workbooks
Sentinel automation rules triggering playbooks — playbooks are Logic Apps workflows that execute the response actions
KQL queries alone
explain: Automation rules react to incidents by triggering playbooks, which are Azure Logic Apps workflows that call APIs — isolating VMs, creating tickets, disabling accounts. Workbooks are dashboards, KQL queries retrieve data, and manual runbooks defeat the automation goal.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A Sentinel analyst sees dozens of separate low-severity alerts that turn out to be stages of one attack. Which Sentinel capability correlates related alerts into a single incident?
options: Data connectors
Workbooks
Scheduled query rules only
Fusion — Microsoft's correlation engine that combines related alerts into unified incidents
explain: Fusion uses machine learning to correlate alerts across sources and time into single incidents representing one attack story. Data connectors ingest the data, workbooks visualize it, and scheduled rules generate the individual alerts — Fusion does the correlating.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A team stores an API's database password, an RSA private key for encryption, and a TLS certificate for its web app in Azure Key Vault. Which vault object types hold these three items?
options: Secrets for the password, keys for the RSA key, certificates for the TLS certificate — each type has purpose-built handling
All three are keys
All three are certificates
All three are secrets
explain: Key Vault distinguishes secrets (passwords, connection strings), keys (cryptographic keys for encrypt, decrypt, and sign operations), and certificates (managed TLS certs with lifecycle). Storing everything as one type loses purpose-built features like certificate auto-renewal and key operations.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants its database passwords in Key Vault rotated automatically every 30 days without human involvement. Which pattern implements this?
options: Manual rotation by an admin
Event Grid notifying an Azure Function on rotation schedule, which generates and stores the new secret — the documented auto-rotation pattern
Storing passwords in code
Disabling the database monthly
explain: The published auto-rotation pattern uses Event Grid (or a timer) to trigger a Function that creates the new credential and writes it to Key Vault — fully automated. Manual rotation doesn't scale, code-stored secrets are the anti-pattern, and disabling the database is downtime, not rotation.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company is adopting Zero Trust and wants to structure the program around Microsoft's published model. Which six pillars does the model cover?
options: Firewalls, antivirus, VPNs, passwords, backups, and patching
Users, groups, roles, policies, locks, and tags
Identities, devices, data, applications, infrastructure, and networks
Regions, zones, VNets, subnets, NSGs, and gateways
explain: Microsoft's Zero Trust model spans six foundational pillars: identities, devices, data, applications, infrastructure, and networks — each protected under 'never trust, always verify.' The other lists mix tools, RBAC concepts, or networking components rather than the model's pillars.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: As part of defense in depth, a company encrypts its VM disks so stolen disk files are unreadable. Which defense-in-depth layer does disk encryption primarily strengthen?
options: The perimeter layer
The network layer
The identity layer
The data layer — protecting information itself, the innermost layer
explain: Defense in depth layers data protection at the center: disk encryption protects the data layer directly, so stolen media yields nothing readable. Perimeter and network layers guard boundaries, identity governs access — but encryption protects the data even when outer layers fail.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A trainer asks students to list the five essential characteristics of cloud computing as defined by NIST. Which list is correct?
options: Unlimited free storage, no passwords required, automatic profit, instant hiring, zero maintenance
Physical servers, on-premises datacenters, perpetual licenses, manual provisioning, fixed capacity
On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service
Virtual machines, containers, serverless functions, databases, and networking
explain: NIST defines exactly these five characteristics: self-service provisioning, access over standard networks, pooled shared resources, elastic scaling, and metered usage. The first option invents fantasy benefits, the second describes on-premises IT, and the fourth lists service types rather than characteristics.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A finance team wants to verify that each department is billed only for the cloud resources it actually consumed last month. Which cloud characteristic makes this possible?
options: Resource pooling — departments share the same hardware
Broad network access — services are reachable from anywhere
Measured service — usage is metered, monitored, and reported for billing
Rapid elasticity — resources scale automatically
explain: Measured service means the provider meters usage and reports it, so billing reflects actual consumption. Resource pooling is about shared infrastructure, broad network access is about reachability, and elasticity is about scaling — none of them produce the bill.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A sales team accesses the company CRM from laptops, tablets, and phones over the public internet, with no VPN or special client software. Which characteristic does this demonstrate?
options: On-demand self-service
Broad network access — services available over the network through standard devices and protocols
Resource pooling
Measured service
explain: Broad network access means capabilities are available over the network and accessed through standard mechanisms by heterogeneous devices. On-demand self-service is about provisioning without human interaction, resource pooling is about shared infrastructure, and measured service is about metering.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A cloud provider runs thousands of customers on shared physical infrastructure, dynamically assigning capacity, and customers generally do not know the exact server or location running their workload. This is:
options: Measured service
Resource pooling — the provider's resources are pooled to serve many customers at once
Rapid elasticity
A community cloud
explain: Resource pooling is the multitenant model: physical and virtual resources are pooled and dynamically assigned, with location independence for the customer. Measured service is metering, elasticity is scaling, and community cloud is a deployment model, not the pooling characteristic.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: Several public universities form a consortium to share a cloud environment for genomics research, restricted to member institutions with shared security and compliance requirements. This deployment model is:
options: A community cloud — infrastructure shared by organizations with common concerns
A public cloud open to any paying customer
A private cloud dedicated to a single university
A hybrid cloud
explain: A community cloud is shared by several organizations with shared mission, policy, or compliance needs — exactly the university consortium. A public cloud is open to all, a private cloud serves one organization, and hybrid mixes deployment models.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A startup worries that sharing cloud hardware with other companies puts its data at risk. How does a public cloud keep one tenant's data separate from another's?
options: Each customer is given physically separate datacenters
Tenants take turns using the hardware on a schedule
Logical isolation — virtualization, encryption, and access controls separate tenants on shared infrastructure
Customer data is only encrypted on the customer's own laptop
explain: Public clouds are multitenant by design; isolation is logical through virtualization boundaries, identity controls, and encryption — not separate buildings. Time-sharing hardware is not how clouds work, and laptop encryption does nothing for data stored in the cloud.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A retailer wants to launch a promotion microsite in a new country this afternoon instead of waiting months for server procurement and shipping. Which cloud benefit makes this possible?
options: Geo-distribution
Economies of scale
Disaster recovery
Agility — provisioning and deploying IT resources in minutes instead of weeks
explain: Agility is the ability to deploy, scale, and reconfigure resources rapidly as business needs change. Geo-distribution is about location, economies of scale about unit cost, and disaster recovery about surviving outages.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An architect says the new system must automatically add capacity during the morning rush and release it at night, while also supporting long-term growth as the user base doubles each year. Which pair of terms describes these two needs, in order?
options: Scalability, then elasticity
Agility, then elasticity
Fault tolerance, then high availability
Elasticity — automatic short-term adjustment to demand — then scalability — the ability to handle increased load over time
explain: Elasticity is dynamic scaling out and in with demand; scalability is the system's capacity to handle growth. The first two options reverse or confuse the terms, and fault tolerance and availability are about surviving failures, not capacity.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A web farm handles a traffic spike by adding more identical servers behind a load balancer, while the database tier is moved to a larger VM with more memory. In order, these are examples of:
options: Scaling up, then scaling out
Scaling out — horizontal, adding more instances — then scaling up — vertical, increasing an instance's size
Elasticity, then agility
Fault tolerance, then disaster recovery
explain: Scaling out (horizontal) adds instances; scaling up (vertical) increases the size of an existing instance. The first option reverses them, and the remaining options name unrelated concepts.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A gaming company deploys game servers in Azure regions on four continents so players connect to nearby servers and each player's data stays in their home country. Which benefit is the company using?
options: Economies of scale
Geo-distribution — global reach for low latency and data-residency needs
Serverless computing
Measured service
explain: Geo-distribution lets you place resources near users to cut latency and satisfy data-residency rules. Economies of scale is about unit cost, serverless about execution model, and measured service about metering.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A hospital's patient-monitoring system must keep running with zero interruption even if a server fails — brief failover gaps are unacceptable because any gap in monitoring risks lives. Which design goal is this?
options: High availability — minimal downtime
Fault tolerance — continued operation with no service interruption despite component failures
Disaster recovery
Backup
explain: Fault tolerance means the system keeps operating through failures with zero interruption, typically via full redundancy. High availability minimizes downtime but can include brief failover gaps; disaster recovery restores operations after a major event; backup is about data copies.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A startup with almost no capital needs to launch its app next month. Buying servers is impossible, but it can afford a monthly cloud bill that rises and falls with usage. Moving from buying hardware to paying monthly shifts spending from:
options: Capital expenditure (CapEx) to operational expenditure (OpEx)
OpEx to CapEx
Fixed cost to fixed cost
Revenue to profit
explain: Buying servers is CapEx — large upfront investment. Paying a monthly usage bill is OpEx — ongoing operational cost with no upfront commitment. The second option reverses the shift, and the others misuse the terms.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company buys $200,000 of servers it expects to use for five years. Which statement about this capital expenditure is true?
options: The cost appears only in months when the servers are heavily used
Unused capacity costs nothing
Spending can be reduced in any given month
It requires significant upfront spending, and the company must guess future capacity needs
explain: CapEx means paying upfront before knowing exact needs — overprovisioning wastes money and underprovisioning risks shortages. Costs are sunk regardless of use, so the first three options describe OpEx, not CapEx.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A virtual machine runs for 37 minutes during a test, then is deleted. Under the consumption-based pricing model, the customer:
options: Pays for a full month of VM time
Pays only for the 37 minutes the VM existed
Pays a flat annual fee regardless of usage
Pays nothing because test workloads are free
explain: Consumption-based (pay-as-you-go) pricing meters actual usage — you pay for what you consume and billing stops when resources are deleted. There is no monthly minimum, no flat fee, and test workloads are billed like any other usage.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company comparing cloud providers asks what an SLA actually promises. The BEST description is:
options: A guarantee that the customer's application code has no bugs
A marketing promise of unlimited performance
Free technical support forever
A formal commitment describing expected uptime or performance, with service credits if targets are missed
explain: An SLA is a contractual commitment to availability or performance levels, backed by service credits — not cash refunds — when missed. It never covers the customer's own code, promises unlimited anything, or includes perpetual free support.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's app goes down because of a bug in its own code deployed that morning. The cloud platform itself stayed healthy the entire time. Can the company claim SLA credits?
options: Yes — SLAs cover all downtime regardless of cause
Yes — any software bug qualifies
No — SLAs cover the provider's platform availability, not the customer's code or configuration
No — SLAs only apply during business hours
explain: SLAs commit to the provider's infrastructure and platform services; the customer's application code, data, and configuration are always the customer's responsibility. The platform met its SLA here, so no credits apply.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An architect is choosing between two designs for an order-processing workflow. Design X uses a single Azure service with a 99.9% SLA. Design Y chains three Azure services, each with a 99.9% SLA. Which design offers higher availability, and why?
options: Design Y — more services means more redundancy
They are equal — every service carries the same SLA
Design Y — chaining services multiplies the SLA upward
Design X — each chained dependency lowers the composite SLA, so the single-service design stays near 99.9% while the chained design drops toward 99.7%
explain: A composite SLA is the product of its dependencies' SLAs, so chaining services in series drives availability down — three 99.9% services yield roughly 99.7%. The distractors confuse series chaining, which weakens availability, with parallel redundancy, which strengthens it.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A team wants SLA coverage for its production database. Which statement about Azure SLAs is true?
options: Free-tier services carry the same SLAs as paid tiers
SLAs apply automatically with no configuration required
SLAs guarantee 100% data durability
Higher SLAs generally require redundant configurations, such as availability zones or scale sets
explain: SLA levels are tied to how you deploy — redundancy across zones or instances earns higher commitments, while single instances get lower or no SLA. Free tiers typically carry no SLA, and no SLA promises perfection.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A photo-sharing app must generate thumbnails the instant a user uploads a photo, then do nothing until the next upload. The team wants no servers to manage and costs only when code runs. The best fit is:
options: Serverless computing — event-driven code that scales to zero with no server management
A dedicated physical server
A virtual machine running 24/7
On-premises storage
explain: Serverless abstracts servers away: code runs on events, scales automatically, and you pay per execution. A dedicated server or always-on VM bills continuously for idle time, and on-premises storage does not process uploads.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A cloud provider buys hardware in massive volume and passes the savings to customers as lower per-unit prices. This benefit is called:
options: Geo-distribution
Agility
Economies of scale
Measured service
explain: Economies of scale: the provider's huge purchasing power and utilization drive down unit costs, letting customers pay less than they could achieve alone. The other options describe location, speed, and metering — not cost structure.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company runs the same database workload 24/7 and expects it to continue for three years; it also runs short marketing campaign workloads a few times a year. The most cost-effective pricing mix is:
options: Pay-as-you-go for everything
Reserved capacity for everything
Spot VMs for the database
Reserved capacity for the steady database, pay-as-you-go for the campaign spikes
explain: Reservations discount predictable long-term usage, while pay-as-you-go fits variable spikes you cannot forecast. Reserving spiky workloads wastes money, pure pay-as-you-go overpays for the steady workload, and Spot VMs can be evicted — unacceptable for a 24/7 database.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A company's datacenter floods. The team fails over to a secondary site and resumes business operations there. Which concept did they exercise?
options: Disaster recovery — restoring operations after a disruptive event
Backup — they restored files
High availability — they avoided downtime
Fault tolerance
explain: Disaster recovery is the plan and process for restoring operations after a major disruption, such as failing over to a secondary site. Backup is point-in-time data copies, high availability minimizes downtime of a running system, and fault tolerance avoids interruption entirely.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A bank's policy states that online banking must be restored within 4 hours of any outage. The 4-hour target is the:
options: Recovery point objective
Backup window
Recovery time objective (RTO) — the maximum acceptable downtime
SLA credit
explain: RTO is how long you can afford to be down; RPO is how much data loss you can tolerate. The backup window is when backups run, and SLA credits are the provider's remedy — none of these set the restoration deadline.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A retailer runs its store on on-premises servers sized for normal days but bursts into Azure for extra capacity during the holiday rush. This pattern is called:
options: Cloud bursting — handling peak demand with public cloud capacity
Multicloud
Community cloud
Serverless computing
explain: Cloud bursting keeps steady workloads on-premises and bursts into the cloud for peaks. Multicloud means using multiple public providers, community cloud is shared by related organizations, and serverless is an execution model.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A factory needs Azure-style virtual machines on its own shop floor because millisecond latency to the robots rules out a distant datacenter, and regulations keep the data on-site. Which option fits?
options: Azure Stack HCI — running Azure services on-premises as a private cloud
A public Azure region
SaaS applications only
Moving the robots to the cloud
explain: Azure Stack brings Azure services into the customer's datacenter for latency-sensitive or regulated workloads — a private/hybrid cloud. A public region cannot meet the latency and data-location constraints, and SaaS does not provide VMs.
