q: A security team needs to collect logs from firewalls, Azure resources, and Microsoft 365, correlate them to detect attacks, and automatically isolate compromised machines. Which Azure service is built for this?
options: Azure Monitor — which collects operational metrics and logs but is not a SIEM/SOAR
Log Analytics — a query workspace, not the full detection-and-response solution
Microsoft Sentinel — a cloud-native SIEM and SOAR for detection, investigation, and automated response
Microsoft Defender for Cloud — which assesses posture rather than correlating multi-source security events
explain: Sentinel is the SIEM (collect and correlate security data) plus SOAR (automated response like isolating machines). Monitor handles operational telemetry, Log Analytics is the underlying query engine, and Defender for Cloud scores posture — none deliver the full detect-and-respond security-operations role.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An operations team wants CPU, memory, and disk metrics plus activity logs collected from all its VMs and apps into one place for dashboards and alerts. Which service collects this telemetry?
options: Azure Service Health — which reports Azure platform incidents, not customer resource metrics
Azure Resource Health — which reports the health of individual resources, not metric collection
Azure Advisor — which gives best-practice recommendations rather than collecting telemetry
Azure Monitor — which collects metrics, logs, and activity data from Azure resources for analysis and alerting
explain: Azure Monitor is the telemetry platform: metrics, logs, and activity data with dashboards and alerts. Service Health covers platform-wide incidents, Resource Health reports per-resource status, and Advisor recommends optimizations — none are the metrics-and-logs collection service.

q: Developers need to know why their web app is slow — which requests fail, where time is spent in code, and how users experience performance. Which monitoring service gives application-level insight?
options: Application Insights — application performance monitoring: request tracking, dependencies, exceptions, and user analytics
Log Analytics alone — a query workspace without the app-centric APM experience
Azure Service Health — platform incident reporting, unrelated to app code
Network Watcher — network diagnostics, not application performance
explain: Application Insights is the APM service: request rates, failures, dependency timing, and user behavior inside the application. Log Analytics is the raw query engine beneath it, Service Health reports Azure outages, and Network Watcher diagnoses networks — none answer 'why is my code slow.'

q: During a widespread Azure outage, an admin wants to know whether the platform incident is affecting her region and view Microsoft's status updates. Which service should she check?
options: Azure Resource Health — which reports on her specific resources rather than platform-wide incidents
Azure Service Health — which publishes Azure-wide service issues, planned maintenance, and health advisories by region
Azure Monitor — which tracks her resources' metrics rather than Microsoft's platform status
Azure Advisor — which recommends optimizations rather than reporting outages
explain: Service Health is the platform-status channel: regional service issues, planned maintenance, and advisories. Resource Health covers the health of her own resources, Monitor collects her telemetry, and Advisor gives recommendations — none publish Microsoft's incident communications.

q: A consultant works from a locked-down laptop with no terminal installed and needs to run Azure CLI commands against a client's subscription. What lets her do this from the browser?
options: The Azure portal's resource blades — which manage resources graphically but do not run CLI commands
A locally installed PowerShell — which the locked-down laptop cannot install
Azure Cloud Shell — a browser-based shell with Azure CLI and PowerShell preinstalled and authenticated
Azure Service Health — which reports incidents rather than running commands
explain: Cloud Shell is a browser-based, authenticated shell with CLI and PowerShell built in — no local install needed. Portal blades are graphical rather than command-line, local PowerShell requires installation, and Service Health only reports platform status.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A team must deploy the same 40-resource environment to development, testing, and production — identically, repeatedly, and without manual portal clicking. Which approach makes deployments repeatable?
options: Manual portal deployment — which is slow and error-prone across environments
Cloud Shell ad-hoc commands — which are manual and not version-controlled
Emailing screenshots of the portal configuration — which deploys nothing
Infrastructure as Code with ARM templates or Bicep — declarative templates deployed identically every time
explain: Infrastructure as Code (ARM templates or Bicep) defines the environment declaratively so all three environments deploy identically and repeatably. Manual portal work, ad-hoc shell commands, and screenshots cannot guarantee consistency or be version-controlled.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An admin wants personalized, prioritized recommendations — shut down idle VMs to save money, enable MFA, add availability zones — across cost, security, and reliability. Which service generates these?
options: Azure Advisor — personalized best-practice recommendations across cost, security, reliability, and performance
Azure Policy — which enforces rules rather than recommending improvements
Microsoft Cost Management — which analyzes spend but does not recommend MFA or zones
Azure Monitor alerts — which fire on metric thresholds rather than suggesting best practices
explain: Advisor produces prioritized, personalized recommendations across cost, security, reliability, operational excellence, and performance. Policy enforces rather than advises, Cost Management reports spend, and Monitor alerts on thresholds — none generate the cross-category best-practice guidance.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: After a phishing attack compromises one password, a company decides administrators must approve sign-ins with a second factor on their phones. What is this authentication requirement called?
options: Single sign-on — which reduces passwords to one but does not add a second factor
Multifactor authentication (MFA) — requiring two or more verification methods, so a stolen password alone is not enough
Role-based access control — which authorizes actions rather than strengthening sign-in
Password rotation — which changes passwords but still relies on a single factor
explain: MFA requires an additional verification factor (phone approval) beyond the password, neutralizing the phished credential. SSO simplifies sign-in without adding factors, RBAC governs authorization after sign-in, and rotation keeps the single factor single — none add the second factor.

q: A security architect designs a network where no user or device is trusted by default — every request is verified, access is least-privilege, and breach is assumed. Which security model is this?
options: Perimeter security — which trusts everything inside the network boundary
VPN-everything — which extends trust rather than verifying each request
Zero Trust — verify explicitly, grant least-privilege access, and assume breach
Security through obscurity — hiding systems rather than verifying access
explain: Zero Trust is built on verify explicitly, least-privilege access, and assume breach — never trusting by network location. Perimeter models trust insiders by default, VPNs extend the trusted boundary, and obscurity is not a security model at all.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: Before migrating a regulated workload, a risk team performs vendor due diligence and wants to review Microsoft's independently audited certifications — ISO 27001, SOC 2 — for Azure. Where are these published?
options: Azure Advisor — which recommends best practices rather than publishing audit certificates
Microsoft Defender for Cloud — which assesses workload posture rather than hosting Microsoft's own certifications
The Azure Policy compliance dashboard — which shows customer resource compliance, not Microsoft's audit reports
The Microsoft Service Trust Portal — the repository for Microsoft's compliance reports, certifications, and audit documents
explain: The Service Trust Portal publishes Microsoft's official compliance documentation — ISO certificates, SOC reports, and regional attestations — the source for vendor due diligence. Advisor recommends, Defender for Cloud scores workloads, and Policy dashboards show customer-resource compliance — none host Microsoft's own audit evidence.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A startup creates its Azure footprint and needs a boundary that groups its billing, lets it set spending limits, and scopes who can manage everything inside. Which Azure construct is this boundary?
options: An Azure subscription — the billing boundary that also scopes access and policy
A resource group — which organizes resources but is not the billing boundary
A management group — which sits above subscriptions rather than being one
A tag — which labels resources but creates no boundary at all
explain: The subscription is the fundamental billing and access boundary in Azure — invoices, quotas, and RBAC scope to it. Resource groups organize within a subscription, management groups govern across subscriptions, and tags merely label — none define the billing boundary.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A European bank's regulators require all workloads to stay in EU datacenters. The cloud team wants Azure itself to reject any deployment outside the EU, automatically. Which governance tool enforces this?
options: A resource lock — which blocks changes or deletion but cannot restrict deployment locations
Azure Policy with an allowed-locations rule — which denies any deployment outside the approved EU regions
A budget — which alerts on spending but restricts nothing
A naming-convention tag — which labels resources without enforcing where they deploy
explain: Azure Policy's allowed-locations effect denies deployments outside the EU automatically — true enforcement of data residency. Locks protect against modification/deletion, budgets only alert, and tags label without enforcing — the classic trap of confusing labeling or alerting with enforcement.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company commits to spending a fixed amount per hour on Azure compute for one year to get a discount, but it wants the flexibility to switch VM sizes and regions as needs change. Which discount option fits?
options: Pay-as-you-go — which offers no commitment discount at all
Spot VMs — which are cheap but can be evicted and offer no commitment pricing
Azure Savings Plans — a commitment to hourly spend (1 or 3 years) that applies flexibly across VM sizes and regions
Free-tier services — which cover only small fixed quantities, not enterprise compute
explain: Savings Plans commit to a dollar-per-hour spend for 1 or 3 years and apply flexibly across sizes and regions — the key distinction from reservations. Pay-as-you-go has no discount, spot is evictible surplus capacity, and free tiers cover only tiny allowances.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company migrates its on-premises databases to Azure SQL Database and wants to reuse its existing SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance instead of paying Azure's built-in SQL license rates. Which benefit makes this possible?
options: Spot pricing — which discounts spare VM capacity, not database licensing
Reserved capacity — which discounts compute commitments, not license reuse
The Azure free account — a trial credit, not a licensing program
Azure Hybrid Benefit — which lets you apply existing SQL Server and Windows Server licenses with Software Assurance to Azure, lowering license costs
explain: Azure Hybrid Benefit covers both Windows Server and SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance — including PaaS databases like Azure SQL Database — so the company avoids paying for licenses twice. Spot discounts spare capacity, reservations discount compute, and the free account is a trial credit — none reuse existing licenses.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company needs a 99.99% connectivity SLA for its virtual machines. According to Microsoft's published SLA, which deployment meets this target?
options: Two or more VMs deployed across availability zones in the same region — the configuration Microsoft backs with a 99.99% SLA
A single VM with premium storage — which carries a 99.9% SLA, not 99.99%
Two VMs in one availability set — which carries a 99.95% SLA
One VM in each of two paired regions with no load balancing — regions do not combine into a VM SLA this way
explain: Microsoft's SLA guarantees 99.99% for two or more VMs across availability zones in a region. A single premium-storage VM is 99.9%, an availability set pair is 99.95%, and scattering single VMs across regions without a designed topology earns no combined VM SLA.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A startup wants the cheapest paid Azure support plan that still includes technical support for troubleshooting (not just billing help). Which plan should it choose?
options: Basic — which is free but covers only billing and subscription support, no technical cases
Developer — the lowest-cost paid plan, with business-hours technical support for trial and non-production workloads
Standard — which adds 24/7 support and faster response times at a higher price
Professional Direct — the premium tier with the fastest response times and ProDirect delivery managers
explain: Developer is the entry-level paid plan with technical support (business hours), making it the cheapest option beyond billing-only help. Basic is free but billing-only, while Standard and Professional Direct add 24/7 coverage and speed at higher cost.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: After a reorganization, an admin needs to move several virtual machines and their disks from the 'legacy' resource group to the 'production' resource group. Is this allowed?
options: No — resources are permanently bound to the resource group where they were created
Only by deleting and recreating the virtual machines from scratch
Yes — most Azure resources can be moved between resource groups and subscriptions, subject to documented limitations
Only if the subscription is cancelled and recreated first
explain: Azure supports moving most resources between resource groups and subscriptions (with some service-specific limitations) — reorganization does not require rebuilds. The 'permanently bound' and 'delete and recreate' options are the classic traps; cancelling the subscription would destroy everything rather than reorganize it.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: An admin deletes the 'old-project' resource group to clean up. What happens to the virtual machines, storage accounts, and databases that were inside it?
options: They are automatically moved to another resource group in the subscription
They are kept but become invisible until reassigned to a new group
Only their tags are removed; the resources keep running
Deleting a resource group deletes everything inside it — the standard way to remove a whole solution at once
explain: Resource groups share a lifecycle: deleting the group deletes all contained resources — which is exactly why teams use one group per solution. Resources are never auto-moved, never linger invisibly, and tags are irrelevant — deletion is total, so it demands caution.

q: An administrator wants one web-based place to create resources, view billing, open Cloud Shell, and manage role assignments. Which Azure tool provides this unified experience?
options: The Azure portal — the web-based console for building, managing, billing, and monitoring Azure resources
The Service Trust Portal — which hosts compliance documents rather than managing resources
The Azure status page — which shows platform health rather than managing anything
The pricing calculator — which estimates costs rather than managing resources
explain: The Azure portal is the unified web console: resource management, billing views, Cloud Shell, and RBAC in one place. The Service Trust Portal hosts audit documents, the status page reports platform health, and the pricing calculator estimates costs — none manage resources.
domain: Domain 3: Describe Azure management and governance

q: A company wants two things: automatically block any deployment that violates its tagging standard, and get an email when monthly spending reaches 80% of budget. Which combination delivers both?
options: Resource locks plus tags — locks block changes but cannot enforce tagging rules on new deployments
RBAC plus Azure Monitor — RBAC scopes who can act but cannot auto-block untagged deployments
Azure Advisor plus Service Health — Advisor recommends and Service Health reports incidents; neither enforces or alerts on spend
Azure Policy to deny non-compliant deployments, plus a budget with an 80% alert threshold to notify on spend
explain: Policy's deny effect blocks deployments missing required tags (enforcement), while budgets send alerts at thresholds like 80% without ever stopping spend (notification). Locks cannot evaluate tagging rules, RBAC cannot judge compliance, and Advisor/Service Health neither enforce policy nor track budget thresholds.

q: A food-truck company opens seasonal kiosks and wants its IT spending to rise and fall with revenue instead of buying servers before each season. Which financial model makes this possible?
options: Shipping the same physical servers between kiosks as locations open and close
OpEx — paying a monthly usage-based bill so costs track revenue instead of large upfront server purchases
Leasing a private datacenter cage on a five-year contract to lock in capacity
CapEx — buying bigger servers before each season so the hardware is owned outright
explain: OpEx (operational expenditure) turns IT into a pay-as-you-go monthly cost that scales with the business, which is exactly what a seasonal company needs. CapEx means large upfront purchases that sit idle off-season; a five-year cage lease is still a fixed commitment; and hauling servers between kiosks is on-premises logistics, not a cloud financial model.

q: A ticketing site is quiet for months, then sells out a stadium in 40 minutes when a tour is announced. The CTO wants capacity to surge automatically for the rush and shrink back afterward with no idle servers in between. Which cloud characteristic is this?
options: Fault tolerance — the system keeps running when a single component fails
Rapid elasticity — resources scale out automatically for the spike and back in when it passes
High availability — the site targets a high percentage of uptime over the month
Geo-distribution — copies of the site run in regions around the world
explain: Rapid elasticity is automatic scale-out and scale-in driven by demand, so the 40-minute spike is absorbed and capacity (and cost) drops afterward. Fault tolerance is about surviving component failure, not demand spikes; geo-distribution reduces latency rather than absorbing surges; and high availability is an uptime percentage, not automatic scaling.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A startup's developer needs a test environment with a database and two app servers today, but the company's procurement process takes six weeks to approve hardware. Which cloud benefit removes that wait?
options: Agility — deploying fully configured environments in minutes through self-service instead of waiting on procurement
Scalability — gradually increasing capacity as the user base grows over years
Economies of scale — the provider's bulk purchasing lowering per-unit hardware costs
Disaster recovery — restoring systems from backup after a regional outage
explain: Agility is the ability to provision and reconfigure IT resources in minutes via self-service, which eliminates the six-week procurement delay. Scalability is about growing capacity over time, not provisioning speed; economies of scale is about the provider's cost advantage; and disaster recovery is about restoring after failure, not deploying quickly.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A payroll SaaS company grows from 2,000 to 20,000 customers over three years and steadily adds database capacity each quarter to match. The capacity planning is manual and gradual, not automatic. Which concept does this describe?
options: Serverless computing — paying only per function execution with no servers to manage
Rapid elasticity — automatic scale-out and scale-in driven by immediate demand
Scalability — the ability to increase capacity over time as demand grows
Fault tolerance — continuing to operate through individual component failures
explain: Scalability is increasing (or decreasing) capacity to match longer-term growth — the quarterly, planned additions here. Rapid elasticity would be automatic and immediate, which this manual process is not; fault tolerance is about surviving failures; and serverless is a compute model, not a capacity-growth concept.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A hospital's patient portal runs across three datacenters in one region. When one datacenter loses power, patients never notice — sessions continue on the other two with no interruption. Which concept kept the portal running?
options: Disaster recovery — restoring service from backups after a declared disaster
Fault tolerance — the system continues operating through the failure of individual components
Geo-distribution — placing copies of data on multiple continents
Rapid elasticity — automatically adding capacity during demand spikes
explain: Fault tolerance means the system keeps working straight through a component failure, which is what happened when the datacenter dropped and sessions continued. Disaster recovery would involve restoring after an outage rather than riding through it; elasticity handles demand spikes, not failures; and geo-distribution is about global placement, not failure survival.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A hurricane destroys a company's primary region. The IT team declares a disaster and brings the business back online from backups replicated in a distant region within hours. Which cloud capability did they use?
options: Disaster recovery — restoring operations in another location after a catastrophic failure
High availability — designing components so the outage would never have happened
Fault tolerance — the system absorbing the hurricane with no interruption at all
Rapid elasticity — automatically scaling resources to handle the recovery workload
explain: Disaster recovery is the plan and capability to restore service from another location after a disaster, which is exactly the declared failover to replicated backups. High availability and fault tolerance aim to prevent or ride through failures, but a destroyed region exceeds both; elasticity scales capacity, it does not restore lost systems.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A small business pays less per gigabyte of cloud storage than it would cost to run its own storage array, largely because its provider buys hardware by the shipload. What is this cost advantage called?
options: Multi-tenancy — many customers sharing the same physical infrastructure
Consumption-based pricing — paying only for the storage actually used
Rapid elasticity — resources automatically scaling with demand
Economies of scale — the provider's massive purchasing power drives down per-unit costs for everyone
explain: Economies of scale is the cost advantage that comes from buying and operating at massive scale, which the provider passes on as lower prices. Elasticity is about scaling, not purchasing power; multi-tenancy describes sharing (a related but different concept); and consumption-based pricing is the billing model, not the reason the unit price is low.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A video-streaming startup's viewers in Asia complain about buffering while US viewers are fine. The team deploys streaming servers in Asian regions so content travels a shorter distance. Which benefit are they using?
options: Geo-distribution — placing resources near users to cut latency
Rapid elasticity — scaling capacity up and down with viewer demand
Fault tolerance — surviving datacenter failures without interruption
High availability — guaranteeing a percentage of monthly uptime
explain: Geo-distribution puts resources close to users so data travels less distance, which fixes the buffering caused by latency. Fault tolerance is about surviving failures; elasticity is about scaling with demand; and high availability is an uptime target — none of them shorten the network distance to Asian viewers.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A law firm buys a $120,000 storage array outright and depreciates it over five years on the balance sheet. How is this spending classified?
options: Capital expenditure (CapEx) — a large upfront investment in a physical asset
Total cost of ownership — the full lifetime cost comparison of two options
Operational expenditure (OpEx) — a recurring cost for running day-to-day operations
Consumption-based pricing — paying per unit of resource consumed
explain: Buying hardware outright is CapEx: upfront capital invested in an asset that depreciates over years. OpEx is the ongoing monthly-bill model; consumption-based pricing is a cloud billing method; and total cost of ownership is an analysis technique, not a spending classification.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A research lab stores 40 TB of experiment data in the cloud and its bill rises and falls each month with the exact gigabytes stored. Which pricing model is the lab using?
options: Perpetual licensing — buying software once and using it forever
Reserved pricing — committing to one or three years of capacity for a discount
Consumption-based pricing — paying only for the resources actually consumed, measured per unit
Capital expenditure — purchasing the underlying storage hardware outright
explain: Consumption-based (pay-as-you-go) pricing bills per unit consumed — here, per gigabyte-month — so the bill tracks actual usage. Reserved pricing requires a term commitment for a discount; perpetual licensing is buying software outright; and CapEx is purchasing hardware, none of which produce a bill that moves with usage.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A retailer runs its storefront on Azure virtual machines. One night, the physical host server underneath its VMs needs a firmware update. Who is responsible for updating that host hardware?
options: Microsoft — under the shared responsibility model, the provider owns the physical hosts, datacenters, and virtualization layer
The retailer — the customer is responsible for the guest OS and applications, not the physical host
The retailer's ISP — network carriers have no role in datacenter hardware maintenance
Nobody — host firmware updates are skipped in the cloud, which is false; Microsoft performs them
explain: The shared responsibility line for IaaS puts physical infrastructure, hosts, and virtualization with Microsoft, while the customer owns the guest OS upward — host firmware is firmly Microsoft's side. The retailer's responsibility starts at the guest OS; the ISP carries traffic; and host maintenance absolutely still happens, performed by the provider.

q: The same company moves its app to Azure App Service (PaaS). Another OS-level security patch is released. Who applies it now?
options: The customer — the OS is always the customer's job regardless of service model
Nobody — PaaS operating systems never require security patches
The application's end users — each user patches their own device's OS
Microsoft — on PaaS, the provider manages the operating system and runtime patching
explain: On PaaS, Microsoft owns the OS and runtime, so it applies OS patches while the customer manages only code and data — the responsibility line moved with the service model. The customer no longer touches the OS; end users are irrelevant to server patching; and PaaS operating systems absolutely still get patched, just by the provider.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A 20-person company uses Microsoft 365 for email and documents. Employees just sign in and work; nobody manages servers, operating systems, or updates. Which service model is this?
options: PaaS — the customer deploys its own code to a managed platform
On-premises — the company runs everything in its own datacenter
SaaS — the provider delivers complete software; the customer only manages its data and user accounts
IaaS — the customer rents virtual machines and manages the operating system
explain: Microsoft 365 is SaaS: fully managed software the customer simply uses, responsible only for its data and accounts. IaaS would mean managing VMs and operating systems; PaaS would mean deploying custom code; and on-premises would mean owning the datacenter — none match signing in and working.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A university research lab runs climate simulations on a custom-compiled Linux kernel with experimental scheduler patches, and the team manages its own patching schedule. Which Azure service model gives them this control?
options: Serverless with Azure Functions — the runtime is fully managed with no OS access at all
PaaS with Azure App Service — Microsoft manages the OS, so custom kernels are impossible
SaaS with Microsoft 365 — finished productivity software with no infrastructure access
IaaS with Azure Virtual Machines — full control of the guest OS, including custom kernels and patch timing
explain: Only IaaS exposes the guest OS for custom kernels and self-managed patching. PaaS hides the OS behind Microsoft's management; SaaS provides finished software; serverless abstracts infrastructure entirely — all three deny the kernel-level control the lab requires.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A development team wants to deploy its web API by pushing code, with no interest in patching operating systems or configuring web servers. Which service model fits?
options: Bare-metal servers — the team would manage hardware, OS, and everything above it
IaaS with virtual machines — the team would still patch and configure the OS itself
SaaS with Dynamics 365 — finished business software, not a place to deploy custom code
PaaS with Azure App Service — deploy code to a managed platform while Microsoft handles the OS and runtime
explain: PaaS is the push-code-and-go model: Microsoft manages the OS, runtime, and web server while the team owns its code. IaaS would force the team back into OS management; SaaS is finished software rather than a deployment target; and bare metal is maximum management burden — the opposite of what the team wants.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A startup with no datacenter runs its entire product on infrastructure owned by Microsoft and shared with thousands of other customers. Which cloud deployment model is this?
options: Community cloud — infrastructure shared by organizations with common concerns
Private cloud — infrastructure dedicated to a single organization
Public cloud — provider-owned infrastructure shared by many customers
Hybrid cloud — on-premises resources combined with public cloud services
explain: Public cloud is provider-owned, multitenant infrastructure — exactly the shared Microsoft infrastructure described. Private cloud would be dedicated to one organization; hybrid requires an on-premises component that does not exist here; and community cloud is shared among a specific community, not the general public.

q: A defense contractor runs cloud software on servers that are used by no other customer, housed in its own guarded datacenter. Which deployment model is this?
options: Hybrid cloud — a mix of on-premises and public cloud working together
Public cloud — infrastructure shared with many customers over the internet
Private cloud — cloud infrastructure dedicated solely to one organization
Multicloud — workloads spread across more than one public cloud provider
explain: Private cloud means the infrastructure serves a single organization exclusively, whether hosted in its own datacenter or by a third party. Public cloud is shared; hybrid mixes on-premises with public cloud; and multicloud means using multiple public providers — none describe dedicated, single-tenant infrastructure.

q: A hospital keeps patient records on servers in its own datacenter to satisfy regulators, but runs its public website and appointment reminders on Azure, with the two environments linked. Which deployment model is this?
options: Public cloud — everything runs on shared provider infrastructure
Hybrid cloud — on-premises resources and public cloud services combined into one coordinated environment
Private cloud — all resources are dedicated to the single organization with no public cloud involved
Multicloud — the hospital uses two different public cloud providers
explain: Hybrid cloud combines on-premises infrastructure with public cloud services in a connected environment — the datacenter plus Azure here. Pure public or private cloud would exclude one side of this setup, and multicloud means multiple public providers rather than on-premises plus one provider.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A retailer runs its storefront on Azure and its analytics platform on a competing provider's cloud to avoid depending on a single vendor. No on-premises servers are involved. Which model is this?
options: Multicloud — using more than one public cloud provider for different workloads
Hybrid cloud — hybrid requires an on-premises or private-cloud component, which is absent here
Private cloud — the infrastructure is shared public infrastructure, not dedicated to one organization
Single cloud — the retailer deliberately uses two providers, not one
explain: Multicloud is the use of multiple public cloud providers, which is exactly the Azure-plus-competitor setup. Hybrid cloud is the common trap, but it requires an on-premises/private element that does not exist here; private cloud would be single-tenant; and single cloud contradicts the two-provider design.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An e-commerce company designs its checkout service with redundant components so it stays reachable 99.95% of the month even during maintenance. Which benefit is the company pursuing?
options: Consumption-based pricing — paying only for resources consumed
Geo-distribution — placing resources near users worldwide
Rapid elasticity — automatically scaling capacity with demand
High availability — designing for a high percentage of uptime over time
explain: High availability is the design goal of maximizing uptime percentage, which the 99.95% target expresses. Elasticity scales with demand rather than targeting uptime; geo-distribution shortens distance to users; and consumption pricing is a billing model — none of them is an uptime percentage goal.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A finance director is tired of surprise infrastructure bills and wants monthly cloud spending to stay within a predictable range with alerts before it drifts. Which cloud benefit addresses this concern?
options: Agility — provisioning resources quickly through self-service
Fault tolerance — continuing to operate through component failures
Predictability — using budgets, alerts, and cost tools to keep spending foreseeable and controlled
Rapid elasticity — automatically scaling resources with demand
explain: Predictability covers both cost predictability (budgets, alerts, forecasts) and performance predictability — the director wants foreseeable bills. Elasticity and agility are about scaling and speed, not bill stability; fault tolerance is about surviving failures, which does nothing for budget surprises.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An IT manager used to drive to three offices to update servers. Now she patches, monitors, and deploys to all locations from one web console and a set of templates. Which cloud benefit is this?
options: Scalability — increasing total capacity as the business grows
Fault tolerance — surviving hardware failures without interruption
Manageability — centrally administering resources through unified tools and automation instead of manual per-site work
Multi-tenancy — sharing physical infrastructure with other customers
explain: Manageability is centralized, template-driven administration of the whole estate from one place — the end of driving between offices. Scalability is about capacity growth; multi-tenancy describes sharing hardware; and fault tolerance is about surviving failures — none describe unified administration.

q: Two unrelated companies' virtual machines run on the same physical Azure host, but neither can see the other's data or traffic. What makes this sharing safe?
options: Private cloud — infrastructure dedicated to one organization, the opposite of this setup
Multi-tenancy with logical isolation — customers share physical infrastructure while hypervisor-level isolation keeps them separate
Hybrid cloud — a mix of on-premises and cloud, which is unrelated to sharing a host
Single-tenancy — each customer would have fully dedicated hardware, which is not the case here
explain: Multi-tenancy is many customers sharing physical infrastructure with strict logical isolation between them. Single-tenancy and private cloud both mean dedicated hardware — contradicted by the shared host; hybrid cloud describes deployment mix, not how a host is shared.

q: A financial firm must prove to auditors that no other customer's workload ever runs on the same physical server as its trading VMs. Which Azure option gives it a whole physical server?
options: Azure Dedicated Host — a physical server devoted entirely to one customer's VMs
Azure Spot VMs — discounted shared capacity that can be evicted at any time
An availability set — which spreads VMs across racks but still on shared hosts
A standard pay-as-you-go virtual machine — which runs on shared physical hosts
explain: Dedicated Host provides a physical server for one customer's exclusive use, satisfying the no-shared-hardware audit requirement. Standard VMs and Spot VMs run on shared hosts; an availability set only spreads VMs across fault/update domains — none guarantee hardware exclusivity.

q: A nonprofit's donation form triggers a short task a few hundred times a day — each run takes two seconds, and the rest of the time nothing runs. It wants to pay nothing when idle. Which approach fits?
options: An App Service premium plan — always-warm instances billed continuously
A dedicated host — an entire physical server for a two-second intermittent task
An always-on virtual machine — which bills for compute around the clock even when idle
Serverless with Azure Functions on the consumption plan — pay per execution with scale to zero when idle
explain: Serverless consumption billing charges per execution and scales to zero, so the idle hours cost nothing — ideal for brief, intermittent work. An always-on VM or premium plan bills continuously; a dedicated host is wildly oversized — all three charge for idle time the nonprofit wants to avoid.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A manufacturer runs its factory systems on-premises at steady load, but during the holiday rush it temporarily extends into Azure for extra order-processing capacity, then pulls back. What is this pattern called?
options: Multicloud — using two public providers, whereas this is on-premises plus one cloud
Full migration — permanently moving everything to the cloud, which is not what happens here
Cloud bursting — a hybrid pattern where on-premises handles the baseline and the cloud absorbs peak demand
Private cloud — dedicated single-organization infrastructure, which describes neither side fully
explain: Cloud bursting is the hybrid pattern of bursting from on-premises into the cloud for peaks and retracting afterward. Full migration would be permanent; multicloud needs two public providers; private cloud is about dedication, not bursting — none describe the temporary extension.

q: A nonprofit's grant covers operating costs but explicitly cannot be used for capital equipment purchases. Why does moving its donor database to Azure fit the grant rules?
options: Azure is free for nonprofits — it is discounted in some programs, but it still bills as an operating expense
CapEx spending is unlimited — the grant explicitly prohibits capital purchases
Reserved instances are capital assets — reservations are billing commitments, not owned hardware, and still OpEx
Azure bills as OpEx — a monthly operating expense — rather than requiring a CapEx hardware purchase the grant forbids
explain: Cloud spending is classified as OpEx, which the grant allows, while buying servers would be prohibited CapEx. Azure is not free; the grant's CapEx ban is the whole constraint; and reservations are prepaid OpEx commitments, not capital assets.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A gaming studio's player count swings wildly week to week. Its CFO asks whether to buy one-year reserved VM capacity for the game servers. What is the right guidance?
options: Buy the reservations anyway — the discount applies even to capacity that sits unused
Buy physical servers instead — that returns to CapEx and removes all scaling flexibility
Stay pay-as-you-go — reservations reward steady, predictable usage, and volatile workloads may not use the committed capacity
Use Spot VMs for the player-facing servers — evictions would disconnect players mid-game
explain: Reserved pricing discounts a one- or three-year commitment, which only pays off for steady-state usage; a wildly variable workload risks paying for unused commitment. Unused reservations still cost money; physical servers abandon cloud flexibility; and Spot evictions would kick players offline — the worst option for live game servers.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: A news site runs its homepage on two identical virtual machines. The architect adds a load balancer in front so if one VM fails, readers still get the page from the other. Which concept is the architect applying?
options: Resource tagging — tags organize billing and management; they do not route traffic or provide failover
Vertical scaling — a bigger single VM would still be a single point of failure
Redundancy for high availability — duplicate components with automatic failover keep the service reachable
Backup and restore — backups recover data after loss; they do not keep the live page serving during a failure
explain: Redundant components behind a load balancer deliver high availability: one VM's failure is invisible to readers. Vertical scaling enlarges one failure point; backups are a disaster-recovery tool, not live failover; and tags are organizational metadata with no traffic role.

q: A startup signs up for a cloud service advertising a 99.9% uptime SLA. The founder assumes this means the service will never go down. What is wrong with that assumption?
options: SLAs cover data loss — they cover service availability, not the customer's data, which needs its own backup strategy
Downtime is impossible in the cloud — all cloud services can experience outages, which is why SLAs exist
The SLA is just a marketing slogan — it is a contractual commitment backed by service credits
An SLA is a committed uptime target, not a guarantee of zero downtime — 99.9% still allows about 43 minutes of downtime per month
explain: A 99.9% SLA permits roughly 43 minutes of monthly downtime; it is a target with remedies, not a promise of perfection. SLAs are contractual, not slogans; they address availability rather than data protection; and outages are possible everywhere — the SLA exists precisely because they happen.

q: A data-science team runs training jobs on Azure Spot VMs because they are cheap. The team lead asks what uptime SLA covers those VMs. What is the answer?
options: 99.95% because they are cheaper — price does not raise the SLA; evictible capacity carries none
No SLA — Spot VMs can be evicted at any time, so Microsoft offers no uptime commitment for them
A per-subscription SLA — SLAs attach to services and their conditions, not to subscriptions
99.9% like all virtual machines — Spot VMs are explicitly excluded from VM SLA coverage
explain: Spot VMs use spare capacity that Azure can reclaim with short notice, so they carry no SLA — the discount trades away the uptime commitment. They do not get the standard VM SLA; lower price never means higher SLA; and SLAs are defined per service, not per subscription.
domain: Domain 1: Describe cloud concepts

q: An application depends on two services, each with a 99.9% SLA. The architect needs the application's composite SLA. How is it calculated?
options: Multiply them: 0.999 x 0.999, giving approximately 99.8% — each additional dependency lowers the combined SLA
Average them — averaging ignores how failures compound across dependencies
Take the higher of the two — the chain is only as strong as its weakest link, and combined availability is lower than either alone
Add them: 99.9% + 99.9% — SLAs cannot exceed 100% and do not add
explain: Composite SLA is the product of the component SLAs, because the app is down if either dependency is down — 99.9% × 99.9% ≈ 99.8%. Adding could exceed 100%, which is meaningless; taking the higher ignores the second failure source; averaging has no mathematical basis here.

q: A European retailer must ensure customer data never leaves Europe. Which Azure construct defines the boundary its data stays within?
options: An availability zone — physically separate datacenters within one region, not a residency boundary
A resource group — a logical management container that can hold resources in any region
An Azure geography — a discrete market area, typically containing two or more regions, that bounds data residency
A virtual network — an isolated network boundary, not a data-residency boundary
explain: Geographies (like Europe) define data-residency and compliance boundaries across their regions. Availability zones are about datacenter-level resilience inside a region; resource groups are management containers spanning regions; VNets are network isolation — none define where data may legally reside.

q: A company deploys its database in a region's paired region as a standby. Why does Azure encourage using the designated pair rather than any random second region?
options: Paired regions are free — the standby still incurs normal service charges
Pairs replace availability zones — zones protect within a region; pairs protect across regions, and both can be used
Pairing doubles the SLA automatically — SLAs depend on the services and architecture deployed, not on pairing alone
Region pairs get staggered platform updates and prioritized recovery — if one region fails, its pair is recovered first
explain: Region pairs are engineered together: platform updates roll to one at a time, and in a broad outage the pair gets recovery priority. Standby resources are still billed; pairs complement rather than replace zones; and pairing alone does not change any service's published SLA.

q: A payment processor must keep authorizing transactions even if an entire datacenter in its region goes dark. Which Azure feature provides datacenter-level isolation inside a region?

Resource groups — logical management containers with no physical isolation at all
Availability sets — which spread VMs across racks inside a single datacenter, not across datacenters
Availability zones — physically separate datacenters within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking
explain: Availability zones are separate physical datacenters in a region, so one datacenter's failure does not take the others down. Availability sets only separate fault/update domains within a datacenter; region pairs are for cross-region recovery; resource groups are purely logical.

q: A small business runs two VMs in a region without availability zones and wants them protected against a single rack failure and against both rebooting during host maintenance. What should it use?

An availability set — spreading VMs across fault domains (racks) and update domains (maintenance groups)
An availability zone — which does not exist in this region
A load balancer — which distributes traffic but does not separate VMs across fault or update domains
explain: Availability sets place VMs in different fault domains (protecting against rack failure) and update domains (protecting against simultaneous maintenance reboots). Zones are unavailable in this region; scale sets are about autoscaling fleets; a load balancer distributes traffic but provides no fault/update domain separation.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A SaaS company needs its web tier to grow from 4 to 40 identical VMs during launches and shrink back automatically, with new VMs configured exactly like the rest. Which service does this?
options: Availability sets — which separate fixed VMs across fault domains but do not autoscale
Virtual Machine Scale Sets — autoscaling fleets of identical, load-balanced VMs
Azure Dedicated Host — a single physical server, the opposite of an elastic fleet
Individual virtual machines — which would require manual creation and configuration of each new VM
explain: VM Scale Sets maintain a fleet of identical VMs that autoscale on metrics and sit behind a load balancer. Availability sets provide no autoscaling; a dedicated host is one fixed server; individual VMs would need manual provisioning — none deliver automatic elastic fleets.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A genomics lab runs DNA sequence analyses that checkpoint every few minutes, so an interruption only loses minutes of work. It wants the lowest possible price for VM capacity. Which purchasing option fits?
options: Dedicated hosts — whole physical servers at premium pricing, the opposite of a discount
Azure Spot VMs — deeply discounted spare capacity for workloads that tolerate eviction, with no SLA
Reserved virtual machines — a one- or three-year commitment for steady workloads, not checkpointed batch jobs
Pay-as-you-go VMs — full price with an SLA, the most expensive way to run interruption-tolerant work
explain: Spot VMs sell unused capacity at steep discounts for workloads that survive eviction — checkpointed analyses qualify perfectly. Reservations need stable usage to pay off; pay-as-you-go is full price; dedicated hosts are premium single-tenant hardware — all far costlier for this pattern.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company's domain controllers run 24/7 at a flat, predictable load and will not change for the next two years. How should it pay for that VM capacity?
options: Spot VMs — evictible spare capacity with no SLA, unsuitable for always-on domain controllers
Pay-as-you-go — full price forever, wasting the discount a stable workload qualifies for
Reserved virtual machine instances — a one- or three-year commitment that discounts steady-state capacity
B-series burstable VMs alone — a size choice, not a pricing model, and it does not discount the commitment
explain: Reserved instances trade a 1- or 3-year commitment for a significant discount — ideal for flat 24/7 workloads like domain controllers. Spot VMs could be evicted and carry no SLA; pay-as-you-go leaves the discount on the table; B-series is a VM size, not a purchasing option.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A consultancy's compute usage shifts constantly between VM sizes, regions, and services, but its overall hourly spend is stable. It wants a discount without locking to specific VMs. Which option fits?
options: Reserved VM instances — which lock the commitment to specific VM types and regions
Pay-as-you-go — no commitment and therefore no discount at all
Azure savings plans — commit to a fixed hourly spend for one or three years and get discounts across eligible compute, flexibly
Spot VMs — evictible spare capacity with no SLA, not a committed-use discount
explain: Savings plans discount an hourly spend commitment that flexes across VM families, regions, and compute services — matching shifting usage. Reservations lock to specific configurations; Spot is interruptible with no SLA; pay-as-you-go offers no discount — none fit variable-but-stable spend.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A software vendor's license terms require its application to run on hardware used by no other customer, and it needs to control VM placement on that hardware. Which option provides this?
options: Azure Dedicated Host — a physical server dedicated to one customer, with control over VM placement on it
Reserved instances — a billing discount on shared-tenant VMs, not dedicated hardware
Virtual Machine Scale Sets — elastic fleets of shared-tenant VMs
Availability zones — separate datacenters that are still multitenant
explain: Dedicated Host is single-tenant physical hardware with placement control, satisfying hardware-exclusivity licensing. Reservations are only pricing on shared hosts; zones are multitenant datacenters; scale sets are elastic shared-tenant fleets — none provide dedicated hardware.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An administrator shuts down a VM from inside the guest OS on Friday and is surprised by a compute charge on Monday. What happened, and how is the charge avoided?
options: Azure bills stopped VMs at double rate — stopped-deallocated VMs incur no compute charge at all
Billing stops the moment the OS shuts down — an OS-level shutdown leaves the VM allocated, so billing continues
The VM was stopped but not deallocated — it still held its host, so compute billing continued; stopping (deallocating) it in the portal or CLI releases the host and stops compute charges
Deleting the network interface stops billing — compute billing follows the VM's allocation state, not its NIC
explain: Shutting down from inside the OS leaves the VM in 'Stopped' (allocated) state, still reserving host capacity and incurring compute charges; 'Stopped (deallocated)' releases it. There is no double-rate penalty; NIC deletion does not change allocation; and OS shutdown alone never stops billing — the classic stopped-vs-deallocated trap.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A team deploys three web apps and wants them to share the same compute capacity, region, and operating system while scaling together. What defines that shared capacity in Azure App Service?

The application code — code does not define compute capacity, region, or scaling
The App Service plan — it sets the region, OS, VM size, and instance count that the apps share and scale on
The free tier's auto-scale — the free/shared tiers do not scale out at all
explain: The App Service plan is the unit of compute: region, OS, size, and instance count shared by its apps. Code cannot define infrastructure; consumption plans are a Functions concept; and free/shared tiers cannot scale — all three misdescribe how App Service capacity works.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A retailer wants a small piece of code to run automatically each time a new product image lands in Blob storage — nothing should run or bill at other times. Which Azure feature triggers this?

An always-on virtual machine polling the container — which bills continuously and adds polling latency
A timer trigger firing every minute — which would run constantly instead of reacting to the actual upload event
Azure Functions triggers and bindings — a Blob trigger fires the function on each upload, scaling to zero otherwise
explain: Functions' Blob trigger executes code in direct response to the upload event and scales to zero when idle. A polling VM bills around the clock; Logic Apps is the workflow-orchestration tool rather than event-driven code; a timer trigger ignores the event and runs on a schedule — none match event-driven, scale-to-zero execution.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An office manager with no coding background needs an automated workflow: when a form is submitted, save the attachment to OneDrive and post a message in Teams. Which service fits best?

Azure Container Instances — which runs containers, not form-to-Teams workflows
Azure App Service — which hosts custom web applications, not visual SaaS workflows
Azure Logic Apps — a visual designer with hundreds of connectors for no-code workflow automation across SaaS apps
explain: Logic Apps is the no-code integration platform: visual designer plus connectors for OneDrive, Teams, and hundreds of services. Functions demands code; App Service hosts custom apps; Container Instances runs containers — none serve a non-coder automating SaaS workflows.

q: A developer needs to run a single Linux container for a two-hour data-conversion task, with no orchestrator to manage and no infrastructure to maintain. Which service is the simplest fit?
options: Azure Kubernetes Service — a full orchestrator, overkill for one short-lived container
Azure Container Instances — run individual containers on demand without managing VMs or orchestrators
Azure App Service — hosts web apps, not arbitrary one-off container tasks
Virtual Machine Scale Sets — elastic VM fleets, far heavier than a single container run
explain: Container Instances is built for exactly this: fire off containers without orchestrators or VM management. AKS adds orchestration overhead for one task; App Service targets web apps; VM scale sets manage VM fleets — all heavier than needed.

q: A logistics company runs thirty containerized services and needs crashed containers restarted automatically, updates rolled out without downtime, and traffic balanced across container replicas. Which Azure service orchestrates this?
options: Azure Functions — event-driven code execution, not container fleet orchestration
Azure App Service — hosts web apps but is not a container orchestrator
Azure Container Instances — runs standalone containers with no orchestration, self-healing, or replica management
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) — managed Kubernetes orchestration with self-healing, rolling updates, and load balancing for container fleets
explain: AKS provides managed Kubernetes: automatic restarts, rolling updates, replica scaling, and service load balancing. Container Instances has no orchestration; App Service is for web apps; Functions is event-driven serverless — none manage a fleet of interdependent containers.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A company wants its web servers and database servers on isolated network segments with private IP addresses, so a compromised web server cannot reach the database directly. Which Azure construct provides this segmentation?
options: A network security group alone — NSGs filter traffic but do not create isolated segments; they attach to VNets/subnets
A virtual network with subnets — segments resources into isolated address spaces with private IPs
Azure DNS — resolves names to addresses but provides no network isolation
A VPN gateway — connects networks together rather than segmenting them
explain: A VNet with subnets is the segmentation boundary: separate address spaces with private IPs and controlled routing between them. An NSG is a filter that lives on a VNet/subnet, not a segment itself; DNS only resolves names; a VPN gateway connects networks instead of dividing them.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: An application in one virtual network needs to query a database in another virtual network. The traffic must stay on Microsoft's private backbone with low latency. How should the networks be connected?
options: A VPN gateway — encrypts traffic over the public internet, adding latency versus peering
Public IP addresses on both ends — exposes the database to the internet instead of keeping traffic private
ExpressRoute — a private on-premises connection, unnecessary and costly for VNet-to-VNet traffic
VNet peering — connects VNets privately over the Microsoft backbone with low latency
explain: VNet peering routes traffic privately across Microsoft's backbone with minimal latency — the designed solution for VNet-to-VNet. VPN gateways traverse the public internet; public IPs expose resources; ExpressRoute is for on-premises connectivity — all wrong tools for this job.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A bank needs a connection between its datacenter and Azure that never traverses the public internet and offers consistent bandwidth for replication traffic. A startup just needs its developers to reach Azure securely from home over the internet. Which pairing is correct?
options: Public IPs with open ports for both — exposes both environments to the internet with no encryption or privacy
ExpressRoute for the bank (private dedicated connection) and VPN Gateway for the startup (encrypted tunnel over the internet)
ExpressRoute for both — overkill and costly for developers working from home
VPN Gateway for the bank and ExpressRoute for the startup — reversed: VPN traverses the internet and ExpressRoute is the private dedicated link
explain: ExpressRoute is the private, dedicated, consistent-bandwidth link suited to the bank; VPN Gateway encrypts traffic over the public internet, fitting the startup's remote developers. Reversing them mismatches the requirements; ExpressRoute for home developers is unjustifiable cost; open public IPs provide neither privacy nor encryption.

q: A company buys the domain shop.example.com and wants Azure to authoritatively answer DNS queries for it with fast, globally distributed resolution. Which service hosts the DNS zone?

Azure DNS — hosts authoritative DNS zones on Microsoft's global anycast network
A VPN gateway — connects networks and has no DNS hosting role
Azure Front Door — a global HTTP entry point, not a DNS hosting service
explain: Azure DNS is the authoritative DNS hosting service on Microsoft's global network. Traffic Manager makes routing decisions using DNS but does not host zones; Front Door is an HTTP-layer entry point; a VPN gateway connects networks — none host DNS zones.

q: Six identical VMs run a stateless API in one region. Client TCP connections must be spread evenly across them at the network layer, including non-HTTP traffic. Which service does this?
options: Application Gateway — a Layer 7 HTTP load balancer, wrong for non-HTTP traffic
Azure Load Balancer — distributes Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) traffic across backend VMs
Azure Front Door — a global Layer 7 entry point, not a regional Layer 4 distributor
NAT Gateway — provides outbound internet access, not inbound traffic distribution
explain: Azure Load Balancer operates at Layer 4, spreading TCP/UDP connections across the VMs. Application Gateway and Front Door are Layer 7 HTTP services; NAT Gateway handles outbound connectivity — none distribute raw TCP connections regionally.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A retailer needs path-based routing to its web app (for example, /shop versus /blog), plus protection against common web attacks like SQL injection. Which service combines both?
options: Azure Firewall — network-layer filtering, not HTTP path routing or web-attack protection
Azure DDoS Protection — absorbs volumetric attacks but does not route by URL path or inspect for SQL injection
Application Gateway with Web Application Firewall — Layer 7 routing plus OWASP-rule protection against web exploits
Azure Load Balancer — Layer 4 distribution with no path-based routing and no WAF
explain: Application Gateway routes by URL path at Layer 7, and its WAF tier blocks OWASP Top 10 attacks including SQL injection. Load Balancer cannot see HTTP paths; Azure Firewall filters at network layers; DDoS Protection handles flood attacks — none combine path routing with web-exploit defense.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A global SaaS app serves users on five continents from one web application. The company wants users to reach the nearest healthy deployment automatically over a single anycast entry point. Which service provides this?

Traffic Manager — DNS-based routing, which resolves names but is not an anycast HTTP entry point
Azure Load Balancer — regional Layer 4 distribution, not global
Azure Front Door — a global Layer 7 entry point with anycast routing to the nearest healthy backend
explain: Front Door is the global anycast front end: users hit one entry point and are routed to the nearest healthy deployment at Layer 7. Traffic Manager routes via DNS responses rather than anycast; Load Balancer is regional; VNet peering is private network connectivity — none serve global users through one entry point.

q: Dozens of VMs in a subnet need outbound internet access for software updates, but security policy forbids assigning public IPs to any VM. Which service gives them shared, scalable outbound connectivity?

A public IP on each VM — directly violates the no-public-IP policy
Azure Bastion — provides inbound RDP/SSH access, not outbound connectivity
A VPN gateway — connects to on-premises networks, not the public internet

q: An auditor needs occasional RDP access to a VM that has no public IP, from a browser, with the session fully encrypted and no inbound ports opened. Which service enables this?
options: A jumpbox VM with a public IP — exposes RDP to the internet, exactly what the policy forbids
Azure Bastion — browser-based RDP/SSH to VMs over TLS with no public IPs or open inbound ports
Opening port 3389 with an NSG rule — exposes RDP directly to the internet
A VPN gateway — requires client VPN setup rather than simple browser access
explain: Bastion provides RDP/SSH through the browser over TLS without public IPs on the VMs or open inbound ports. A public jumpbox and an open 3389 both expose RDP to the internet; a VPN gateway needs client configuration — none deliver browser-based access with zero exposed ports.

q: A team wants its Azure SQL Database reachable only through a private IP inside its virtual network, with no public endpoint at all. Another team is fine with the public endpoint as long as traffic from its VNet is recognized. Which two features map to these needs, in order?

Private Link for both — the second team does not need a private IP, so Private Link is more than required
Service endpoints for the first team — service endpoints keep the public endpoint; they cannot give the database a private IP
Private Link for the first team (private IP in the VNet, public endpoint disabled) and service endpoints for the second (VNet identity recognized over the optimized Azure path)
explain: Private Link assigns the PaaS service a private IP inside the VNet and can disable the public endpoint; service endpoints extend the VNet's identity to the service while its public endpoint remains. q: A photo app stores millions of user-uploaded images and videos — large, unstructured files accessed by URL. Which storage service is designed for this?

Table storage — NoSQL key-value storage, not binary object storage

q: A company archives seven years of compliance logs it almost never reads but must retain. It wants the cheapest storage tier and understands retrieval will be slow. Which tier and caveat apply?

Hot tier — optimized for frequent access and priced higher, the opposite of cheapest
explain: Archive is the cheapest tier for data kept months or years, but archived blobs are offline and must be rehydrated — taking hours — before reading. Hot and premium tiers charge for performance this workload does not need; cool is a middle tier, still pricier than archive for long retention.

q: A company is retiring its on-premises file server but its applications require traditional SMB file shares with drive-letter mappings. Which Azure storage service replaces it with minimal rework?

Queue storage — messaging between application components, not file shares
Blob storage — object storage accessed by URL/API, not mountable SMB shares
Azure Files — fully managed SMB (and NFS) file shares that applications can mount like the old file server
explain: Azure Files provides SMB/NFS shares that mount like traditional file servers, enabling lift-and-shift of file-dependent apps. Blob storage is object-based, not SMB; Queue storage is messaging; managed disks are VM-attached volumes — none present network file shares.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A database VM needs 20,000 IOPS for its data volume. The architect attaches an Ultra Disk to the VM. Which statement about this storage is correct?

Managed disks provide persistent block storage for VMs, and Ultra Disk is the tier for the highest IOPS/throughput needs
Blob storage should back the database volume — databases need low-latency block storage, not object storage
VM data must live on the temporary disk — the temporary disk is ephemeral and loses data on maintenance or redeploy
explain: Managed disks are persistent VM block storage, and Ultra Disk sits at the top for IOPS/throughput. The temporary disk is ephemeral and unsafe for data; Blob storage is object storage with the wrong access pattern for database volumes; Ultra Disk is managed, not unmanaged.
domain: Domain 2: Describe Azure architecture and services

q: A media archive must survive a full regional outage, and editors in the secondary region need read access to the replicated copy during drills. Which redundancy option meets both needs?
options: Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) — copies across zones in one region; still lost if the whole region fails
Locally redundant storage (LRS) — three copies inside one datacenter; a regional outage loses everything
Read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS) — replicates to the paired region and allows read access to the secondary copy
Geo-redundant storage (GRS) without read access — replicates to the paired region but the secondary cannot be read until failover
explain: RA-GRS replicates to the paired region and uniquely allows reading the secondary copy anytime — covering both survival and drill access. LRS keeps all copies in one datacenter; ZRS stays within one region; plain GRS replicates but blocks secondary reads — none satisfy both requirements.
